name: Notes - Bacterial structure, classification & growth
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 6 2 BACTERIAL STRUCTURE, CLASSIFICATION & GROWTH ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Classify clinically important bacteria according to their morphology, Gram-stain characteristics, and oxygen requirements, using findings from clinical and laboratory contexts. 2. Differentiate the structural features of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria and explain how these differences influence their susceptibility to antibiotics. 3. Analyse the contribution of major bacterial structures—including the cell wall, capsule, pili, flagella, plasmids, cell membrane, and endospores—to bacterial survival, colonization, virulence, antimicrobial resistance, and persistence in clinical settings. 4. Interpret bacterial growth-curve data and predict how the different growth phases and environmental conditions may influence bacterial multiplication and the effectiveness of antimicrobial therapy. Bacterial size and shape The small size (0.5 – 5 µm) and nearly colorless nature of bacteria require the use of stains (Gram stain) for visualization with a light microscope. Hence, bacteria are generally referred to Gram positive (violet) and Gram negative (red). The major morphologic forms are spheres, rods, bent or curved rods, and spirals. Spherical or oval bacteria are called cocci and are typically arranged in clusters or chains. Rods are called bacilli and may be straight or curved. Bacilli that are small and pleomorphic to the point of resembling cocci are often called coccobacilli. Structure of Bacteria The major structures of the bacterial cell consist of the multilayered envelope and its appendages and the interior core consisting of the nucleoid (or nuclear body) and the cytoplasm. Figure 1: Structure of bacteria 1. Envelope and appendages A. Cell Wall A rigid cell wall surrounds all bacterial cells except bacteria lacking cell walls such as the mycoplasmas. The structure and function of the bacterial wall is a hallmark of the prokaryotes; it is absent in human cell. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 6 The cell wall (1) protects the cell from mechanical disruption and from bursting caused by the internal pressure of the cell. (2) It also provides a barrier against certain toxic chemical and biologic agents. (3) Its form is responsible for the shape of the cell. (4) Site of action of beta lactams (penicillin binding proteins; PBP) (5) Contains receptor for phages. The structure, chemical composition, and thickness of the cell wall differ in gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. The peptidoglycan layer is much thicker in Gram-positive than in Gram-negative bacteria. Gram-positive bacteria also have teichoic acid that protrude outside the peptidoglycan, whereas gram-negative bacteria do not. Besides the major wall components—peptidoglycan and teichoic acids—gram-positive walls usually have lesser amounts of other molecules characteristic of their species. Some are polysaccharides, such as the group-specific antigens of streptococci; others are proteins, such as the M protein of group A streptococci. In contrast, Gram-negative bacteria have a complex outer membrane layer consisting of outer leaflet of lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin), lipoprotein, and inner leaflet of phospholipid. Special structural proteins, called porins, form pores through the outer membrane that make it possible for nutrients to diffuse through it and into the periplasm. Lying between the outer-membrane layer and the cytoplasmic membrane in Gram-negative bacteria is the periplasmic space, which is the site, in some species, of enzymes called β-lactamases that degrade penicillins and other β-lactam drugs. Peptidoglycan Peptidoglycan consists of a linear glycan chain of two alternating sugars, N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM). Adjacent glycan chains are cross-linked into sheets by peptide amino acids side chains. Most enzymes found in mammalian hosts and other biologic systems do not degrade peptidoglycan; one important exception is lysozyme, the hydrolase in tears and other secretions. Treatment of a gram-positive cell with penicillin (which blocks formation of the peptide cross-links) destroys the peptidoglycan, and bacteria is lysed, but If the cell is protected from lysis by suspension in a medium isotonic with the cell interior, the cell becomes round and forms a sphere called a protoplast surrounded by cell membrane. A B Figure 2. A. Peptidoglycan structure. B. Protoplast Teichoic acid These compounds are polymers of either glycerol phosphate or ribitol phosphate. A type of teichoic acid called lipoteichoic acid and appears to play a role in anchoring the wall to the cell membrane and as an epithelial cell adhesin. It is also the major antigen of Gram-positive bacteria. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 6 Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) LPS consists of: (1) lipid A (the endotoxin), (2) a core polysaccharide, and (3) O antigen polysaccharide side chains (the major surface antigen of gram-negative bacteria). LPS of the outer membrane of the cell wall of gram-negative bacteria is endotoxin. It is responsible for many of the features of disease, such as fever and shock (especially hypotension), caused by these organisms. B. Cell membrane The cell (plasma) membrane of bacteria is similar to the familiar bi-leaflet membrane of most cells, containing phospholipids. However, bacterial cell membrane does not contain sterols (except mycoplasmas). The cell membrane: (1) plays a role in the segregation of daughter chromosomes at cell division. (2) is the site of synthesis of DNA, cell wall polymers. (3) It contains the entire electron transport system of the cell (and, hence, is functionally analogous to the mitochondria of eukaryotes). (4) It contains receptor proteins that function in chemotaxis. (5) it is a permeability barrier and contains proteins involved in the selective and active transport of solutes. (6) It is also involved in secretion of proteins including exotoxins and hydrolytic enzymes involved in the pathogenesis of disease. The bacterial cell membrane is therefore the functional equivalent of most of the organelles of the eukaryotic cell and is vital to the growth and maintenance of the cell. C. Capsule Many bacterial cells surround themselves with some kind of hydrophilic gel. If the material forms a reasonably discrete layer, it is called a capsule; if it is amorphous, it is referred to as a slime layer. Most capsules are polysaccharides; a few are simple polypeptides. Capsules provide some general protection for bacteria, but their major function in pathogenic bacteria is protection from the immune system (antiphagocytic). Capsular polysaccharides can also form the basis of serotyping and vaccine targets. D. Pili (or Fimbriae) Hair-like projections found on the surface of cells of many Gram-positive and Gram-negative species. There are two general classes, common pili and sex pili. Common pili are adhesins, which are responsible for the ability of bacteria to colonize surfaces and cells. The sex pilus is involved in the exchange of genetic material between some Gram-negative bacteria (conjugation). E. Flagella Flagella are organelles of motility found in many species of bacteria, both Gram- positive and Gram-negative. They may be distributed around the cell, at one pole or at both ends of the cell. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 4 of 6 2. Core A. Cytoplasm It is densely packed with ribosomes, which are much more abundant than in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells. This is a reflection of the higher growth rate of bacteria. The overall subunit structure of the 70 S bacterial ribosome resembles that of eukaryotic ribosomes, but is smaller and differs sufficiently in function that a very large number of antimicrobial agents have the prokaryotic ribosome as their target. name: Notes - Pathogenesis of bacterial infection
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 6 3 PATHOGENESIS OF BACTERIAL INFECTION ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Interpret clinical findings to distinguish bacterial colonization from infection and relate them to pathogenicity and virulence. 2. Analyze the sequential mechanisms by which bacteria enter the host, adhere to target cells, invade tissues, and evade host defenses. 3. Predict the contribution of specific bacterial virulence mechanisms to the development and severity of clinical disease. 4. Compare the mechanisms and clinical consequences of bacterial exotoxins and endotoxin-mediated injury. 1. Important definitions • Adherence (adhesion, attachment): The process by which bacteria stick to the surfaces of host cells. It is a major initial step in the infection process. • Colonization: colonization is the presence of multiplying bacteria on a body surface (like on the skin, mouth, intestines or airway) without causing disease in the person. • Infection: Invasion & multiplication of an infectious agent within the body to cause disease. • Pathogenicity: The ability of any bacterial species to cause disease in a susceptible human host. • Pathogen: A bacterial species able to cause such disease when presented with favorable circumstances (for the organism). • Opportunistic pathogen: An agent capable of causing disease only when the host resistance is impaired (ie, when the patient is “immunocompromised”). • Virulence: A term which presumes pathogenicity, but allows expression of degrees from low to extremely high, for example: • Low virulence—Streptococcus salivarius is universally present in the oropharyngeal flora of humans. On its own, it seems incapable of disease production, but if during a transient bacteremia it lands on a damaged heart valve, it can stick and cause infective endocarditis. • Moderate virulence—Escherichia coli is universally found in the colon, but if displacement to other sites such as adjacent tissues or the urinary bladder regularly causes acute infection. • High virulence—Bordetella pertussis, the cause of whooping cough, is not found in the resident flora, but if encountered it is highly infectious and causes disease in almost every nonimmune person it contacts. • Extremely high virulence—Yersinia pestis, the cause of plague, is also highly infectious, but in addition leads to death in a few days in over 70% of cases. Bacterial pathogenesis is influenced by both microbial virulence factors and host factors. The same organism may cause asymptomatic colonization in one host but invasive disease in another, depending on inoculum, portal of entry, host immunity, underlying disease, and the local microbiome. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 6 Attributes of bacterial pathogenicity Whether a microbe is a primary or opportunistic pathogen, it must be able to enter a host; find a unique niche; avoid, circumvent, or subvert normal host defenses; multiply; and injure the host. For long-term success as a pathogen, it must also establish itself in the host or somewhere else long enough to eventually be transmitted to a new susceptible host. 1. Entry Each of the portals in the body that communicates with the outside world becomes a potential site of microbial entry. Human have various protective mechanisms to prevent microbial entry. a. A simple, though relatively efficient mechanical barrier to microbial invasion is provided by the epithelial borders of the internal and external body surfaces. Of these, the skin is the most formidable with its tough keratinized superficial layer. Organisms can gain access to the underlying tissues only by breaks or by way of hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and sweat glands that traverse the stratified layers. Bacteria have no known mechanism for passing the unbroken skin. b. For the internal surfaces a viscous mucin secreted by goblet cells protects the epithelium lining of the respiratory tract, the gastrointestinal tract, and the urogenital system. Microorganisms become trapped in this thick network of protein and polysaccharide and may be swept away before they reach the epithelial cell surface. c. Secretory IgA (sIgA) secreted into the mucus and other secreted antimicrobials such as lysozyme and lactoferrin aid this cleansing process. Some bacteria excrete an enzyme sIgA protease, which cleaves human sIgA1. (e.g. Streptococcus pneumoniae). This enzyme may play an important role in establishing microbial species at the mucosal surface. d. The epithelium of the intestinal tract below the esophagus is a less efficient mechanical barrier than the skin, but there are other effective defense mechanisms. The high level of hydrochloric acid and gastric enzymes in the normal stomach kill many ingested bacteria. Other bacteria are susceptible to pancreatic digestive enzymes or to bile salts. How efficiently bacterial pathogens navigate all these barriers before their initial encounter with their target cell type is in some ways measured by their infecting dose. How many organisms must be given to a host to ensure infection in some proportion of the individuals? In general, pathogens that have environmental or animal reservoirs can overwhelm innate defenses with large numbers. Pathogens with no reservoir or amplification mechanism must be transmitted human-to-human and thus require the lowest infecting doses. Without this advantage, these pathogens would eventually die out in the population. 2. Adherence The first major interaction between a pathogenic microorganism and its host entails attachment to a eukaryotic cell surface. In its simplest form, adherence requires the participation of two factors: an adhesin on the invading microbe and a receptor on the host cell. The adhesin must be exposed on the bacterial surface either alone or in association with appendages like pili. In gram-negative bacteria, the outer membrane is a major site for adhesins. Most adhesins are proteins, but carbohydrates and teichoic acids may also be involved. Two of the most common receptors, mannose and fibronectin, are widely present on human epithelial cell surfaces. Many bacteria have NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 6 more than one mechanism of host cell attachment. Biofilms may also act as an adherence mechanism by binding to catheters, prosthetic devices, or mucosal surfaces. A. B. Figure 1. A. Bacterial attachment. B. Bacterial invasion 3. Invasion A few bacteria (as Chlamydia), like viruses, are obligate intracellular pathogens. Other bacteria are facultative intracellular pathogens and can grow as free-living cells in the environment as well as within host cells. Generally, invasive organisms adhere to host cells by one or more adhesins but use a class of molecules, called invasins, which interact with integrins or other families of cell adhesion molecules. The integrins in turn interact with elements of the cell cytoskeleton stimulating modifications which end in uptake of the bacterial cell. Invasive bacteria enter cells initially within a membrane-bound, host-vesicular structure but then follow one of two pathways; 1) Some bacteria (Listeria, Shigella) enzymatically lyse the phagosome membrane and escape to the nutrient-rich host cell cytoplasm. These bacteria may continue to multiply there, infect adjacent cells, or move through the cell to the submucosa. 2) Other invasive pathogenic species (Salmonella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis) remain in the phagosome and replicate even in phagocytes by preventing phagosome–lysosome fusion or, if fused, blocking acidification to the optimum pH for digestive enzyme activity. 4. Evading the immune system The host immune system evolved in large part because of the selective pressure of microbial attack. name: Notes - Bacterial genetics
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 5 4 BACTERIAL GENETICS ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Identify the major forms of bacterial genetic material and relate their genetic organization to clinically important bacterial characteristics. 2. Analyze how mutations, recombination, and transposable elements can generate phenotypic changes relevant to bacterial survival and antimicrobial resistance. 3. Differentiate transformation, transduction, and conjugation according to their mechanisms and clinical consequences for horizontal gene transfer. 4. Evaluate the applications of recombinant DNA technology in medicine, including the role of vectors and DNA-modifying enzymes. Types of Bacterial DNA 1. Chromosome Single circular double stranded supercoiled DNA molecule. 2. Plasmids Extrachromosomal, double-stranded, circular DNA molecules that are capable of replicating independently of the bacterial chromosome. Although plasmids are usually extrachromosomal, they can be integrated into the bacterial chromosome. Plasmids occur in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Types of plasmids: (1) Transmissible plasmids (Conjugative plasmids) e.g. F plasmids can be transferred from cell to cell by conjugation. they contain genes responsible for synthesis of the sex pilus and for the enzymes required for transfer. (2) Nontransmissible (Non conjugative) plasmids do not contain the transfer genes. Plasmids carry the genes for the following functions:(1) Antibiotic resistance, (e.g. R plasmids) which is mediated by a variety of enzymes, such as the beta-lactamases. (2) Exotoxins, such as the exfoliative toxin of S. aureus and tetanus toxin of Clostridium tetani. (3) Pili (fimbriae), which mediate the adherence of bacteria to epithelial cells. 3. Transposable elements Transposons are pieces of DNA that move readily from one site to another either within or between the DNAs of bacteria, plasmids, and bacteriophages. They are nicknamed “jumping genes.” In contrast to plasmids, transposons are not capable of independent replication; they replicate as part of the DNA in which they are integrated. Transposons can code for drug- resistant enzymes, toxins, or a variety of metabolic enzymes and can either cause mutations in the gene into which they insert or alter the expression of nearby genes. Genetic change Bacteria use mutation and recombination for genomic change, as do eukaryotic cells. In addition, they have powerful mechanisms for exchange of genes between cells that do not even have to be closely related. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 5 1. Mutation The spontaneous development of mutations is a major factor in the evolution of bacteria. Mutations occur in nature at a low frequency (one mutation in every million cells for any one gene), but the large size of microbial populations ensures the presence of many mutants. Because bacteria are haploid, the consequences of a mutation, are immediately evident in the mutant cell. Because the generation time of bacteria is short, it does not take many hours for a mutant cell that has arisen by chance to grow to the dominant cell type if the mutation gives it a survival advantage. 2. Recombination Recombination is the process in which nucleic acid molecules from different sources are combined or rearranged to produce a new nucleotide sequence. The source of recombinant DNA may be another part of the same chromosome or from outside the cell from one of the genetic transfer mechanisms described later. There are two types of recombination: homologous and nonhomologous. a. Homologous recombination occurs between closely related DNA sequences and generally substitutes one sequence for another. The process requires a set of enzymes produced by the rec genes. b. Site-specific recombination occurs between dissimilar DNA sequences and generally produces insertions or deletions or both. This process usually requires specialized recombination enzymes, such as those produced by many transposons and lysogenic bacteriophages. 3. Genetic transfer within bacterial cell Transposition Transposition involves transposable elements that are genetic units capable of mediating their own transfer from one chromosome to another, from one location to another on the same chromosome, or between chromosome and plasmid within the same bacterial cell. This transposition relies on their ability to synthesize their own site-specific recombination enzymes, called transposases. Transposons (1) when inserted in a new site they cause insertional mutation. (2) Sometimes they insert into genes and inactivate gene that encodes an essential protein, then the cell dies. (3) The transfer of a transposon to a plasmid and the subsequent transfer of the plasmid to another bacterium by conjugation contributes significantly to the spread of antibiotic resistance. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 5 4. Genetic exchange between bacterial cells 1. Transformation It involves the release of DNA into the environment by the lysis of some bacterial cells, followed by the direct uptake of that DNA by the recipient cells. The ability to take up DNA from the environment is called competence, and in many species of bacteria. The fate of the internalized DNA fragment then depends on whether it shares homology (the same or similar base sequences) with a portion of the recipient cell’s DNA. If so, recombination can occur. Heterologous DNA is degraded and causes no heritable change in the recipient cell. 2. Transduction Transduction is the transfer of genetic information from donor to recipient cell by viruses of bacteria called bacteriophages. Transduction can be classified as specialized if the phages in question transfer particular genes (usually those adjacent to their integration sites in the genome) or generalized if incorporation of DNA sequences is random because of accidental packaging of host DNA into the phage capsid. The encapsulated DNA, instead of phage DNA, is injected into a new host cell, where it can recombine with the homologous host DNA. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 4 of 5 A. B. 3. Conjugation The transfer of DNA from the donor to a recipient bacterial cell in a process that requires intimate cell contact. By themselves, bacteria cannot conjugate. Only when a bacterial cell contains a self-transmissible plasmid does DNA transfer occur. In most cases, conjugation involves transfer only of plasmid DNA. Conjugative plasmids in gram-negative bacteria contain a set of genes which encode for the sex pilus. The sex pilus has the ability to draw the donor and recipient cell into an intimate contact needed to form a conjugal bridge through which DNA can pass. The plasmid DNA is then enzymatically cleaved, and one strand is guided through the conjugation pilus into the recipient cell. Both the introduced strand and the strand remaining behind in the donor cell direct the synthesis of their complementary strand, resulting in complete copies in both donor and recipient cells. Both cells can now function as donor cells. Conjugation can involve more than simple F-plasmid transfer. Hfr strains have the F factor integrated into the chromosome and can transfer adjacent chromosomal genes. Fʹ plasmids arise when an integrated F factor excises incorrectly and carries bacterial genes with it. Conjugative plasmids are clinically important because they can disseminate multiple antimicrobial-resistance genes. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 5 of 5 Genetic Engineering The use of genetic engineering or recombinant DNA technology and “cloning” has revolutionized biology and medicine. name: Notes - Antibacterial agents
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 9 5 ANTIBACTERIAL AGENTS ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Differentiate major antibacterial agents according to their molecular targets and mechanisms of action. 2. Interpret the relationship between antimicrobial spectrum, bacterial characteristics, and clinical site of infection when choosing therapy. 3. Analyze clinical scenarios to select an appropriate antibacterial agent based on efficacy, resistance, tissue penetration, and toxicity. 4. Evaluate the advantages and limitations of major antibacterial classes in the management of common and serious bacterial infections. Sources of antibacterial agents There are three main sources of antibacterial agents: First are antibiotics, which are molecules of biological origin. Penicillin, for example, is produced by several molds of the genus Penicillium. Second are the chemically synthesized antimicrobial agents. e.g. the sulfonamides. A third source of antimicrobials arises from the molecular manipulation of previously discovered antibiotics to broaden their range and degree of activity against microorganisms or to improve their pharmacologic characteristics. e.g. penicillinase-resistant and broad-spectrum penicillins, aminoglycosides and cephalosporins Spectrum of action The spectrum of activity of each antimicrobial agent describes the genera and species against which it is typically active. Some antibacterial antimicrobials are known as (1) narrow-spectrum agents; (benzyl penicillin is highly active against many gram-positive cocci but has little activity against enteric gram-negative bacilli), (2) broad-spectrum agents that inhibit a wide range of gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria (tetracyclines, cephalosporins, and carbapenems) Bactericidal antibiotics actively kill bacteria, typically by disrupting an essential structure or process the cell cannot survive without (β-lactams, glycopeptides, aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones). Bacteriostatic antibiotics, by contrast, merely inhibit bacterial growth and reproduction without directly killing the organism (tetracyclines, and macrolides). Because the bacteria remain alive (just unable to multiply), bacteriostatic drugs rely on the host's own immune system to finish clearing the infection, which makes them less suitable for patients who are immunocompromised, neutropenic, or fighting infections in poorly accessible sites like heart valves (endocarditis) or the meninges, where a bactericidal agent is generally preferred. N.B. Clinically effective antimicrobial agents exhibit selective toxicity toward the microbe rather than the host. In most cases, selectivity is explained by action on microbial processes or structures that differ from those of mammalian cells. For example, agents inhibit the synthesis of the bacterial cell wall (an organelle not present in human cell). NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 9 SELECTED ANTIBACTERIAL AGENTS I. Antimicrobials acting on cell wall synthesis 1. β-Lactams The β-lactam antimicrobial agents comprise the penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, and monobactams. They are named after the β-lactam ring in their structure; this ring is essential for their antibacterial activity. The cephalosporins are classified by generation—first, second, third, fourth, fifth, or “unclassified.” In general, a cephalosporin of a higher generation has a wider spectrum. The carbapenems imipenem, meropenem, have the broadest spectrum of all β-lactam antibiotics due to the combination of easy penetration of gram-negative and gram-positive bacterial cells and high level of resistance to β-lactamases. Action: The β-lactam antibacterial agents interfere with the transpeptidation reactions that seal the peptide crosslinks between glycan chains. The targets of all the β-lactams are penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs). The PBP interacts with β-lactam ring and are not available for the synthesis of new peptidoglycan. The disruption of peptidoglycan layer leads to the lysis of bacterium (bactericidal effect). It is important to remember that all antibiotics inhibiting cell wall synthesis are effective only on growing cells (metabolically active cells). Beta lactam antibiotics Action I. Penicillins Natural penicillins: penicillin G, penicillin V Active against gram-positive bacteria Penicillinase-resistant: methicillin, dicloxicillin Similar to the natural penicillins, but resistant to inactivation by the penicillinase of staphylococci Broad-spectrum: ampicillin, amoxicillin Similar to the natural penicillins, but more active against gram-negative organisms Extended-spectrum: piperacillin Increased activity against gram-negative rods, including Pseudomonas spp. II. Cephalosporins First-generation: cefazolin and cephalexin Active against gram-positive organisms. In addition, they are active against some of the Enterobacterales Second-generation: cefoxitin and cefaclor Resistant to β-lactamases of some gram-negative organisms that inactivate first-generation compounds. Expanded activity against Enterobacterales Third-generation: ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, and ceftazidime Have wider spectrum; they are active against gram-negative organisms. Of these three agents, only ceftazidime is active against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The potency, broad spectrum, and low toxicity of the third-generation cephalosporins have made them preferred agents in life-threatening infections in which the causative organism has not yet been isolated (ex: meningitis) Fourth-generation: Cefepime Have activity against a wider spectrum of Enterobacterales as well as Pseudomonas aeruginosa Fifth generation: Ceftaroline It has the unique ability to bind avidly to PBP-2A, the altered penicillin-binding protein that confers resistance to other β-lactam antibiotics in methicillin-resistant S aureus (MRSA). III. Carbapenems Meropenem, imipenem Resistant to inactivation by β-lactamases. Active against many gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria including anaerobes. IV. Monobactams Aztreonam Resistant to β-lactamases. Purely gram-negative coverage, primarily active against members of Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas aeruginosa NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 9 β-Lactamase Inhibitors. e.g. clavulanic acid, sulbactam, tazobactam, and avibactam are referred to as suicide inhibitors, because they must first be hydrolyzed by a β-lactamase before becoming effective inactivators of the enzyme. Combinations of one of these inhibitors with an appropriate β-lactam antimicrobial agent protects the therapeutic agent from destruction by many β-lactamases and significantly enhances its spectrum. (e.g. amoxicillin/clavulanate, ampicillin/sulbactam, piperacillin/tazobactam, Ceftazidime/avibactam). 2. Glycopeptides Action: Vancomycin and teicoplanin belong to this group. The effect is the same as with β-lactams: they inhibit cell wall peptidoglycan synthesis by blocking transpeptidation but by a mechanism different from that of the β-lactam drugs. Vancomycin binds directly to the d-alanyl-d-alanine portion of the pentapeptide, which blocks the transpeptidase from binding, whereas the β-lactam drugs bind to the transpeptidase itself. Both agents are bactericidal, but are primarily active only against gram-positive bacteria. Their main use has been against multidrug-resistant gram-positive infections including MRSA. Neither agent is absorbed by mouth; this feature allows these medications to be given orally to treat Clostridium difficile infections of the bowel. Figure 1. Rarely, these agents cause immediate hypersensitivity reactions consisting of rash, urticaria, or anaphylaxis. name: Notes - Antimicrobial resistance
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 5 6 ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Explain the major genetic and phenotypic mechanisms responsible for bacterial antibiotic resistance in clinical infections. 2. Analyze clinical and microbiological findings to identify the most likely mechanism of antibiotic resistance. 3. Select appropriate indications and strategies for antibiotic use, including prophylactic, preemptive, empiric, and therapeutic approaches. 4. Evaluate empiric antibiotic choices and determine when modification to targeted therapy is appropriate based on microbiological results and local resistance patterns. There are no direct connections between resistance and virulence: some highly drug- resistant bacteria may cause relatively indolent infections, whereas susceptible organisms may cause severe infections. The resistance to antimicrobials may be (1) Inherent (intrinsic) to the organism as such as permeability barriers, a lack of cell wall. Mycoplasma → no cell wall → β-lactams ineffective. Enterococci → intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins. Gram-negative bacteria → outer membrane limits entry of many antibiotics. (2) Acquired; appear in a previously susceptible species by mutation (chromosomal resistance) or the acquisition of new genes (plasmids and transposons) through gene transfer. Genetic basis and spread of acquired resistance • Mutation: spontaneous chromosomal mutations may alter an antimicrobial target, permeability, or regulatory pathways. • Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is a major mechanism for rapid dissemination of resistance genes between bacteria through conjugation, transformation or transduction. • Resistance genes may be carried on plasmids, transposons, integrons, and other mobile genetic elements. • A single mobile genetic element may carry multiple resistance genes, producing multidrug resistance. Mechanisms of antibiotic resistance 1. Enzyme inactivation Enzymatic inactivation of antimicrobial agents is the most powerful and robust resistance mechanism. a. β-Lactamases. β-Lactamase is a general term referring to any one of many bacterial enzymes able to break open the β-lactam ring and inactivate various members of the β-lactam group. The first, penicillinase, was discovered when penicillin-resistant strains of Staphylococcus aureus emerged and were found to inactivate penicillin in vitro. Each β-lactamase is a distinct enzyme with its own physical characteristics and substrate profile. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 5 A class of gram-negative extended- spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) hydrolyses multiple cephalosporins. From a clinical perspective, they are significant because treatment with any generation of cephalosporin may lead to clinical failure. Carbapenems are important treatment options for serious infections caused by ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, particularly when susceptibility and clinical circumstances support their use. However, antimicrobial selection should be guided by the site of infection, susceptibility results, patient factors and current treatment guidelines. Most concerning of all among the gram-negative are the carbapenemases. These genes have made carbapenem- resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) one of the most important challenges facing infectious diseases medicine today. b. Modifying Enzymes. The most common cause of acquired bacterial resistance to aminoglycosides is through the production of enzymes that acetylate, adenylate, or phosphorylate the aminoglycoside molecule. The resistance conveyed by these actions is usually high level; the chemically modified aminoglycoside no longer binds to the ribosome. Inactivating enzymes have been described for a number of other antimicrobials; erythromycin (esterase, phosphotransferase) and chloramphenicol (acetyltransferase). 2. Exclusion (A) The cell wall, particularly the outer membrane, of gram-negative bacteria presents a barrier for access to the interior of the cell. Inability to traverse the outer membrane is the primary reason most β-lactams are less active against gram-negative than gram-positive bacteria. Some antimicrobials must be actively transported into the cell. For example, bacteria which lack the metabolic pathways required for transport of aminoglycosides across the cytoplasmic membrane (streptococci, enterococci, anaerobes) are intrinsically resistant. (B) Other antimicrobials are actively transported out of the cell. A number of bacterial species have energy-dependent efflux mechanisms that literally pump antimicrobial agents which have entered the cell back out. The membrane transporter systems which drive these efflux pumps often affect antimicrobials of several classes. e.g tetracycline and quinolones resistance 3. Altered target If the antimicrobial target is altered in a way that decreases its affinity for the antimicrobial, the inhibitory effect will be proportionately decreased. These changes could be due to point mutations, substitutions of amino acid sequences. Examples of altered antimicrobial targets • MRSA: altered PBP → PBP2a → reduced β-lactam binding. • Penicillin-resistant pneumococci: altered PBPs. • Macrolide resistance: modification of 23S rRNA → reduced macrolide binding. • Fluoroquinolone resistance: mutations affecting DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 5 Figure 1. Mechanisms of antibiotic resistance Non-genetic causes of antibiotic resistance There are several nongenetic reasons for the failure of drugs to inhibit the growth of bacteria: (1) Bacteria can be walled off within an abscess cavity that the drug cannot penetrate effectively. Surgical drainage is therefore a necessary adjunct to chemotherapy. (2) Bacteria can be in a resting state (i.e., not growing); they are therefore insensitive to cell wall inhibitors such as penicillins and cephalosporins. (3) Under certain circumstances, organisms that would ordinarily be killed by penicillin can lose their cell walls, survive as protoplasts, and be insensitive to cell wall–active drugs. Later, if such organisms resynthesize their cell walls, they are fully susceptible to these drugs. (4) The presence of foreign bodies makes successful antibiotic treatment more difficult. This applies to foreign bodies such as surgical implants and catheters as well as materials that enter the body at the time of penetrating injuries, such as splinters. (5) Several artifacts can make it appear that the organisms are resistant (e.g., administration of the wrong drug or the wrong dose or failure of the drug to reach the appropriate site in the body). A good example of the latter is the poor penetration into spinal fluid by several early-generation cephalosporins. Biofilm-associated resistance/tolerance • Bacteria growing in biofilms are often much less susceptible to antimicrobial treatment than free-living bacteria. • The extracellular matrix can reduce penetration of some antimicrobials. • Biofilms contain metabolically inactive or slow-growing cells that are less susceptible to antibiotics targeting actively growing bacteria. • Biofilms facilitate persistence on: o urinary catheters o central venous catheters o prosthetic joints o prosthetic heart valves o other implanted devices. • Biofilm-associated infections may require removal of the infected device in addition to antimicrobial therapy. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 4 of 5 The problem of antibiotic resistance Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global health threat. It requires urgent multisectoral action. WHO has declared that AMR is one of the top 10 global public health threats facing humanity. Misuse and overuse of antimicrobials are the main drivers in the development of drug- resistant pathogens. Review on AMR estimates that by 2050, as many as ten million people could die each year as a result of AMR. The e

name: Notes - Viral structure & classification
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 5 7 VIRAL STRUCTURE & CLASSIFICATION ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Analyze the structural and genomic features of clinically relevant viruses to predict their behavior during infection and transmission. 2. Differentiate enveloped from naked viruses and interpret how their structural differences influence environmental stability, disinfectant susceptibility, and host-cell entry. 3. Apply principles of defective viruses and viral classification to clinical situations involving viral coinfection and viral taxonomy. 4. Evaluate bacteriophage characteristics and propagation patterns to select appropriate phages for potential therapeutic use against bacterial infections. Viruses are the smallest replicating intracellular microorganisms that are comprised of sets of genes either DNA (DNA viruses) or RNA (RNA viruses) packaged in a capsid (protein shell) or in a capsid and an outer lipid bilayer envelope. The resulting complete virus particle is called a virion. Viruses have an obligate requirement for intracellular growth and a heavy dependence on host cell structural and metabolic components. Therefore, viruses are also referred to as obligate intracellular parasites. Viruses do not have a nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, or other cell organelles. Structure of viruses Viruses are approximately 20-400 nm in diameter. The basic structure of all viruses places the nucleic acid genome (DNA or RNA) on the inside of a protein shell called a capsid. Some human viruses are further packaged into a lipid membrane, or envelope, which is usually acquired from the plasma or cytoplasmic membrane of the infected cell during release from the cell. The genomes of enveloped viruses form a protein complex and a structure called a nucleocapsid, which is often surrounded by a matrix protein that serves as a bridge between the nucleocapsid and the inside of the envelope. Viruses that are not enveloped have a defined external capsid and are referred to as naked viruses. Protein or glycoprotein structures called spikes, which often protrude from the surface of virus particles, are involved in the initial contact with receptor on host cells. The simplest viral structures that can be built stepwise are symmetric and include helical and icosahedral (cubic) structures. Viral genomes Viral genomes can be made of either RNA or DNA and also can be either single-stranded or double-stranded. The RNA viruses can be either positive sense (+) (same polarity of mRNA) or negative sense (–) (complementary to or antisense of mRNA), double- stranded (one strand + and the second strand –) or ambisense (both + and – polarity on the same strand). Although the RNA genomes of most viruses are linear, some RNA viruses may also have segmented genomes (several segments or pieces of RNA), with each segment responsible for encoding a protein. The DNA genome of viruses can be both linear and circular genomes. Most viruses contain a single copy of their genome, except that retroviruses (e.g HIV) carry two identical copies of its genome and are, therefore, diploid. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 5 Viral capsids The capsids or nucleocapsids are virus-encoded specific proteins that protect the genome and confer shapes to viruses. The capsids of all viruses are composed of many copies of one or, at most, several different kinds of protein subunits. The presence of many identical protein subunits in viral capsids or the existence of many identical spikes in the membrane of enveloped viruses has important implications for adsorption, hemagglutination, and recognition of viruses by neutralizing antibodies. The protein shell forming the capsid or the nucleocapsid assumes one of two basic shapes: helical or icosahedral. Viral envelope Many human viruses have an outer lipid bilayer membrane that is derived from host plasma membrane. The viral envelope lipid layer membrane contains virus-encoded glycoproteins called “spikes” or “peplomers” or “viral envelope proteins.” The envelope spikes bind to the receptor on the host cells, help the virus envelope membrane fuse with the cellular membrane of the host cells, and act as principal antigens against which the host mounts immune response for the recognition of the virus. Enveloped viruses are more sensitive to detergents, solvents, ethanol, ether, and heat compared with nonenveloped (naked capsid) viruses whose outer coat is capsid protein. Both envelope glycoproteins, and naked capsid viruses’ spikes become antigens after infection and the host mounts both cell-mediated and humoral immune responses for the elimination of virus-infected cells and cell-free virus, respectively. These antigens also determine the viral serotypes that are based on antigenic variation and are type-specific such as poliovirus serotypes 1, 2, and 3. The capsid or envelope of viruses functions (1) to protect the nucleic acid genome from damage during the extracellular passage of the virus from one cell to another, (2) to aid in the process of entry into the cell, and (3) in some cases, to package viral enzymes essential for the early steps of the infection process. Figure 1. Structure of viruses Defective viruses Viruses which lack a complete genome so that they cannot completely replicate or cannot form a protein coat. Some are host-dependent defectives, meaning they can replicate only in cell systems which provide the particular genetic function which they lack. Others, called Satellite viruses, are able to replicate only when their genetic defect is complemented by a helper virus (is the hepatitis D virus which replicates only in the presence of surface antigen from a co-infecting hepatitis B virus). NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 5 Reaction to physical and chemical agents Heat and cold Naked viruses tend to be stable, losing little infectivity after several hours at 37°C. Enveloped viruses are much more heat labile, rapidly at 37°C. Viral infectivity is generally destroyed by heating at 50–60°C for 30 minutes, although there are some exceptions (eg, hepatitis B virus). Viruses can be preserved by storage at freezing temperatures, pH Viruses are usually stable between pH values of 5 – 9. Some viruses (eg, enteroviruses) are resistant to acidic conditions. All viruses are destroyed by alkaline conditions. Radiation Ultraviolet, x-ray inactivate viruses. Formaldehyde It destroys viral infectivity by reacting with nucleic acid. Viruses with single-stranded genomes are inactivated much more readily than those with double-stranded genomes. Formaldehyde has minimal adverse effects on the antigenicity of proteins and therefore has been used in the production of inactivated viral vaccines. Chlorine Larger concentrations of chlorine are required to destroy viruses than to kill bacteria, especially in the presence of extraneous proteins. For example, the chlorine treatment of stools adequate to inactivate typhoid bacilli is inadequate to destroy poliomyelitis virus present in feces. Quaternary ammonium compounds and organic iodine compounds not effective against viruses Alcohol Alcohols, such as isopropanol and ethanol, are relatively ineffective against certain viruses, especially picornaviruses. Classification of viruses The International Committee for Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) considered various properties, including virions, genome, proteins, envelope, replication, and physical and biologic properties. Based on these properties, virus families are designated with the suffix, -viridae (as in Herpesviridae), virus subfamilies with suffix virinae (Herpesvirinae), virus genera with suffix virus (Herpesvirus), and virus species designated by a virus type (herpes simplex virus 1). name: Notes - Viral replication
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 5 8 VIRAL REPLICATION ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Outline the major stages of the viral replication cycle and predict the consequence of disruption at each stage. 2. Analyse how differences in viral genome type and cellular machinery determine the strategy of DNA and RNA viral replication. 3. Interpret how viral attachment, entry, replication, assembly, and release contribute to viral pathogenesis and potential immune protection. 4. Differentiate lytic and lysogenic bacteriophage replication and explain their clinical consequences, including lysogenic conversion. Virus replication depends on virus–host cell interaction and the type of cells it infects—whether permissive or nonpermissive cells. 1) Permissive cells are those that permit production of progeny virus particles and/or viral transformation. 2) Nonpermissive cells do not allow virus replication, but may allow virus transformation. Some viruses enter cells that do not support virus replication, but some early viral proteins cause cell death; this infection is termed abortive infection. Viral replication cycle Virus replication cycle typically consists of six discrete phases: (1) adsorption or attachment to the host cell, (2) penetration or entry, and uncoating to release the genome, (3) synthetic or virion component production, (4) assembly, and (5) release from the cell. The eclipse phase in virus replication is the time interval between when a virus infects a host cell and when the first new, infectious virus particles (virions) are assembled inside the cell. Figure 1. Viral replication cycle 1. Adsorption or attachment The first step in every viral infection is the attachment or adsorption of the infecting virus particle to the surface of the host cell. A prerequisite for this interaction is a collision between the virion and the cell. Viruses do not have any capacity for locomotion and, therefore, the collision event is simply a random process determined by diffusion and by the concentrations of both the virions and the cells. It involves interaction between virion attachment proteins (VAP) or spikes and cell receptors. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 5 For some viruses, two different surface molecules, receptor and coreceptor, are involved in adsorption (ex; HIV). A particular kind of virus is capable of infecting only a limited spectrum of cell types called its host range. In many cases, human viruses infect only a particular subset of the cells found in their host organism. This kind of tissue tropism is clearly an important determinant of viral pathogenesis. In most cases studied, the specific host range of a virus and its associated tissue tropism are determined at the level of the binding between the cell receptors and virion attachment proteins. When a virus particle has penetrated to the inside of a cell, it is hidden from the host immune system. Thus, if protection from a virus infection is to be accomplished at the level of antibody binding to the virions, it must occur before adsorption and prevent the virus from attaching to and penetrating the cell. Thus, most neutralizing antibodies—whether elicited as a result of natural infection or vaccination— are specific for virion attachment proteins. 2. Penetration, Entry and uncoating After entry, uncoating releases the viral genome or replication-competent nucleocapsid. Uncoating step (capsid disassembly from the viral genome) may be simultaneous with entry or may occur in a series of steps. There are two basic mechanisms for the entry of an enveloped virus into the cell. Both mechanisms involve fusion of the viral envelope with a cellular membrane, and the end result in both cases is the release of the free nucleocapsid into the cytoplasm. 1. Some viruses (ex; measles, HIV) enter by a process called direct fusion. The envelopes of these viruses contain protein spikes that promote fusion of the viral membrane with the plasma membrane of the cell, releasing the nucleocapsid directly into the cytoplasm. 2. Other enveloped viruses (influenza virus, coronavirus), after adsorption, the virus particles are taken up by receptor-mediated endocytosis, which is normally responsible for internalizing growth factors, hormones, and some nutrients. When it involves viruses, the process is referred to as viropexis. The nucleocapsid is now surrounded by two membranes: the original viral envelope and the newly acquired endosomal membrane. Low pH of the endosome leads to a conformational change in a viral spike protein, which results in the fusion of the two membranes and release of the nucleocapsid into the cytoplasm. Naked viruses, also appear to enter the cell by viropexis Figure 2. Entry of viruses by direct fusion & by viropexis NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 5 3. Synthetic or virion component production Most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm—the immediate site of entry with the exception of influenza viruses and the retroviruses that replicate in the nucleus. All DNA viruses must move from the cytoplasm to the nucleus to replicate, except the poxviruses that replicate in the cytoplasm. A. Transcription & translation An essential step in every virus infection is the production of virus-specific mRNAs that program the cellular ribosomes to synthesize viral proteins. Viral gene expression is often temporally regulated. Early proteins commonly include regulatory proteins and enzymes needed for genome replication, whereas late proteins are predominantly structural proteins required for assembly of progeny virions. • The genomes of most DNA viruses are transcribed by the host DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RNA polymerase II) in the nucleus to yield the viral mRNAs which are exported to the cytoplasm for translation. • The (+) sense RNA viruses, possess genomes that can be used directly as mRNAs and are translated immediately on entry into the cytoplasm of the cell. • The (–) sense RNA viruses, to make mRNAs must provide their own transcription machinery (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) to produce the viral mRNAs at the beginning of the infection process. B. Genome replication DNA viruses The extent to which viruses use the cell replication machinery depends on their protein-coding potential and, thus, on the size of their genome. • The smallest of the DNA viruses (parvoviruses) are completely dependent on host machinery that they require the infected cells to be dividing to ensure that a normal S phase occurs and replicates the viral DNA together with the cellular DNA. • The largest DNA viruses (poxviruses) are independent of the host. Because they replicate in the cytoplasm, they must code for almost all of the enzymes and other proteins required for replicating their DNA. • All other DNA human viruses are at least partially dependent on host cell machinery for the replication of their genomes (code for a protein expressed early in infection that induces an unscheduled cycle of cellular DNA replication (S phase). RNA viruses RNA viruses mostly replicate in the cytoplasm. Moreover, human cells do not have RNA polymerases that can copy RNA templates (RNA-based RNA replication). Therefore, RNA viruses must provide the replicases or polymerases required to duplicate the RNA genome into daughter RNA genomes. 4. Assembly of naked viruses and nucleocapsids The process of enclosing the viral genome in a protein capsid is called assembly or encapsidation. Four general principles govern the construction of capsids and nucleocapsids. First, the process generally involves self-assembly of the component parts. Second, assembly is stepwise and ordered. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 4 of 5 Third, individual protein structural subunits or protomers are usually preformed into capsomeres in preparation for the final assembly process. Fourth, assembly often initiates at

name: Notes - Pathogenesis of viral infection
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 7 9 PATHIGENESIS OF VIRAL INFECTION ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Distinguish the major routes of viral transmission and entry and relate them to the clinical presentation of viral infections. 2. Explain how viral tropism and host-cell receptor/coreceptor interactions determine the cells and tissues susceptible to viral infection. 3. Analyze the relationships among viral pathogenicity, virulence, cytopathogenicity, and patterns of viral infection in determining clinical disease. 4. Appraise the contribution of host immune responses to virus-induced immunopathology and immunosuppression in selected viral diseases. Viral pathogenesis comprises of several stages, including (1) transmission and entry of the virus into the host, (2) spread in the host, (3) tropism, (4) virulence and cytopathogenicity, (5) patterns of viral infection and disease, (6) virus-induced immunopathology. (7) Virus-induced immunosuppression. 1. TRANSMISSION & ENTRY Viruses are transmitted via horizontal (common route of transmission: person to person), and vertical (mother-to-child transmission) routes or vector transmission (from mosquitoes, animals). Human viruses enter the host through a variety of routes, including direct inoculation (break in skin, mucous membranes) as well as respiratory, conjunctival, gastrointestinal, and genital routes. Mother-to-child transmission (vertical transmission) can occur in utero, during delivery (via birth canal), and through breast-feeding. Zoonotic (animal-to-human) transmission of viral infections can occur from the bite of animals (eg, rabies) or insects (eg, dengue, yellow fever) or from inhalation of animal excreta (eg, roboviruses). After virus entry into the host, viruses have variable incubation periods. Incubation period is the time between exposure to the organism and appearance of the first symptoms of the disease. Viruses generally multiply at the site of entry to establish infection in the host. Some viruses have short incubation periods (influenza—2-4 days), whereas others have long incubation periods (eg, hepatitis B virus—weeks to several months). 2. SPREAD IN THE HOST • Viral infections produce either localized infection at the site of entry or disseminated infection spread throughout the body. • Localized infections include influenza, parainfluenza, common cold (rhinoviruses, coronaviruses), gastrointestinal infections (rotaviruses), and skin infections (papillomaviruses). In localized infections, the virus spreads mainly by infecting adjacent or neighboring cells. • Several viruses that cause systemic disease in the host spread from the site of entry to the target tissue, where they cause cell injury after multiplication. Viruses use two major routes to spread and cause systemic infection, that is, hematogenous (via the bloodstream) and NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 7 neural (via neurons) spread. Some of the viruses that cause systemic or disseminated infection are poliovirus, rabies virus, HBV, HCV, HIV, measles, varicella zoster virus, and others. 3. TROPISM • Tropism is the capability of viruses to infect a discrete population of cells within an organ. • Cellular or tissue tropism is most often determined by the specific interaction of viral surface proteins (spikes) and cellular receptors on the host cells. However, it should be kept in mind that the presence of a receptor for a virus is not always sufficient for viral infection in the target cells. For example, the presence of CD4 (HIV receptor) alone on target cells does not allow virus entry into these cells, but it requires that target cells also express coreceptors, CXCR4 or CCR5 (chemokine receptors) for efficient viral attachment. • Different viruses may use the same cellular molecule as receptors. Some examples are sialic acid residues functioning as important components of the receptor for influenza, corona. 4. VIRULENCE AND CYTOPATHOGENICITY • Pathogenicity: The ability of a virus to cause disease in an infected host. • Viral virulence: is the degree of pathogenicity of a virus. A virus may be of high or low virulence for a particular host. Different strains of the same virus may differ in the degree of pathogenicity. • Cytopathogenicity: The ability of a virus to cause degenerative changes in cells or cell death. • Virulent viruses: Viral strains that kill target cells and cause disease. • Avirulent or attenuated strains: strains that have mutated and lost their ability to cause cytopathic effects (CPE) and disease. Some attenuated strains can be used as live vaccines. • Interference: If two closely related viruses infect a host, then infection by the first virus can inhibit the function of the second virus Replication of the virus results in alterations of cellular morphology and function as well as antigenicity of the virus. When a lytic virus infects a permissive cell, lots of daughter viruses are produced and this is followed by lysis of the infected cells, called cytopathic effects (CPE) of the virus. The features of CPE are morphologic changes of the cell (inclusion bodies, thickening of the nucleus, swelling, cell fusion [syncytia]), followed by cellular lysis. Some viruses encode a new class of proteins called virokines and viroreceptors, which contribute to viral virulence by mimicking cellular proteins. Virokines are secreted from infected cells and act as cytokines, helping the cells to proliferate and increase virus production. Viroreceptors resemble cytokine receptors and attract cellular cytokines. E.g. Herpesviruses 5. PATTERNS OF VIRAL INFECTION & DISEASE Three major outcomes can be attributed to a viral infection: (1) abortive infection, in which no progeny virus particles are produced, but the cell may die because early viral functions can occur. (2) lytic infection, in which active virus production is followed by cell death. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 7 (3) persistent infection, in which small numbers of virus particles are produced with little or no CPE. Persistent infections include: a. latent infection, in which viral genetic material remains in host cell without production of virus and may be activated at a later time to produce virus and/or transform the host cell. b. chronic infection, which involves low level of virus production with little or no CPE; and viral transformation, in which viral infection or viral gene product induces unregulated cellular growth, and cells form tumors in the host. Based on patterns and levels of detectable infectious virus in the host and the role of immune response in clearing the virus, viral infections can be divided into five categories: (Figure 1) (1) acute infection that is cleared by the immune response. In acute infection, the virus enters the host, then multiplies at the site of entry and in the target tissue, and this is followed by viremia and cytopathic effects. This type of infection is a lytic infection. The immune system mounts both cellular and humoral responses and successfully eliminates the virus from the host. Examples of acute viral infections followed by clearance of the virus from the host by immune responses are hepatitis A, influenza, parainfluenza, rhino, and corona viruses. (2) acute infection that becomes latent and periodically reactivated. In some viral infections, acute infection may result in either asymptomatic or symptomatic disease followed by latent infection in which the viral genome persists without any infectious virus production. Most of the viruses opting to persist in the host have evolved various mechanisms for persistence, including restriction of viral cytopathic effects, infection of immunologically privileged sites, maintenance of viral genomes without full viral gene expression, antigenic variation, suppression of immune components. name: Notes - Antiviral agents & resistance
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 5 10 ANTIVIRAL AGENTS & RESISTANCE ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Classify antiviral agents according to their molecular target and stage of the viral replication cycle. 2. Explain the relationship between the mechanism of action of selected antiviral agents and their clinical indications. 3. Select an appropriate antiviral agent for a patient according to the causative virus, mechanism of action, and clinically relevant drug characteristics. 4. Analyze the causes and clinical consequences of antiviral resistance and appropriate strategies to minimize or manage it. Unlike viruses, bacteria do not rely on host cellular machinery for replication, so processes specific to these organisms provide ideal targets for the development of antibacterial drugs. Because viruses are obligate intracellular parasites, antiviral agents must be capable of selectively inhibiting viral functions without damaging the host, making the development of such drugs very difficult. Another limitation is that many rounds of virus replication occur during the incubation period and the virus has spread before symptoms appear, making drug treatment after the development of clinical symptoms relatively ineffective. Thus, the challenges in the development of antiviral agents is identification of the steps in viral replication that are unique to the virus and not used by the normal cell. Among the unique viral events are attachment, penetration, uncoating, RNA-directed DNA synthesis (reverse transcription) or RNA-directed RNA synthesis (RNA viruses), and assembly and release of the intact virion. There is a need for antiviral drugs active against viruses for which vaccines are not available or not highly effective because of a multiplicity of serotypes (eg, rhinoviruses) or because of constantly changing viral antigens (eg, influenza, HIV). Antivirals are usually most effective when started early, because viral replication may peak before or around symptom onset. Clinical benefit depends on the virus, site of infection, host factors, and timing. Combination therapy is particularly important for viruses with high mutation rates, such as HIV and HCV, because it suppresses replication more effectively and reduces the probability of resistance. ANTIVIRAL DRUGSInhibition of early eventsInhibition of viral nucleic acid synthesisInhibition of late eventsInhibitors of UncoatingFusion inhibitorsPolymerase inhibitorsReverse transcriptase inhibitorsProtease inhibitorsNeuraminidase inhibitorsNucleoside analogsNon-nucleoside NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 5 SELECTED ANTIVIRAL AGENTS 1. Inhibitors of Uncoating Amantadine and rimantadine, which are thought to inhibit viral uncoating as their primary antiviral effect. They are extremely selective, with activity against only influenza A, where they act as inhibitors of the viral M2 protein. They have been used either as prophylaxis or for therapy. Unfortunately, since 2001, the rates of resistance to amantadine/rimantadine have increased so sharply (up to 100% for some strains) that they are no longer routinely recommended. 2. Fusion inhibitors HIV fusion inhibitors act by disrupting the fusion of viral envelope with the cell membrane, preventing cellular infection. The prototype agent is enfuvirtide. 3. Inhibitors of nucleic acid synthesis a. Nucleoside analogues Most antiviral agents are nucleoside analogues that are active against virus-specific nucleic acid polymerases or reverse transcriptases and have much less activity against analogueous host enzymes. Some of these agents serve as nucleic acid chain terminators after incorporation into nucleic acids. Nucleoside analogues cause selective inhibition of viral replication: § by binding better to viral DNA polymerase, rather than to the cellular DNA polymerase; and § by being utilized more extensively in virus-infected cells due to the more rapid synthesis of DNA in infected cells. 1. Acyclovir A guanosine analogue. The key to its benefit is that it must be phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase to be active. Therefore, the compound is essentially nontoxic because it is not phosphorylated or activated in uninfected host cells. Viral thymidine kinase catalyzes the phosphorylation of acyclovir to a monophosphate, then host cell enzymes complete the progression to the diphosphate and, finally, the triphosphate. Acyclovir triphosphate inhibits viral replication by competing with guanosine triphosphate and inhibiting the function of the virally encoded DNA polymerase. Susceptible strains of herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 (HSV-1 and -2) are the most active thymidine kinase inducers and are the most readily inhibited by acyclovir. Resistant strains of HSV have been recovered from immunocompromised patients, including patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); in most instances, resistance results from mutations in the viral thymidine kinase gene or viral DNA polymerase. 2. Ganciclovir A guanosine analogue. It confers activity against cytomegalovirus (CMV). Acyclovir has low activity against CMV because it is not well phosphorylated in CMV-infected cells due to the absence of the gene for thymidine kinase in CMV. However, ganciclovir is active against CMV because another viral-encoded phosphorylating enzyme (UL97) is present in CMV-infected cells that is, capable of phosphorylating ganciclovir and converting it to the monophosphate. Then, cellular enzymes convert it to the active compound, ganciclovir triphosphate, which inhibits the viral DNA polymerase. Since NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 5 ganciclovir can be phosphorylated in normal, uninfected, host cells, toxicity, especially neutropenia, frequently limits therapy. 3. Zidovudine Thymidine analogue, inhibits the reverse transcriptase of HIV by terminating the developing DNA chain. As with other nucleosides, AZT must be phosphorylated; host cell enzymes carry out the process. The basis for the relatively selective therapeutic effect of AZT is that HIV reverse transcriptase is more than 100 times more sensitive to AZT than is host cell DNA polymerase. It is also used for treatment of pregnant HIV-infected women. It has been shown to reduce or prevent the transmission of HIV from the mother to the baby. The drug, however, is toxic and costly. 4. Lamivudine Lamivudine is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor with activity against HIV and HBV to disrupt viral DNA synthesis. Lamivudine is phosphorylated intracellularly to its active triphosphate metabolite. This nucleoside analogueue is incorporated into viral DNA by HIV reverse transcriptase and HBV polymerase, resulting in DNA chain termination. 5. Ribavirin A guanosine analogue. Similar to other nucleoside analogues, ribavirin must be phosphorylated to mono, di-, and triphosphate forms, but cellular enzymes can carry out each of these, thus, heightening the risk of toxicity. It is an inhibitor of RNA polymerase. It was used used in treatment of HCV. Aerosol administration is used for treatment of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). 6. Idoxuridine and Trifluorothymidine Idoxuridine blocks nucleic acid synthesis by being incorporated into DNA in place of thymidine and producing a non- functional molecule. It is phosphorylated by cellular thymidine kinase to the active compound, which inhibits both viral and cellular DNA polymerase. The resulting host toxicity precludes systemic administration in humans. Idoxuridine can be used topically as effective treatment of herpetic keratitis. Trifluorothymidine, a related pyrimidine analogue, is effective in treating herpetic corneal infections, including those that fail to respond to Idoxuridine. Figure 1.
