name: Notes - Introduction to medical mycology
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 7 11 INTRODUCTION TO MEDICAL MYCOLOGY ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Interpret the major morphological features of medically important fungi and relate them to their mode of growth and pathogenic potential. 2. Differentiate superficial, subcutaneous, systemic, and opportunistic mycoses using clinical presentation, host factors, and tissue involvement. 3. Apply appropriate laboratory diagnostic approaches to common superficial and opportunistic fungal infections based on specimen type and fungal characteristics. 4. Analyze the relationship between fungal virulence mechanisms, host immune status, route of transmission, and the resulting clinical manifestations. Medical mycology is the study of fungi that cause human disease, including their morphology, classification, pathogenesis, laboratory diagnosis, treatment and prevention. Differences of Fungi from bacteria • Fungi are eukaryotic organisms with a true nucleus. • They have chitin and β-glucans in the cell wall. • The cell membrane contains ergosterol, an important antifungal drug target. • Most pathogenic fungi grow more slowly than bacteria. • Fungi reproduce by asexual (production of spores, budding) and/or sexual spores (production of zygotes).. • Fungal spores are important for environmental survival and transmission, but they should not be confused with bacterial endospores. Structure of fungal cell The fungal cell has many typical eukaryotic features, including a nucleus with a nucleolus, nuclear membrane, and linear chromosomes. The cytoplasm contains a cytoskeleton, ribosomes and organelles, such as mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, and the Golgi apparatus. Fungal cells have a rigid cell wall (made of complex polysaccharides such as mannans, glucans, and chitins in close association with each other and with structural proteins) external to the cytoplasmic membrane (made of ergosterol). Mannoproteins of the cell wall are composed of mannan found on the cell surface where they are linked to various proteins. Mannoproteins are very important since antibodies are readily developed against these molecules on the cell surface. Figure 1. Structure of fungal cell NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 7 Morphology & classification of fungi The size of fungi varies from bacterial size (2-4 μm) to a macroscopically visible structure. The morphologic forms of growth vary from colonies superficially resembling those of bacteria to some of the most complex, multicellular, colorful, structures seen in nature. Fungi that cause human infections can be divided based on their morphological forms into: 1. Yeasts are fungi that primarily grow in a round cellular form. The yeasts tend to have the simplest cellular forms, reproducing by a process of asexual budding, constriction, and cell separation similar to many bacteria. e.g. Cryptococcus 2. Molds are fungi that primarily grow as filamentous, tube-like structures called hyphae. As the hyphae extend, they form an intertwined mass called a mycelium. Most molds form hyphal septa, which are cross-walls perpendicular to the cell walls, dividing the hypha into subunit cells (septate molds), others do not form septa (aseptate molds). They reproduce asexually (spores), or sexually (zygote). e.g. Aspergillus 3. Pseudohyphae which are actually elongated yeast cells growing end-to-end. Pseudohyphae are distinguished from true hyphae by having recurring bud-like constrictions and less rigid cell walls. e.g. Candida. 4. Dimorphic can transition between morphological forms depending on environmental conditions. A distinct group of human pathogens are the thermally dimorphic fungi, shifting from tissue-associated form (as yeast-like) (37°C) in mammalian host to hyphal growth (ambient temperature) in their environmental reservoir, based on temperature. e.g. Histoplasma capsulatum Yeasts Figure 2. Morphology of fungi Grouping of medically important fungi based on the types of tissues they infect and the diseases they produce, is as follows: 1. The superficial mycoses, such as the dermatophytes, cause indolent lesions of the skin and its appendages, commonly known as ringworm and athlete’s foot, without typically spreading to deeper tissues. 2. The subcutaneous mycoses characteristically cause infection through the skin, followed by subcutaneous or lymphatic spread. e.g. mycetoma NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 7 3. The opportunistic mycoses are those found in the environment or in the resident flora that produce disease primarily in immunocompromised hosts. E.g. Aspergillus, Candida, Cryptococcus, Pneumocystis, Mucor. 4. The systemic mycoses are the most virulent fungi and may cause serious and progressive systemic disease in previously healthy persons. They are not found in the human microbiota. Although their major potential is to produce deep-seated visceral infections and systemic spread. e.g. Histoplasma N.B. Many opportunistic fungal infections are primarily diseases of patients with impaired host defenses rather than highly virulent pathogens in healthy individuals. Figure 3. Dermatophytes causing superficial mycoses Figure 4. Fungi causing opportunistic mycoses NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 4 of 7 Infections caused by fungi The diseases caused by fungi are called mycoses. These infections vary greatly in their manifestations but tend to present with subacute or chronic features, often relapsing over time. Acute disease, such as that produced by many viruses and bacteria, is uncommon with fungal infections. 1. Superficial mycoses Dermatophytes General term for species invading superficial layers of skin. Of the many species involved, those belonging to Epidermophyton, Microsporum and Trichophyton are of greatest importance. Characteristics Filamentous fungi invading surface keratinized structures: skin, hair, nails. Hyphae penetrate between cells. Dermatophytes utilize keratin and generally remain in keratinized tissues rather than invading viable tissue. Epidermophyton → skin and nails, not hair Microsporum → skin and hair, generally not nails Trichophyton → skin, hair and nails Transmission By contact with fungal material on skin scales. Pathogenesis Skin inflammation, pruritus – sometimes localized hypersensitivity reactions. Diseases Tinea, ringworm, athlete’s foot. Laboratory identification Examination of KOH-treated skin scrapings for hyphae; fluorescence under Wood’s lamp. Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) Treatment Topical (imidazoles) and oral antifungal agents (griseofulvin, itraconazole, terbinafine). 2. Opportunistic mycoses A. Aspergillus spp. Aspergillus species are molds found readily in the environment. Invasive aspergillosis occurs in highly immunocompromised persons, often rapidly resulting in death. Aspergillus fumigatus is the most important of three common species, the others being Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus niger. Characteristics Filamentous fungi causing opportunistic infections in immunocompromised patients. Occur widely in external environment. Invade lungs and blood vessels. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 5 of 7 Transmission Inhalation of airborne conidia. Pathogenesis Causes thrombosis and infarction when blood vessels invaded. Partial blockage of airways from fungal mass. Allergic bronchopulmonary reactions. Host factors favoring Aspergillus growth include anatomic abnormalities of the lungs (eg, bronchiectasis, severe emphysema) and immunosuppression (neutropenia, lung transplantation). Diseases Aspergillus fumigatus: pulmonary aspergillosis; 1) Aspergillus pneumonia, (2) disseminated aspergillosis, (3) allergic respiratory disease, and (4)aspergilloma (fungus ball). Aspergillus niger: Otomycosis Laboratory identification Presence of hyphae in tissue smears. Culture on SDA. PCR. Serology. Treatment Amphoteric

name: Notes - Antifungal agents & resistance
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 4 12 ANTIFUNGAL AGENTS & RESISTANCE ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Differentiate the mechanisms of action of major antifungal drug classes based on their fungal cellular targets. 2. Interpret the clinical spectrum and pharmacologic properties of antifungal agents to guide treatment of common and life-threatening fungal infections. 3. Select an appropriate antifungal agent for a patient according to the fungal pathogen, site/severity of infection, and important drug toxicities. 4. Analyze antifungal resistance mechanisms by relating changes in drug targets, drug uptake, efflux, or biosynthetic pathways to therapeutic failure. Compared with antibacterial agents, relatively few antifungals are available for treatment of fungal infections. Many substances with antifungal activity have proved to be unstable, to be toxic to humans, or to have undesirable pharmacologic characteristics, such as poor diffusion into tissues. Newer antifungal agents target fungal-specific cellular features and demonstrate lower toxicity than older drug classes. 1. Antifungals acting on cytoplasmic membrane A. Polyenes Action: The polyenes nystatin and amphotericin B are lipophilic and bind to ergosterol, the dominant sterol in the cytoplasmic membrane of fungal cells. After binding, they form annular channels, which penetrate the membrane and lead to leakage of essential small molecules from the cytoplasm and cell death. Spectrum of activity: Almost all fungi are susceptible to amphotericin B, and the development of resistance is rare. Use of amphotericin B is limited to progressive, life-threatening fungal infections. Amphotericin B is insoluble in water and must be administered intravenously as a colloidal suspension. Side effects: The major limitation to amphotericin B therapy is the toxicity created by its affinity for mammalian as well as fungal membranes. Intravenous Infusion is commonly followed by chills, fever, headache, and dyspnea. The most serious toxic effect is renal dysfunction. The even greater toxicity of nystatin limits its use to topical preparations. Preparations that complex amphotericin B with lipids (liposomal amphotericin) have been used as a means to limit toxicity. B. Azoles Action: Their activity is based on inhibition of the enzyme “lanosterol 14-α-demethylase” responsible for conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol, the major component of the fungal cell membrane. This leads to ergosterol depletion and lanosterol accumulation, forming defective membranes. Azoles are generally fungistatic against many fungi rather than uniformly fungicidal. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 4 Spectrum of activity: Fluconazole is primarily active against yeasts, including many Cryptococcus and Candida species. Mold-active azoles (itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, and isavuconazole) have extended activity against molds such as Aspergillus species. These Most of these agents can be given orally or parenterally. Topical agents (ketoconazole, clotrimazole, and miconazole) are available as topical preparations for superficial mycoses. Side effects: Azoles can cause varying degrees of liver toxicity. Additionally, many systemic azoles, can adversely affect cardiac myocyte repolarization and therefore prolong the QTc interval on an ECG, placing patients at increased risk for cardiac arrhythmias. Azoles can also affect the precursors of some hormones and may therefore cause endocrinological side effects, restricting their use in pregnancy. C. Allylamaines Action: The allylamines act by inhibition of an enzyme (squalene epoxidase) in the early stages of ergosterol synthesis. Spectrum of activity: The allylamine group includes an oral and topical agent. Terbinafine is particularly effective against dermatophytes and accumulates in keratinized tissues, making it an important treatment for tinea infections and onychomycosis. 2. Antifungals acting on nucleic acid synthesis Action: 5-Flucytosine (5FC) is an analog of cytosine. It is a potent inhibitor of RNA transcription and DNA synthesis. Spectrum of activity: Flucytosine is well absorbed after oral administration. It is active against most clinically important yeasts, including Candida albicans and Cryptococcus neoformans, but it has little activity against molds. Side effects: The frequent development of mutational resistance during therapy limits its application to mild yeast infections or its use in combination with amphotericin B for cryptococcal meningitis. The primary toxic effect of flucytosine is a reversible bone marrow suppression that can lead to neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. 3. Antifungals acting on cell wall synthesis The unique chemical nature of the fungal cell wall, with its interwoven layers of mannans, glucans, and chitin, makes it an ideal target for chemotherapeutic attack. The echinocandins, which block glucan synthesis, are now in widespread clinical use due to their potent antifungal effect and comparatively low adverse effect profile. Other cell wall-active antifungals are in preclinical development. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 4 Echinocandins Action: Echinocandins inhibit a glucan biosynthetic enzyme (β-1,3-D-glucan synthase) required for the synthesis of fungal cell wall. Echinocandin administration, therefore, causes morphologic distortions and osmotic instability in yeasts and molds, similar to the effect of β-lactams on bacteria. Spectrum of activity: Caspofungin, has activity against Candida and Aspergillus. Although highly active against many Candida species, the echinocandins tend to be used as second-line agents for invasive aspergillosis. Cryptococcus neoformans whose cell wall glucans have a slightly different structure, are more tolerant of echinocandins. Newer echinocandins, micafungin and anidulafungin, have the same mode of action and a similar spectrum of antifungal activity. Side effects: Since there are no similar glucans in humans, echinocandin toxicity is minimal. 4. Others Griseofulvin Action: acts on the microtubules and associated proteins that make up the mitotic spindle. It interferes with cell division. Spectrum of activity: after oral administration, it is absorbed from GIT and concentrates in the keratinized layers of the skin. It is active only against the agents of superficial mycoses. Side effects: Clinical response is slow. Prolonged therapy may be required. Antifungal resistance Many of the same resistance mechanisms observed in bacteria are also found in fungi. Fungi tend to primarily inactivate drug activity using efflux pumps and by altering their biosynthetic pathways. In contrast to bacteria, fungi do not make hydrolytic enzymes to inactivate antibiotics to the same extent as bacteria. Polyene Resistance Because amphotericin B binds directly to the ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane, the only means to resist this action is to change the membrane sterol composition. Therefore, resistance is rare. Flucytosine Resistance Flucytosine (5-FC) requires a permease for entry into the cell and then multiple enzymes to modify it to the active metabolites that inhibit nucleic acid synthesis. Mutation in any one of these enzymes renders the drug ineffective. This is the reason that its use is mostly limited to combination therapy with other antifungals. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 4 of 4 Azole Resistance The most well-characterized mechanism is through the induction of efflux pumps that transport the drug out of the cell. Mutation of demethylase enzyme, effectively decreasing the affinity of the azole for its enzyme target. Some azole-resistant strains have also been shown to accomplish ergosterol synthesis by an alternate pathway, thus bypassing the azole target enzyme. Echinocandin Resistance Although the echinocandins are relatively new, resistance has already been obs

name: Notes - Principles of vaccines
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 6 13 PRINCIPLES OF VACCINES ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Explain the immunological principles underlying vaccination and vaccine-induced protection in clinical contexts. 2. Differentiate major vaccine platforms according to their composition, immune response, advantages, limitations, and clinical applications. 3. Interpret clinical situations to select an appropriate vaccine type based on host factors, route of administration, and expected immune response. 4. Evaluate the benefits and limitations of vaccination strategies, including herd immunity, adjuvant use, conjugation, and vaccine interference. What is a vaccine? The word “vaccine” originates from the Latin Variolae vaccinae (cowpox), which Edward Jenner demonstrated in 1798 could prevent smallpox in humans. Today the term ‘vaccine’ applies to all biological preparations, produced from living organisms, that enhance immunity against disease and either prevent (prophylactic vaccines) or, in some cases, treat disease (therapeutic vaccines). Vaccines are administered in liquid form, either by injection, by oral, or by intranasal routes. Principle of vaccination -Vaccines artificially stimulate immunity through exposure to an antigenic substance. An effective vaccine does not protect against disease until it is administered in the proper dosage to susceptible individuals. -Vaccination is a form of active immunization in which exposure to a vaccine antigen stimulates the recipient's own adaptive immune response, producing immunological memory and protection against subsequent infection or disease. - The major goal of vaccination is to generate immunological memory through activation of antigen-specific B and T lymphocytes. Subsequent exposure to the pathogen produces a faster and stronger secondary immune response, which prevents infection, severe disease, or complications. -Vaccines may protect by inducing neutralizing antibodies, opsonizing antibodies, cytotoxic T-cell responses, mucosal immunity, or combinations of these mechanisms, depending on the pathogen and vaccine platform. Herd immunity refers to the fact that the risk of infection among susceptible individuals in a population is reduced by the presence of adequate numbers of immune individuals. However, the threshold of immunity needed for this indirect protective effect depends on many factors, including the transmissibility of the infectious agent, the nature of the vaccine-induced immunity, and the distribution of the immune individuals. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 6 Figure 1. What is herd immunity? Vaccines are composed of either the entire disease-causing microorganism or some of its components. They may be constructed in several ways: • From living organisms that have been weakened, usually from cultivation under sub-optimal conditions (also called attenuation), or from genetic modification, which has the effect of reducing their ability to cause disease; • From whole organisms that have been inactivated by chemical, thermal or other means; • From components of the disease-causing organism, such as specific proteins and polysaccharides, or nucleic acid • From inactivated toxins of toxin-producing bacteria, called toxoid. • From the conjugation of polysaccharides to proteins (this increases the effectiveness of polysaccharide vaccines in young children) Types of Vaccines 1. Whole-organism vaccines – live attenuated or inactivated 2. Component/subunit vaccines – protein, polysaccharide, toxoid and conjugate vaccines. 3. Recombinant and vector-based vaccines 4. Nucleic-acid vaccines – DNA and mRNA vaccines A. Live Attenuated Vaccines Live vaccines use mutants that antigenically overlap with wild-type organism but are restricted in some step in the pathogenesis of disease. These wild viruses or bacteria are attenuated (weakened) in a laboratory, by serial passages in animals or cell cultures. As more is learned about microbial genes involved in disease pathogenesis, attenuated vaccines can be engineered in the laboratory. To produce an immune response, live, attenuated vaccines must replicate in the vaccinated person. Attenuated live vaccines have the advantage of acting more like the natural infection with regard to their effect on immunity. Because live attenuated organisms replicate within the host, they can activate both MHC class I and class II pathways, resulting in both cellular and humoral immune responses. When administered through a mucosal route, live attenuated vaccines can stimulate local secretory IgA and mucosal immune responses. Disadvantages of attenuated live vaccines include (1) a risk of reversion to greater virulence, (2) severe infection in immunocompromised hosts, and (3) limited storage and shelf life in some cases (destroyed by heat and light). (4) Active immunity from a live, attenuated vaccine may not develop because of interference with the vaccine virus by NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 6 circulating antibody. Antibody from any source (e.g., transplacental transfer to infants, transfusion of blood products) can interfere with replication of the vaccine organism and lead to poor response or no response to the vaccine. The live, attenuated viral vaccines as MMR (measles, mumps, rubella), varicella. Bacterial live attenuated vaccines as typhoid vaccine (Ty21a), and Bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG). B. Inactivated (killed) vaccines They are made by purifying bacterial or viral preparations to a certain extent and then inactivating their infectivity in a way that does minimal damage to the important proteins; mild chemical (formalin) or thermal treatment is frequently used. Adjuvant is added to boost the immunogenicity, as they enhance uptake by presenting cells e.g. aluminium hydroxide or aluminium phosphate. [Adjuvants enhance vaccine immunogenicity by promoting innate immune activation, antigen uptake and presentation, and cytokine production. They may allow a stronger and more durable adaptive immune response and can reduce the amount of antigen required per vaccine dose]. The immunity provided by inactivated vaccines is generally not as long-lasting as that obtained from live, attenuated vaccines. Multiple doses over time are needed to obtain ongoing immunity. Unlike live vaccines, which produce an immune response that closely resembles natural infection, the immune response to an inactivated vaccine is mostly antibody production. Little or no cellular immunity results. As a result, some inactivated vaccines may require periodic supplemental doses (Booster doses). Advantages of inactivated vaccines are that there is no reversion to virulence by the vaccine form. Disadvantages of inactivated vaccines include relatively brief immunity requiring boosting shots to maintain effectiveness, poor cell-mediated response. Inactivated viral vaccines as Influenza, Polio (Salk), Hepatitis A, Rabies, bacterial vaccines as Cholera. Table 1. Difference between inactivated and live attenuated vaccines Inactivated vaccine Live attenuated vaccine Duration of immunity Shorter Longer Immunoglobulins produced IgG IgG, IgA Mucosal immunity Poor Present Cell mediated immunity Poor Present Reversion to virulence No Possible Interference with other viruses No Possible Excretion of vaccine virus & herd immunity No Possible Number of doses often requires a primary series and/or boosters one or a small number of doses Stability High Low NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Toxoids Toxoids are bacterial toxins that have been chemically inactivated such as Clostridium tetani or Corynebacterium diphtheriae toxins. name: Notes - Gram positive cocci of medical importance
ref: file:L14 Gram positive cocci of medical importance.pdf
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 4 14 GRAM POSITIVE COCCI OF MEDICAL IMPORTANCE ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Differentiate clinically important Gram-positive cocci according to their morphology, transmission, laboratory characteristics, and associated infections. 2. Analyze how major virulence factors of Gram-positive cocci contribute to the development and severity of specific infections. 3. Interpret clinical and laboratory findings to determine the most likely Gram-positive coccus responsible for a patient's infection and its probable mode of transmission. 4. Select appropriate antimicrobial or preventive strategies for clinically important infections caused by Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, and Enterococcus species. The aerobic gram-positive cocci are a heterogeneous collection of spherical bacteria that are common residents in the mouth, gastrointestinal tract, genitourinary tract, and skin surface. The most important genera are Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, and Enterococcus. Genus Staphylococcus Genus contains over 30 species, of which three are of greatest medical importance: Staph. aureus, Staph. epidermidis, Staph. saprophyticus. 1. Staphylococcus aureus Characteristics Gram-positive cocci in clusters. Some strains produce capsules. Non-fastidious; facultative anaerobe (capable of aerobic and anaerobic respiration) Transmission Normal habitat: humans (and animals associated with them); skin, especially nose and perineum (carriage rates higher in hospital patients and staff). Spread is mainly by contact. Pathogenesis Virulence multifactorial: • cell-associated: capsule, protein A, fibronectin-binding protein, collagen-binding proteins • many strains have protein A bound to the mucopeptide of the cell wall. This protein interacts non-specifically with host IgG antibodies reducing opsonization and causing local activation of complement. • Enzymes: coagulase, catalase. • Extracellular toxins: enterotoxins, exfoliative toxin, toxic shock syndrome toxin (superantigen), membrane-damaging toxins (haemolysins), leukocidin, Diseases Boils; skin sepsis; postoperative wound infection; osteomyelitis; pneumonia endocarditis, sepsis Scalded skin syndrome; food-borne infection, toxic shock syndrome Laboratory identification White or golden colonies on blood agar. Catalase positive, coagulase positive, most strains ferment mannitol. Treatment In susceptible isolates, antibiotics of choice are beta-lactamase-stable penicillins; however, the vast majority of hospital isolates are beta-lactamase NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 4 producers. Multiple drug resistance (including methicillin and tolerance or resistance to vancomycin) is a worldwide problem. Vancomycin is the drug of choice for MRSA. Mupirocin can be used for topical treatment of carriage. Prevention of spread by isolation and / or treatment of carriers in high-risk areas in hospital. 2. Staphylococcus epidermidis Characteristics Gram-positive cocci in clusters. Non-fastidious; facultative anaerobe Transmission Normal habitat: skin (carriage rate approximately 100%). Spread by contact with self, other patients or hospital personnel. Almost all infections acquired in hospital, but may be endogenous. Pathogenesis Extracellular slime production may be a marker of virulence and aid in the colonization of plastic implants (e.g. intravenous catheters and prostheses). Diseases Opportunist pathogen associated with device-related sepsis (e.g. catheter-related sepsis; prosthetic valve endocarditis; infection of artificial joints; shunt infections) Laboratory identification White colonies on blood agar; catalase positive, coagulase negative, mannitol not fermented. Treatment Antibiotic resistance: often multiresistant (including penicillin and methicillin). Prevention of infection: catheter care. Genus Streptococcus A large group of Gram-positive cocci distributed widely in humans and animals, mostly forming part of the normal flora, but some species responsible for some major infections. Individual cells occur in pairs and chains. The medically significant streptococci may be divided on the basis of either haemolysis on blood agar (complete haemolysis, beta; partial haemolysis, alpha; no haemolysis, gamma) or by the presence or absence of a group- specific carbohydrate antigen (i.e. the Lancefield group labelled alphabetically A to V). 1. Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A beta hemolytic streptococci) Characteristics Gram-positive cocci in chains, non-motile, facultative anaerobe Transmission Normal habitat is the human upper respiratory tract and skin. Spread by airborne droplets and by contact. Pathogenesis Elaborates many enzymes and exotoxins, which may play a role in infection: erythrogenic toxin (lysogenic phage mediated); toxic shock syndrome toxin (TSST) (Superantigen); streptolysins; streptokinase A and B (therapeutic applications); deoxyribonuclease; hyaluronidase (spreading factor). Diseases Infections of upper respiratory tract and of skin and soft tissue (e.g. pharyngitis, cellulitis, erysipelas, lymphadenitis). Toxic manifestations include scarlet fever and toxic shock syndrome. Non-suppurative sequelae (acute glomerulonephritis and rheumatic fever) are important complications of both skin and throat infections. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 4 Laboratory identification Pronounced beta haemolytic activity on blood agar, Catalase negative. Susceptible to Bacitracin (0.04 units); detection of group-specific carbohydrate (A antigen) by rapid antigen test Treatment Penicillin is the drug of choice. Oral cephalosporin or clindamycin is an alternative for penicillin-allergic patients. 2. Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B beta hemolytic streptococci) Characteristics Gram-positive cocci in chains, non-motile, facultative anaerobe Transmission Normal habitat; gut and vagina. Babies acquire organism from colonized mother at birth or by contact spread between babies in nursery after birth. Diseases Neonatal meningitis and septicaemia. Laboratory identification Beta-haemolytic on blood agar. Positive Hippurate hydrolysis. Positive CAMP (Christie, Atkins, Munch–Peterson) test. Group-specific carbohydrate (group B) detected by commercially available antigen or molecular tests for definitive identification. Treatment Susceptible to penicillin, combination of penicillin and gentamicin for serious infections. Screening pregnant women recommended; prophylactic antibiotics may be given to babies (especially premature) or carriers. 3. Streptococcus pneumoniae (alpha hemolytic streptococci) Characteristics Gram-positive coccus in pairs (diplococci), capsulated, facultative anaerobe. Transmission Normal habitat is the human respiratory tract; 5% of population may carry in small numbers. Transmission via droplet spread. Pathogenesis Capsule protects the organism from phagocytosis. Pneumolysin may have a role as a virulence factor, but to date no known exotoxins. Splenectomy may predispose to infection. Viral infection may be a precursor to pneumonia. Diseases Pneumonia, bacteremia and meningitis. Otitis media and sinusitis in children. Laboratory identification On blood agar alpha-haemolytic colonies that may autolyse within 48 h at 35°C. Catalase negative. Positive for bile solubility test and susceptible to Optochin. Polysaccharide capsules can be demonstrated by appropriate staining techniques Treatment Penicillin remains the antibiotic of choice, but resistance is increasing rapidly, and susceptibility test results should be used to guide therapy. Vaccine available (polysaccharide capsular antigen) 4. Oral streptococci There are several other species of alpha-haemolytic streptococci that in the past have been lumped together under the heading ‘viridans streptococci’. Most species are commensal in the mouth. Several species are capable of causing infective endocarditis. Most strains are

name: Notes - Gram negative bacilli of medical importance
ref: file:L15 Gram negative bacilli of medical importance.pdf
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 4 15 GRAM NEGATIVE BACILLI OF MEDICAL IMPORTANCE ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Differentiate clinically important Gram-negative bacilli according to their characteristic microbiological, epidemiological, and clinical features. 2. Analyze the relationship between major virulence factors of Gram-negative bacilli and the resulting disease manifestations. 3. Interpret the transmission and environmental characteristics of Gram-negative bacilli to explain the development of infection in individual patients. 4. Select an appropriate antimicrobial management approach for infections caused by Gram-negative bacilli based on the organism and the need for susceptibility testing. Introduction • Gram-negative bacteria are among the world's most significant public health problems due to their high resistance to antibiotics. These microorganisms have significant clinical importance in hospitals because they often require patients to be in the intensive care unit (ICU), and patients are at high risk of morbidity and mortality. Two large groups, Enterobacterales (Lactose and non-lactose fermenters) and the aerobic non-fermenters (Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter), are responsible for most clinical isolates; nevertheless, other clinically pertinent gram-negative organisms exist. • Large number of genera are inhabitants of the large intestine (e.g. E. coli, Proteus, Klebsiella); some are adapted to the respiratory tract (e.g. Klebsiella); others live in soil and water (e.g. Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter). • It is important to distinguish between true pathogens (e.g. Salmonella, Shigella) and the opportunists (e.g. Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter). Figure 1. Classification of Gram-negative bacilli NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 4 1. Escherichia coli Genus Escherichia contains only one species of medical importance: E. coli. Characteristics Gram-negative rod; motile; with or without capsule; non-fastidious, facultative anaerobe Transmission Normal habitat is gut of humans and animals; may colonize lower end of urethra and vagina. Spread is by contact and ingestion (faecal–oral route); may be food-associated; may be endogenous. Possesses O (somatic), H (flagellar), K (capsular) and F (fimbrial) antigens, which can be used to characterize strains by serotyping. Pathogenesis A variety of virulence factors have been identified: • Endotoxin: present in all strains • Adhesins: P fimbriae (pili) associated with UTIs; colonization factors (e.g. CFA I) associated with gastrointestinal tract infection. • Capsule present in some strains; may be associated with adhesion; K1 capsular type associated with neonatal meningitis • Enterotoxins associated with diarrhoeal disease: ETEC (enterotoxigenic E. coli) produce heat-stable (ST) and cholera-like heat-labile (LT) toxins; EHEC (enterohaemorrhagic E. coli) produce verotoxin-associated with haemolytic uraemic syndrome. Diseases Urinary tract infection; neonatal meningitis, septicaemia, diarrhoeal diseases (diarrheagenic strains) Laboratory identification Grows readily on routine laboratory media and on bile-containing selective media (MacConkey’s agar) as Lactose fermenter. Indole test positive Treatment Wide range of antibacterial agents potentially available, but incidence of resistance variable and often plasmid-mediated; must be determined by susceptibility testing. Specific treatment of diarrhoeal disease usually not required. 2. Klebsiella This genus contains several species, of which the most important is K. pneumoniae Characteristics Gram-negative rods, non-fastidious facultative anaerobe, capsulated Transmission Normal habitat is gut of humans and animals and moist inanimate environments, especially soil and water. Infection may be endogenous or acquired by contact spread. Klebsiella have remarkable capacity for survival on hands. Pathogenesis All possess endotoxin and fimbriae or other adhesins. Capsules are important in inhibiting phagocytosis. Diseases Opportunistic infections in the compromised (usually hospitalized) host. Respiratory and urinary tracts are most common sites of infection. Laboratory identification Mucoid Lactose-fermenting, on MacConkey’s agar. Grow readily on routine laboratory media. Treatment Multiple antibiotic resistance, usually plasmid-mediated, is common, and susceptibility must be determined by laboratory tests if treatment is indicated. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 4 3. Proteus This genus contains several species, of which two are of medical importance: P. mirabilis and P. vulgaris. Characteristics Gram-negative rod, non-fastidious, facultative anaerobe, bile tolerant; characteristic unpleasant odour; highly motile and swarms on blood agar Transmission Normal habitat is human gut, soil and water. Contact spread; infection often endogenous. Pathogenesis Characterized virulence factors include endotoxin and urease. Diseases Urinary tract infection; hospital-acquired wound infection, septicemia, pneumonia in the compromised host. Laboratory identification Lactose non-fermenter, swarms on blood agar, produces urease (urea to ammonia). Treatment Range of antimicrobial agents are available. 4. Pseudomonas aeruginosa Characteristics Aerobic Gram-negative rod, motile by means of polar flagella. Able to utilize a very wide range of carbon and energy sources and to grow over a wide temperature range. Does not ferment carbohydrates. Transmission P. aeruginosa is widespread in moist areas in the environment; patients usually become infected by contact spread, directly or indirectly, from these environmental sites. Pathogenesis A number of virulence factors have been identified, including endotoxin and exotoxin A, which acts as an inhibitor of elongation factor in eukaryotic protein synthesis. Extracellular polysaccharide capsule helps to prevent phagocytosis (e.g. massive amounts of alginate produced by strains specifically in cystic fibrosis patients). Pigments may have a role in pathogenicity. Diseases P. aeruginosa is an opportunist pathogen that can infect almost any body site given the right predisposing conditions. It causes infections of skin and burns, it is a major lung pathogen in cystic fibrosis, and can cause pneumonia in intubated patients. It can also cause UTIs, septicaemia, osteomyelitis and endocarditis. Laboratory identification Grows readily on routine media including MacConkey. Produces irregular iridescent colonies and a characteristic smell. Most strains produce a green pigment, oxidase positive. Treatment Resistant to many antibacterial agents; propensity to develop resistance during therapy. Combination antimicrobial chemotherapy based on susceptibility testing is required (e.g. aminoglycoside and beta- lactam antibiotic). or prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment and prophylaxis. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 4 of 4 5. Acinetobacter baumannii Characteristics Aerobic Gram-negative rod, non-motile. Transmission Acinetobacter are ubiquitous saprophytes present in the environment inside and outside the hospital; able to survive on both moist surfaces such as mechanical ventilation equipment, and on dry surfaces such as the human skin. Patients usually become infected by contact spread, directly or indirectly, from these environmental sites. Diseases Opportunistic pathogen causing infections in the respiratory tract, urinary tract, wounds, and sepsis Laboratory identification Gram stain morphology is characteristic—large, Gram variable coccobacilli. Treatment Treatment must be guided by in vitro susceptibility tests because multidrug resistance is common.

name: Notes - Introduction to medical Parasitology
ref: file:L 16 notes - Introduction to medical Parasitology .pdf
text: Page 1 of 6 L16 Introduction to Medical Parasitology SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Identify the concept of Parasitology. 2. Define the terms related to human – parasite relationship. 3. Differentiate between types of parasites and hosts. 4. Discuss the pathogenesis of parasitic diseases. 5. Classify parasites of medical importance. What is Parasitology It is the study of parasites and their relationship to their hosts. It is one of the most fascinating areas of biology. It is entirely proper to classify many bacteria and fungi and all viruses as parasites, however, Parasitology has traditionally been limited to parasitic protozoa, helminths, and arthropods. Global Importance of Parasitology The World Health Organization (WHO) has declared that five out of six major unbeaten human tropical diseases are parasitic. They are schistosomiasis, malaria, filariasis, African trypanosomiasis, and leishmaniasis. NB: Leprosy is the sixth major disease caused by a bacterium. Host -Parasite relationship Symbiosis Literally, the word symbiosis means “living together”. When the two organisms (partners) live in close association, commonly one living in or on the body of the other, they are termed to be symbiotic, as contrasted with free-living organisms. Each of these two organisms is termed a symbiont. Usually, but not necessarily, the symbionts are of different species. Mutualism Mutualism describes a type of symbiosis in which both partners benefit from the association. Mutualism is usually obligatory since in most cases physiological dependence has evolved to such a degree that one organism cannot survive without the other. Page 2 of 6 Commensalism Another type of symbiosis in which one partner benefits from the association, but the other is neither helped nor harmed. The term means “eating at the same table,” and many commens Mutualism describes a type of symbiosis in which both partners benefit from the association. al relationships involve feeding on the wasted food of the host. Parasitism It is a symbiotic relationship in which one of the partners, the parasite, lives on or in the other, the host. The parasite either harms its host or lives at the expense of the host. What is a parasite? A living organism which lives on or in another organism (host) and derives nutrition directly from it. This implies that the parasite benefits and the host is harmed but usually not killed. Types of parasites According to their location in the host, parasites are either; ectoparasites or endoparasites. If a parasite lives on the surface of its host, it is called an ectoparasite (e.g., lice), whereas if the parasite lives in the host, it is an endoparasite (e.g., malaria). Endoparasites are of the following types: • Obligate parasites: they can't exist without being parasitic in their hosts. (e.g., malaria) • Facultative parasites: they can lead a free-living life or live a parasitic life according to environmental conditions. (e.g., Strongyloides stercoralis) • Accidental parasites: they are parasites that infect an unusual host by accident. E.g., Toxocara canis is a worm of the dog w hen accidentally infects human, it does not complete its whole life cycle (reproduction) as it would in its specific host (the dog). Some parasites live their entire adult lives within or on their hosts and may be called permanent parasites, whereas a temporary, or intermittent, parasite, such as a mosquito or bed bug, only feeds on the host and then leaves. Temporary parasites are often referred to as micro-predators, in recognition of the fact that they usually “prey” on several different hosts (or the same host at several discrete times). What is a host? An organism that harbors the parasite and provides nourishment and shelter. Page 3 of 6 Types of hosts • Definitive host: is the host in which the parasite replicates sexually, or the adult stage of parasite (helminth) is present. • Intermediate host: is the host required by the parasite to complete the asexual stage of its life cycle and the larval stage of the parasite is present in it, e.g., the beef is the intermediate host for Taenia saginata (larvae develop in it), whereas, human is the definitive host for that helminth (adults develop in it). • Vector: the term vector is applied usually to arthropods which transmit parasites from one host to another. Effects of parasite on the host 1. Utilization of the host’s food Diphyllobothrium latum in man has been known to cause anemia like pernicious anemia, because of the affinity this tapeworm has for Vitamin B12. This tapeworm can absorb 10 -50 times as much vitamin B12 as other tapeworms. 2. Utilization of host’s non-nutritional materials. In some blood-feeding parasitic hookworms (e.g., Ancylostoma duodenale), the haemoglobin may drop 30% below normal. 3. Damage to host’s tissue. The parasites destroy the host’s tissue in two ways: (a) Some parasites destroy (injure) the host’s tissue when they enter the host. The cercariae of certain schistosomes that cause “Swimmer’s Itch” while penetrating the host skin cause inflammation and damage to the surrounding host tissues. (b) Others inflict tissue damage after they have successfully entered. Entamoeba histolytica which causes a moebic dysentery, secrets histolytic enzymes that digest the epithelial cells lining the host’s large intestine, causing ulcerations. 4. Abnormal growth. (a) Hyperplasia (Increase in the rate of cell division): The eggs of Schistosoma haematobium with their spiny projections are known to irritate the transitional epithelium of the human urinary bladder causing hyperplasia. (b) Neoplasia (Cancer or tumor formation Page 4 of 6 5. Effect of toxins, secretions, excretion, poisons. Specific toxins or poisons, egested, secreted, or excreted by parasites are considered causes of irritation and damage to hosts. • An example of a parasite that elicits an allergic reaction in the host is Schistosoma cercaria which causes a severe inflammatory reaction leading to what is called cercarial dermatitis. • In case of blood-sucking insects such as mosquitoes, the reaction resulting from the bites represents the host’s response to the irritating salivary secretions of the insect. 6. Mechanical interference. Mechanical damage by nematode is also demonstrated by Ascaris lumbricoides in the intestine of their host. This intestinal parasite which measures up to 50 cm in length, when present in large numbers, can disturb intestinal motility leading to volvulus and intestinal obstruction. 7. Host-tissue reaction. Another example of host -tissue reaction is demonstrated by Trichinella spiralis encystment in mammalian muscles. Once the nematode larvae reach the musculature, it is surrounded by connective tissue cells and eosinophils. These host cells soon form a capsule around the coiled worm (larvae) hence the cyst is completely of host origin. Parasite Life Cycles. The life cycle of a parasite is the cycle of its development from the definitive host back to the same or another definitive host. It is termed a direct life cycle when a parasite requires only one specific species of the host in which it completes its development. When two or more species of hosts are required, the life cycle is referred to as an indirect life cycle, and this requires the presence of one or two intermediate hosts. Sources of infection - Man: Man is the source or reservoir for many parasitic infections (e.g., amoebiasis.) The infection is transmitted from one infected man to another man. - Animal: The infection which is transmitted from infected animals to humans is called zoonoses. The infection can be transmitted to humans either directly or indirectly via vectors. (e.g., toxoplasmosis from cats) - Vectors: Vector is an agent, usually an arthropod that transmits the infection from one infected human being to another. Vector can be biological or mechanical. An infected blood sucking insect can transmit the parasite directly into the

name: Notes - what are helminths? what are protozoa
text: Page 1 of 12 L 17 What are Helminths? What are Protozoa? SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Classify medically important parasites 2. Define the terms related parasitic helminths and protozoa 3. Differentiate between different helminths and protozoa 4. Discuss the general morphologic characters of trematodes, cestodes and nematodes 5. Different elements of the life cycle Medical parasitology traditionally has included the study of three major groups of animals: parasitic helminths (worms), parasitic protozoa and those arthropods that directly cause disease or act as vectors of various pathogens. Medical Helminthology The term helminth is derived from the Greek language meaning worm. The helminths are multicellular, bilaterally symmetrical parasites having three germ layers – ectoderm, mesoderm, and entoderm. Helminths have the following characters: • The outer covering, known as cuticle, is tough. It is resistant to intestinal digestion and may be armed with spines or hooks. • Digestive and nervous systems are underdeveloped, whereas their reproductive system is well developed. The parasites may be hermaphrodite or have separate sexes. They also produce eggs in great number to help them survive. • Since they do not possess definite organs of locomotion, they generally move by muscular contraction and relaxation. Classification of Helminthes The helminths of medical importance are classified into two phylums: 1. Phylum Platyhelminthes (Flat worms) They have a dorso-ventrally flattened body, which is either leaf -shaped (Trematoda) or tape-shaped (Cestoda). 2. Phylum Nemathelminths (Round worms) Of which Nematoda (Round worms) are of medical importance Page 2 of 12 Trematodes (Flukes) General characters (Fig.1) Adults are leaf-like worms, covered externally by a cuticle that may be smooth, spiny, or tuberculated. All trematodes possess at least two suckers as organs of attachment. Depending on their habitat they feed on blood, intestinal contents, biliary secreti ons, or tissue juices. Almost all parasitic trematodes are hermaphrodites except bilharzia worms or schistosomes which have separate sexes. General Life Cycle of Trematodes (Fig.2) • All Trematode species are biohelminths (develop in two living organisms) and develop by alternation of hosts and develop adult, egg s, and larval stages. Definitive hosts can be humans and sometimes animals (mammals) that harbor the adult worm. The first or the only intermediate host is the fre shwater snail. A second intermediate host (fish, crab, or ant) in the life cycle of some flukes is sometimes required. • The eggs liberated by the definitive host usually pass to water. A ciliated embryo called miracidium develops from the egg. It enters th e intermediate host (snail), where larval stages develop and escape from the snail to water in the form of cercaria. The fates of cercariae: • Encasement on aquatic vegetation. • Enter the second intermediate host (if present) and transform into metacercaria, • Directly infect the definitive host. On entering the definitive host, the young worms develop to adult stages in their final habitat. After sexual maturity adults lay eggs and the cycle is repeated. Figure 1. General morphology of a trematode Page 3 of 12 Figure 2. General life cycle of trematodes Cestodes (Tapeworms) General characters (Fig.3) • Cestodes have segmented tape-like body, the size ranging between a few millimeters and meters. • Adult worms have three distinct parts: a head or scolex, a neck, and a segmented tape- like body . T he segments are called proglottids. The scolex possesses organs of attachment such as bothria (sucking grooves), or four circular suckers with or without hooks. The neck is the growth zone, from where the proglottids are budded off. • Three types of proglottids are present: immature, mature, and gravid. Immature segments are close to the neck and do not yet have sex glands, mature ones are hermaphrodite (both male and female reproductive organs are present in each proglottid) and locate in the midpart of the body, and gravid proglottids contain a uterus filled with fertilized eggs and are in the terminal part of the body. • The cestodes lack gastrointestinal tract and do not produce digestive enzymes, and must absorb already digested nutrients, therefore their habitat is restricted to the lumen of the small intestine in the definitive host. • Tapeworms are all hermaphrodites. Page 4 of 12 Figure 3. general segmented shape of a tapeworm (A) and details of an adul segment (B) General Life Cycle (Fig.4) • Cestodes develop in three stages: adult, egg and larva. They are biohelminthes, their life cycles involve definitive and intermediate hosts. • Humans can be definitive or/and intermediate hosts for the parasite. In most cestode infections (e.g., Taenia solium, Taeni a saginata, Diphyllobothrium species, Hymenolepis nana) humans are the definitive hosts. Adult worms survive inside their small intestine. • In the remaining cestodes (e.g., Echinococcus), humans function as intermediate hosts. Larvae exist within the tissu es and migrate through different organ systems. Hymenolepis species and T. solium are the cestodes for which humans can function as both definitive and intermediate hosts. • The intermediate host is infected by ingesting eggs that contain six-hooked embryo, which may develop into larvae in the tissues of the intermediate host depending on the species of cestode: 1. Plerocercoid. A larval form of D. latum. In the life cycle of th is parasite there are two intermediate hosts, the plerocercoid being found in the second of them (fish). These are elongated larvae with solid bodies. 2. Cysticercus. A larval form of Taenia solium, Taenia saginata . It is a vesicle with the invaginated scolex and a central cavity containing a little fluid. 3. Cysticercoid. A larval form of Hymenolepis nana . A smaller bladder with an invaginated scolex and a tail-like appendage. 4. Hydatid Cyst. A larval form of Echinococcus. The hydatid cyst is typically a unilocular (single locus) and fluid filled. It is surrounded by double-membrane. The outer layer is smooth, and the inner one is germinal layer, which gives rise to daughter hydatids A B Page 5 of 12 filled with daughter scolices and cyst fluid. The hydatid fluid is highly toxic and allergenic. Figure 4. General life cycle of Cestodes Page 6 of 12 Nematodes (Round worms) General characters (Fig.5) Nematodes or the round worms are thread -like helminths, which include both parasitic and free-living species of which sexes are separate. 1. Their size ranges from 1-2 mm in length up to 1 m, females are longer than males. 2. They are round in cross-section because and have a cuticle to contain this high pressure inside the worm. 3. The head part has a mouth with three lips and sometimes has few teeth. The gut ends up with the anus. 4. Females may be termed viviparous when they give birth to larvae; oviparous when they lay eggs, or ovo -viviparous when the eggs laid contain larvae which immediately hatch out. 5. Young nematodes hatch from eggs and molt in larval stages before they become adults. Figure 5. General morphology of a nematode Page 7 of 12 General Life cycle (Fig.6) • Most of the Nematodes are Geohelminths that develop in a human as the only host. Their eggs hatch into larvae which mature in soil and affect humans. Inside the human host, nematodes may either migrate (Ascaris lumbricoides, Ancylostoma duodenale) or pass the cycle without migration (Trichuris tricura). • A single nematode (Enterobius vermicularis - pin worm) causes contact helminthosis. • Some nematodes that are biohelminthes ( Trichinella spiralis and Filarial nematodes), however, require more than one host to complete their life cycle. Figure 6. General life cycle of nematodes Page 8 of 12 Medical Protozoology General characters • Protozoa are microscopic, one-celled organisms that can be free-living or parasitic. They can multiply and p

name: Notes - Overview of arthropods
text: Page 1 of 4 18 General overview of arthropods SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Determine the general morphological characteristics of arthropods. 2. List the different types of arthropod development. 3. Identify arthropods’ relation to diseases. 4. List different methods by which arthropods can transfer organisms to man. 1. Introduction Arthropods are invertebrates in the phylum Arthropoda which are characterized by being bilaterally symmetrical, with external skeletons, and jointed appendages. The word “arthropod” is derived from the Greek arthron which means “joint” and podos which means “foot” or “leg” and together it means “jointed leg” . The exoskeleton or cuticle mainly consists of chitin, a polymer of glucosamine. The growth is accomplished through a series of molts because of the presence of this tough cuticle which protects the internal organs. They possess a complete digestive tract with the mouth and salivary glands and a complete digestive tract with an anus. The circulatory system is open with a body cavity (the haemocoel) containing a clear colourless fluid (the hemolymph). Sexes are separate and the reproduction is typically sexual . After fertilization, females deposit eggs or larvae. Classification of Arthropods: Arthropods of medical importance are classified into the following classes: I. Class Crustacea e.g. cyclops. II. Class Arachnida e.g. scorpions, spiders, ticks and mites. III. Class Insecta or Hexapoda e.g. fleas, lice, bugs, mosquitoes and flies. General morphological criteria of arthropods: Identification of arthropods is essential to measure the risk of potential human threats. Arthropods are so diverse in their morphology; however, a brief description is listed below: I- Crustacea - Body formed of fused cephalothorax and segmented abdomen. - 5 pairs of legs. - 2 pairs of antennae. - No wings Ex: Cyclops II- Arachnida - Body formed of fused cephalothorax and segmented abdomen or fused together without any segmentation. Page 2 of 4 - 4 pairs of legs. - No antennae. Ex: Scorpion, ticks, and mites. III- Insecta - Body is segmented into head, thorax and abdomen. - 3 pairs of legs. - One pair of antennae. - Winged or not Ex: Fleas, lice, bugs, mosquitoes, and flies. Two different types of development take place (Figure. 1): 1 - Incomplete Metamorphosis: In this type of development, newly hatched larvae resemble adults but are smaller in size and sexually immature. Then they steadily increase in size through successive moltings, such as scorpions, ticks, mites, bugs, and lice. 2- Complete Metamorphosis: The newly hatched larvae are morphologically distinct from the adults. They may be worm-like and develop into the inactive pupal stage from which adults emerge, such as fleas, flies, and mosquitoes. Figure. 1: a. Incomplete metamorphosis (ticks), b. Complete metamorphosis (flies) Arthropods and their relation to disease Medically important arthropods are agents transmitting and /or causing diseases to man. I. Arthropods as Vectors of Pathogens (Disease Transmitters): They might act as mechanical vectors of the etiologic agent or as biological vectors that play an important part in the life cycle. 1. Mechanical Transmission When the arthropods transport the various pathogens in or on their bodies (their legs, hairs and antennae) and drop them unchanged on human food, drink or tissues, for example, the role of house fly in the transmission of enteric pathogens such as polio a b Page 3 of 4 virus and cholera, cysts of protozoa and eggs of helminths. 2. Biological Transmission This method of transmission occurs when the arthropod actively participates in the transmission of the organism. This type of transmission can be divided into: a. Propagative: The organism only multiplies in the arthropod without any cyclical development like in a culture tube, such as the multiplication of Yersinia pestis (causing plague) in fleas. b. Cyclodevelopmental: The organism undergoes developmental or morphological changes only without multiplication in the arthropod, such as the development of microfilaria of filarial worms within the mosquitoes. c. Cyclopropagative: The organism undergoes both developmental changes and multiplication in the arthropod, e.g. Plasmodia in the female Anopheles mosquito and Leishmania species in sand fly. Arthropods can transfer the organisms to man by different methods: 1. Salivary Secretion: Pathogens are discharged in minute droplets with the salivary secretion at when the arthropod is taking a blood meal, e.g., Plasmodia by female Anopheles mosquitoes. 2. Vomit -drop: Non-blood-sucking flies (e.g., house flies) may deposit pathogen-containing vomit drops on human food or drink, such as Entamoeba histolytica cysts. On the other hand, blood-sucking arthropods may obtain the pathogenic organisms in a blood meal from an infected person and deposit them in vomit drops in the puncture wound made in the skin of an uninfected person, e.g., Leishmania species by sandflies and Yersinia pestis causing the plague by fleas. 3. Faeces: Non-blood-sucking flies (e.g., house flies) may deposit their pathogen-containing faeces on human food or drink, such as Entamoeba histolytica cysts. 4. Crushing: Contamination from the infected haemolymph may occur when the arthropod is crushed on the skin, e.g., Rickettsia by lice. 5. Coxal Fluid: During the act of feeding, soft ticks produce infective fluids from their coxal glands that contaminate the bite wound or skin, e.g., diseases transmitted by soft ticks. II. Arthropods as Etiological Agents of Disease (Causing Disease) In addition to their importance in the transmission of pathogens to man, arthropods themselves play a significant role as disease-producing agents. 1. Toxins and venoms: introduced into the skin by tick bites or scorpion stings cause local and/or systemic reactions. 2. Allergic reactions: These reactions may occur due to the injection of the saliva of blood- sucking arthropods into the skin of the host, e.g., dermatitis caused by the bites of female mosquitoes and fleas. In addition, house dust mites may cause rhinitis or asthma by serving directly as allergens or by concentrating highly antigenic material. However, the degree of reaction can vary remarkably between individuals, from little or no reaction to quite severe dermal and systemic effects which may require medical attention. 3. Specific diseases: Certain arthropods produce lesions in humans through their presence in Page 4 of 4 the tissues (the adult or any developmental stage), for example, the presence of larvae of higher diptera in the tissues causing myiasis and the presence of itch mites in skin tissue causing scabies. Additionally, lice infestation can cause pediculosis. 4. Entomophobia: Fear of large arthropods can be extremely important as a cause of severe neurosis. For example, arachnophobia (excessive fear of spiders) is a well-recognized condition.

name: Notes - Clinically important arthropods
text: Page 1 of 10 L 19 Clinically important arthropods SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Discuss diagnosis and management of scorpion sting. 2. Identify arthropods that cause allergic dermatitis. 3. Recognise tick paralysis and its management. 4. Understand pediculosis and its treatment. 5. Differentiate between scabies and other allergic conditions. 1. A- Arthropods that cause toxaemia. They include scorpion and ticks. 1. Scorpion sting A scorpion sting is an injury caused by the stinger of a scorpion resulting in a painful condition that may vary in severity. The sting may cause redness and swelling along with a burning sensation. Scorpions sting to defend and protect themselves. Manifestations The severity of the sting depends on the species of scorpion, the amount of venom injected, and the individual's reaction to the venom. Local effects: - immediate intense aching pain or burning sensation at the sting site - lymphadenitis - Redness, swelling, and warmth around the sting area - Numbness or tingling Systemic effects (in severe cases): - Sweating and salivation - Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain - Muscle twitching, spasms, or convulsions - glossopharyngeal involvement so that speech and swallowing become difficult, - Respiratory distress. - Tachycardia, hypertension, or hypotension - Neurological symptoms such as seizures, paralysis, or altered consciousness. The patient may die by shock or respiratory failure. Page 2 of 10 Diagnosis • Diagnosis is made when the patient gives a history of being stung by a scorpion together with the typical clinical picture. Treatment You usually won’t need medical treatment for a sting. You can typically treat a sting at home with ice, elevation, pain medication, and antihistamines. • First aid measures: - Clean the sting site with soap and water. - Apply a cold compress to reduce pain and swelling. - Keep the affected limb elevated. • Pain management: - Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or acetaminophen may be used to alleviate pain. • Antivenom therapy: - Specific scorpion antivenom may be administered in severe cases of envenomation to neutralize the venom and prevent further toxicity. • Supportive care: - Maintain hydration with intravenous fluids. - Monitor vital signs and provide respiratory support if needed. - Treat complications such as allergic reactions, cardiac arrhythmias, or respiratory failure. Prevention Educate the patient on ways to prevent scorpion stings, such as avoiding areas where scorpions are commonly found, shaking out clothing and bedding before use, and using insecticides or professional pest control services if necessary. Figure 1. scorpion Page 3 of 10 2. Tick bite • Toxins in hard ticks can develop motor paralysis particularly if bitten at the base of the skull. Prompt removal of the engorging tick prevents the progression of ascending paralysis. On biting, hard ticks insert their mouth part in the skin layers to take a blood meal. (Fig. 2) • This f eeding activity lead s to inflammation, cell infiltration, hyperemia, edema, and haemorrhage which worsen by the forcible removal of the tick (Tick dermatosis). • If the tick is present in the back of the neck or along the spinal cord, it will inject its neurotoxin with the saliva causing ‘ Tick Paralysis ’ The condition is characterized by generalized toxaemia with a rise in temperature and rapid ascending flaccid paralysis leading to difficulty in swallowing and breathing, which may be fatal. Toxaemia, ascending flaccid paralysis, and respiratory failure are the causes of death. • Heavy tick infestation can lead to blood loss and anemia. Treatment If you find a tick attached to your skin, simply remove the tick as soon as possible using a plain set of fine-tipped tweezers. How to remove a tick (Fig. 3) 1. Use clean, fine -tipped tweezers to grasp the tick as close to the skin’s surface as possible. 2. Pull upward with steady, even pressure. Don’t twist or jerk the tick; this can cause the mouth-parts to break off and remain in the skin. If this happens, remove the mouth - parts with tweezers. 3. After removing the tick, thoroughly clean the bite area and your hands with rubbing alcohol or soap and water. 4. Few drops of chloroform or ether placed on the tick will usually cause it to relax its hold and will allow it to be easily removed by traction. 5. Never crush a tick with your fingers. Dispose of a live tick by o Putting it in alcohol, o Placing it in a sealed bag/container, o Wrapping it tightly in tape, or o Flushing it down the toilet. 6. Follow-up Page 4 of 10 Figure 2. Hard tick Figure. 3. Mouthpart of the hard tick and its removal B- Arthropods that cause allergy 1. Arthropods causing allergic dermatitis a. Mosquitoes b. Fleas c. Bugs d. Lice e. Itch mite (Sarcoptes scabiei) a. Mosquito dermatitis (Fig. 4) It is caused by a local allergic reaction against the salivary secretion of mosquitoes. This can proceed to severe allergic reactions in highly susceptible individuals. b. Flea dermatitis (Fig. 5) Fleas can cause discomfort and local allergic reactions. The lesion is reddish, oedematous, indurated or even pustular. c. Bug dermatitis Bed bugs crawl out at night to have a blood meal leading to annoyance, dermatitis (allergy to saliva) and anaemia. Page 5 of 10 Figure 4. Mosquito bites 980 × 735 Figure 5. Flea dermatitis d. Lice (Pediculosis) • The presence of body, head, or pubic lice on a person is sometimes referred to as pediculosis. • Three types of blood -sucking lice occur in humans, the body louse, the head louse and the pubic or crab louse. • Morphologically the body and head lice are indistinguishable. (Fig. 6). All three species of lice have a worldwide distribution, but they are often more common in temperate areas. • Body lice are vectors of louse-borne typhus and louse-born relapsing fever. The body louse Infestation of the skin by body lice causes chronic irritation of the skin by prolonged exposure to salivary secretions following frequent biting. The patient becomes hypersensitive, and the skin develops a peculiar form of dermatitis characterized by Page 6 of 10 bronzed pigmentation and pustular formation. Years of infe station lead to darkened skin; a condition known as vagabond’s disease. Control - Louse-infested clothing is subjected to a minimum temperature of 70 °C for at least an hour. - Insecticidal dusts, such as carbaryl, propoxur, malathion or permethrin applied to a person’s body. - Impregnation of clothing with a pyrethroid insecticide may provide long-lasting protection against louse infestations, and such treated clothing may remain effective after several washings. The head louse (Fig. 7) Head lice are a serious public health problem in some areas in the world and in many countries prevalence has been increasing. In some schools in the USA and the UK almost 50% of pupils have head lice. Often there are higher infestation rates in overcrowded homes and where hygiene is poor. Control - Regular combing with an ordinary comb, although not removing the eggs, may reduce the number of nymphs and adults. - A plastic louse comb is much better but may not remove all lice and their eggs. - Most commercial preparations for controlling head lice contain pyrethroids such as phenothrin or permethrin, or organophosphates such as malathion. Insecticidal formulations include dusts, emulsions and lotions. - Treatment should be repeated after 7 –10 days whatever insecticide is used, because it is difficult to kill all eggs with just a single application. - It is recommended that all members of a household are treated, not just those detected as having lice. The pubic louse Infestations of pubic lice are sometimes known as pediculosis pubis. Severe allergic reactions (pruritus) can develop in response to their bites, due to the injection of saliva and the deposition of feces around the feeding sites. Small characteristic bluish spots may appear on infested parts of the body. C

name: Notes - Myiasis
text: Page 1 of 6 L 20 Myiasis SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Define the term “Myiasis” considering causes and risks. 2. Distinguish the different types of myiasis according to the causes and clinical picture. 3. Correlate each type of myiasis to the possible complications. 4. Interpret the suitable treatment of each type of myiasis. 5. Deduce the preventive plan for myiasis. 6. Explain with evidences for myiasis in terms of harms and benefits. 1. Definition Myiasis is a zoonosis derived from the Greek word (mya, or fly) . Myiasis is the infestation of live vertebrates (humans and/or animals) with larvae of medium -sized and large dipterous flies. These larvae (Maggots) can feed on the host's living or dead tissue, liquid body substance, or ingested food. Risk factors Myiasis in humans is distributed world wide but more common in tropics and sub-tropical regions. Low socioeconomic state and poor hygienic measures are main risk factors. Myiasis is considered an important Traveler-associated skin disease. Nosocomial infestations are not uncommon. Causative agent Larvae of flies (Maggots) are the causative agents of myiasis. (Figure 1) Several types of flies can cause myiasis. (Figure 2) Classification of Myiasis Anatomical and ecological classifications are used to study myiasis. Figur e 2: Myiasis pr oducing flies Musca domestica Calliphora Lucilia Sarcophaga Wohlfahrtia Cordylobia Page 2 of 6 1. Anatomical classification: 2. Ecological classification: This is used to facilitate the clinical diagnosis depending on the location of the larvae in the body. This is used to understand the biological habits of myiasis -producing flies and hence design the suitable measures for prevention of myiasis. ➢ Cutaneous myiasis Furuncular Creeping (migratory) Wound ➢ Cavitary myiasis Intestinal Urogenital Cerebral Ophthalmic Aural Nasopharyngeal ➢ Specific/Obligatory myiasis ➢ Semi-specific/Facultative myiasis ➢ Accidental myiasis Anatomical classification: Cutaneous myiasis This is the most common clinical form of myiasis. 1. Furuncular myiasis The main clinical presentation in this form is a boil -like lesion (furuncle) that occurs due to penetration of healthy skin with the larvae of bot flies (screw worms) mainly Dermatobia hominis and Cordylobia anthropophaga. Wohlfahrtia s pp. were reported to cause furuncular lesions mainly in children.The larvae will remain and develop in the lesion until the time of pupation when they will drop out of the host to complete their life cycle. The main symptoms include pain, itching and movem ent sensation. The condition can be complicated by bacterial infection, sanguinopurulent discharge and can heal by hyperpigmentation. Figure 3 Page 3 of 6 2. Migratory (Creeping) myiasis This type of myiasis occurs when the maggots accidentally infest unnatural host. T hey start to migrate aimlessly in irregular (serpentine) tunnels under the skin of unnatural host.The larvae will not undergo any further development and will die in the tissues of the host. Figure 4 3. Wound myiasis This form of myiasis occurs when flies oviposit or larviposit on open wounds especially those necrotic and pus-filled. Wound myiasis is common in neglected individuals. Elderly debilitated patients, psychiatric illness, wars and human natural disasters are the common risk factors for wound myiasis. The condition can be complicated by destruction and deep invasion in tissues together with superadded bacterial infection. The most common flies causing wound myiasis are Sarcophaga, Lucilia and Calliphora flies. Cavitary myiasis This term applies to infestation of body cavities and internal organs with maggots. 1. Intestinal myiasis Intestinal infestation with maggots occurs accidentally when ingesting food or drinks contaminated with eggs or larvae of flies. The condition is facilitated by low gastric acidity. The passage of larvae in stool samples is diagnostic. Larvae can pass to t he intestinal passages up from anal orifice while sleeping outdoors (naked children) or by the use of open latrines. The condition can be associated with nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain. Pruritus ani and rectal bleeding are not uncommon. Common flies causing intestinal myiasis are Musca domestica and Fannia spp. 2. Urogenital myiasis This is a form of accidental myiasis where the flies deposit their eggs or larvae on the external urinary or genital orifices. Maggots can cause lesions in the external genitalia or ascends up and cause internal urogenital myiasis. The condition is more common in females and children. The main risk factors are low hygienic measures, the use of open latrines and sleeping outdoors, especially children lacking underwear. The main clinical presentations include dysuria, haematuria, pruritus and ureteric obstruction and all are relieved by extrusion of maggots in urine. Page 4 of 6 3. Ophthalmomyiasis This condition is considered when there is a foreign body sensation in the eye with an abrupt pain. The conjunctiva is mostly affected. Redness, excessive lacrimation and superadded infection are the main clinical presentation. Oestrus spp. (sheep flies) are the main agents responsible and the condition can be more common in shepherds, children and neglected debilitated individuals. Other flies can be also responsible as: Lucilia, Calliphora and Wohlfahrtia. The main complications are superadded bacterial infection, deep invasion in the orbital tissues, panophthalmitis and cerebral myiasis. 4. Aural myiasis Flies deposit the eggs or larvae in the external auditory canal and the larvae can cause otitis externa or otitis media with foreign body sensation, otalgia, otorrhea and rarely perforation of the tympanic membrane. Deeper invasion into the surrounding tissues and cerebral myiasis are the main complications. 5. Nasopharyngeal and oral myiasis Neglected, debilitated patients, low socioeconomic conditions, sleeping outdoors and chronic cases of atrophic rhinitis are the main predisposing factors with these types of myiasis. Pain, nasal bleeding and mucopurulent discharge are the main symptoms and the main fatal complication is deeper invasion and cerebral myiasis. Ecological classification: Specific/Obligatory myiasis The fly is obligatory dependent on the host to complete its life cycle and the larvae are usually provided with strong and sharp mouth parts to screw into healthy host tissues. The larvae feed on the host till the time of pupation and then drop out to complete its life cycle. Dermatobia hominis and Cordylobia anthropophaga are the main examples causing furuncular myiasis in humans. Hypoderma and Gastrophilus flies cause specific creeping myiasis in man. Risk factors: Moving with bare feet or sitting naked on sandy soil soaked with urine. The flies are attracted and deposit their eggs on these areas and hence the eggs hatch and larvae are attracted to the warmth of the skin. Larvae penetrate healthy skin with their sharp mouth parts and cause furuncular lesion. Wearing clothes soaked with urine that were left to dry outdoors without being ironed. The eggs deposited on the clothes will hatch releasing the maggots that can invade the skin. Semi-specific/Facultative myiasis In this type of myiasis the fly leads a non parasitic life but it is attracted to necrotic tissues and purulent discharges from neglected wounds and ulcers. The fly deposits its eggs or larvae on neglected these necrotic tissues and larvae feed on these tissues till the time of pupation and they leave the host to complete their life cycle. Page 5 of 6 Larvae of Sarcophaga, Lucilia and Calliphora can cause semispecific myiasis. Note: Cavitary myiasis can be either specific if healthy tissues were invaded by the fly larvae or non - specific if myiasis occurs on top of neglected wounds or ulcers.
