name: PDF - Practical parasitology class 3 notes
text: Page 1 of 18 P APPROACH TO DIAGNOSIS OF PARASITIC INFECTIONS SLOs By the end of this practical class, students will be able to 1. Determine the diagnostic approach for parasitic infections. 2. Select the appropriate sample according to the patient’s clinical manifestations. 3. Recognize different methods for parasite detection. 4. Identify the arthropods of medical importance. Introduction Diagnosis of parasitic infections can be achieved by: 1. History taking which includes travel history to endemic places, the patient's geographic location, history of exposure to contaminated water or arthropod bites, and family history. 2. Clinical diagnosis depends on the characteristic signs and symptoms related to the parasitic infection, such as diarrhea, dysentery, or blood in the stool or urine. 3. Laboratory diagnosis can be obtained by the following methods: • Direct methods: include macroscopic and microscopic examination of the patient’s samples. • Indirect methods: include immunological tests. • Molecular methods. Laboratory diagnosis of parasitic infections I. Direct methods for diagnosis of parasitic infections: This is based on the examination of excreta, body fluids, and tissues and the visualization of the different diagnostic stages of parasites. The samples examined could be one of the following: stool, urine, aspirates, sputum, biopsy, and blood. A. Stool Examination: It aids in the identification of parasite infections of the small and large intestines, as well as the biliary tract. Samples should be collected in a wide- mouthed container with a screw top. The sample should not be contaminated with urine or water because urine can kill some parasites and water can contain ciliates, which can lead to false diagnosis. It is also important to ensure that the patient is not receiving antibiotics or has had a barium enema, as both will hide any parasitic infection. Three stool samples should be examined as one sample every other day. 1. Macroscopic Examination a. The consistency should be noted whether formed, semi-formed, or liquid, since trophic forms of protozoa are found in liquid or diarrheic stools, while cystic forms are found more in the formed and semi-formed samples. b. The composition of the sample is also important whether there is blood and/or mucus a Page 2 of 18 such as in dysentery. c. The colour is pale as in steatorrhoeic conditions, e.g., Giardia lamblia infection. It can also be black or red in colour when iron is taken or when there is intestinal haemorrhage. d. The presence of adult parasites or segments is also diagnostic (Figure 1 ). Figure 1: a. Segments of Taenia worm (cestode), b. adult Ascaris (nematode). 2. Microscopic Examination a. Direct Saline Smear: It is prepared by mixing a small portion of stool with a drop of normal saline. It is most useful for the detection of motility of protozoa, e.g., Trophozoites of amoeba and Giardia lamblia, if the stool sample is examined within one hour after discharge (Figure 2). Helminthic eggs may also be seen if they are present in large numbers (Figures 3-5). Figure 2: Protozoan Trophozoite in Saline Smear (Giardia lamblia). b a Page 3 of 18 Eggs Eggs of Trematodes (Figure 3) • Operculated (a) or provided with a spine (b) • Mature or immature (may or may not contain a fully developed embryo called miracidium) Figure 3: Eggs of Trematodes Eggs of Cestodes (Figure 4) • Mature • Contain the hexacanth embryo (Oncosphere). • The embryo has six hooks. Figure 4: Eggs of Cestodes a b Page 4 of 18 Eggs of Nematodes (Figure 5) • Medium-sized eggs • Immature or mature containing embryo (larva) • Oval or barrel-shaped • Non-operculated, non- spined Figure 5: Eggs of Nematodes b. Iodine Smear In this method stool samples are emulsified in 1% iodine solution. The iodine stains the cysts of protozoa revealing their details (Figure 6). Its main disadvantage is that the trophozoites are rapidly killed by the iodine and therefore become non-motile. Figure 6: Protozoan Cyst Stained with Iodine (Giardia lamblia) Direct saline smear and iodine smear are useful only when helminth eggs and protozoa are in large numbers. If they are scarce or scanty then concentration techniques are required. The concentration methods fall into two general categories: sedimentation and floatation methods. Page 5 of 18 c. Concentration Techniques i. Sedimentation Methods Principle: Most helminthic eggs and protozoal cysts are heavier than the suspending liquid and so they sink and concentrate at the bottom of the tube i.e sediment, which is taken and examined. • Formol Ether Concentration Technique It includes centrifugation of the stool sample after the addition of ether and formalin (Figure 7). The ether adsorbs the faecal debris which becomes lighter than water and floats to the top, while the addition of formalin fixes and preserves the specimens. Figure 7: Formol Ether Concentration Technique. ii. Floatation Method Principle: This involves the use of solutions that have a higher specific gravity than the organisms to be floated so that the organisms rise to the top and the debris sinks to the bottom giving a cleaner preparation. The floatation procedure permits the separation of protozoan cysts and eggs of some helminths by using concentrated saline or zinc sulphate solution. The main disadvantage is that heavy eggs and operculated eggs do not concentrate well with this technique. d. Permanent Stained Smears: These can be used for the identification of intestinal protozoa (Figures 8- 10). Protozoa Phylum Sarcomastigophora Sub-phylum Sarcodina • They have two stages: trophozoites and cysts. • Trophozoites move with the aid of pseudopodia. • e.g: Entamoeba histolytica (Figure 8). Page 6 of 18 Figure 8: a. Entamoeba histolytica trophozoite with a vesicular single nucleus and pseudopodia, b. Entamoeba histolytica cyst with multiple nuclei. Sub-phylum Mastigophora (Flagellates) • Trophozoites move by the aid of hair-like structures called flagella. • e.g: Giardia lamblia (Figure 9). Figure 9: a. Giardia lamblia trophozoite with flagella, b. Giardia lamblia cyst. Phylum Ciliophora (Ciliates) • Trophozoites move with the aid of cilia, which are short hair-like structures. • e.g: Balantidium coli (Figure 10). a b Nucleus a b Page 7 of 18 Figure 10: Trophozoite of Balantidium coli with a single kidney-shaped nucleus (green arrow) and cilia (red arrows). Phylum Apicomplexa • They do not have a specific organ of locomotion. e. Additional Techniques Used for Identification of Intestinal Parasites i. Quantitative Estimation of Helminthic Ova in Stools: Correlation of egg production with adult worm burden is possible in intestinal nematodes, e.g., Ascaris lumbricoides. Estimation of the intensity of infection of schistosomes as a test of cure after treatment is also important. • Kato Katz Technique (Figure 11) In this technique a portion of a sieved stool sample is transferred to a hole of a template on a slide. After filling the hole, the template is removed, and the sample is covered with a piece of cellophane soaked in glycerine to clear the fecal material from around the eggs. The eggs, e.g., Schistosoma eggs, are then counted and the egg number per gram of faeces is calculated. Page 8 of 18 Figure 11: Kato Katz Technique ii. Adhesive Tape Technique (Cellotape): This is used to diagnose Enterobius vermicularis eggs in the perianal region. It is best done in the morning before bathing. Perianal swab is performed using the adhesive surface of cellophane tape that is pressed against the perianal skin at several places (Figure 12). Then it is placed on a slide and examined microscopically. Figure 12: Adhesive Tape Technique. B. Urine Examination 1. Macroscopic Examination The colour of urine can aid in the preliminary diagnosis of a parasitic infection (Figure 13). Page 9 of 18 a. Smoky urine denotes the presence of blood, and this can mask Schistosoma haematobium eggs. A drop of diluted acetic acid causes haemolysis of the red

name: PDF: L21  Hepatitis Viruses (B, D)
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 10 21 HEPATITIS VIRUSES (B, D) ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Analyze the molecular biology and structural characteristics of HBV and HDV to explain their replication cycles and mechanisms of therapeutic resistance. 2. Differentiate between the immunopathological mechanisms driving acute liver injury, extrahepatic immune-complex manifestations, and age-dependent chronicity in viral hepatitis. 3. Interpret complex virologic and serologic profiles to classify chronic hepatitis B infection phases (Phases 1–4, occult infection, window period) and guide clinical disease management. 4. Formulate appropriate evidence-based strategies for treatment, pre-exposure vaccination, and post-exposure prophylaxis for HBV and HDV in diverse clinical scenarios. HEPATITIS B VIRUS Structure - HBV is the major member of the hepadnaviruses. Other members of this family include woodchuck, ground squirrel, and duck hepatitis viruses. HBV infects the liver and, to a lesser extent, the kidneys and pancreas of only humans and chimpanzees. - HBV is a small enveloped DNA virus. Specifically, the genome is a small, circular, partly double-stranded DNA. Although a DNA virus, it encodes a reverse transcriptase and replicates through an RNA intermediate. - The virion, also called the Dane particle, is 42 nm in diameter. The virions are unusually stable for an enveloped virus. They resist treatment with ether, low pH, freezing, and moderate heating. These characteristics assist transmission from one person to another and hamper disinfection. - The viral genome encodes four overlapping open reading frames (ORFs), C, P , S, and X, from which funcQonal viral proteins are produced: o Hepatitis B Core antigen HBc and its relatives such as E antigen (HBe); HBc: viral capsid protein which is only present inside hepatocytes and detected in liver biopsies and not detected in serum. HBe; It is secreted in a soluble form and detected only in infected patient’s serum. o Pol from P (Polymerase with reverse transcriptase and ribonuclease H acQvity); o three types of Surface an@gens, L-HBs, M-HBs, and S-HBs, (Large, medium and small) from S; o HBV X protein (HBx) from X. Regulatory protein for transcription and is required for initiation of infection. It can be detected only in the cells replicating the virus. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 10 Figure 1. Structure and genome organiza3on of Hepa33s B virus Replica@on - The aYachment of HBV to hepatocytes is mediated by the HBsAg glycoproteins. - On penetraQon into the cell, the nucleocapsid delivers the genome to the nucleus, where the parQal DNA strand of the genome is completed to form a complete double-stranded DNA circle (covalently closed circular DNA; cccDNA) - TranscripQon of the genome is controlled by cellular transcripQon elements found in hepatocytes. - Viral genome can be integrated randomly in the host genome. This is not required for viral replicaQon but it is one of the important mechanisms for hepatocyte transformaQon and HCC development. - Viral genome is subjected to frequent muta@ons leading to existence of disQnct viral species in infected individuals. Figure 2. Replica3on of HBV Pathogenesis & Immunity HBV can cause acute or chronic, symptomatic or asymptomatic disease. Which of these occurs seems to be determined by the person’s immune response to the infection. The major source of infectious virus is blood, but HBV can be found in semen, saliva, milk, vaginal secretions, and amniotic fluid. The most efficient way to acquire HBV is through: (1) injection of the virus into the bloodstream [Per-cutaneous transmission including intramuscular, intravenous, NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 10 subcutaneous or intra-dermal injections, tattooing, ear piercing and needle stick. Contamination of skin lesions (fresh cutaneous scratch, abrasion and burns). Infected blood and blood products through transfusion or dialysis. (2) Common but less efficient routes of infection are sexual contact and birth (Perinatal transmission when mothers are HBsAg positive due to leak of maternal blood to infant’s circulation during birth. Transplacental transmission is rare). The virus starts to replicate in hepatocytes of the liver within 3 days of its acquisition, with minimal cytopathic effect. Symptoms may not be observed for 45 days or longer because they are primarily caused by immunopathology. The infectious dose, the route of infection, and the person determine the incubation period. Infection proceeds for a relatively long time without causing liver damage (i.e., elevation of liver enzyme levels) or symptoms. Copies of the HBV genome integrate into the hepatocyte DNA and can remain latent. HBsAg particles continue to be released into the blood even after virion release has ended and until the infection is resolved. An individual is infectious when both the HBsAg and the HBeAg components of the virion can be detected in the blood. Cell-mediated immunity and inflammation are responsible for causing the symptoms and effecting resolution of the HBV infection by eliminating the infected hepatocyte. An insufficient T-cell response to the infection generally results in the occurrence of mild symptoms, an inability to resolve the infection, and development of chronic hepatitis. Chronic infection also exhausts CD8 T cells, preventing them from killing infected cells. Infants and young children have an immature cell- mediated immune response and are less able to resolve the infection, but they suffer less tissue damage and milder symptoms. As many as 90% of infants infected perinatally become chronic carriers. Viral replication persists in these people for long periods. Antibodies can protect against initial infection by preventing delivery of the virus to the liver. Later in the infection, the large amount of HBsAg in serum binds to and blocks the action of neutralizing antibody, which limits the antibody’s ability to resolve an infection. Immune complexes formed between HBsAg and anti-HBs contribute to the development of hypersensitivity reactions (type III), leading to problems such as vasculitis, arthralgia, rash, and renal damage. Antibodies to HBc and HBe are present in serum but are nonprotective. The HBeAg protein, like HBsAg, is released into serum, and during its production, anti-HBe is bound to the antigen and undetectable. The HBc antigen is present in cells or virions and inaccessible to the antibody in blood. As a result, anti-HBc is detectable upon production, throughout and after the course of the infection. Genetic variability of HBV: The lack of reverse transcriptase proofreading activity leads to frequent mutations of the viral genome. This results in the coexistence of genetically distinct viral species in infected individuals, also called viral quasispecies, which evolve depending on the pressure from the host environment. The interplay between the virus, hepatocyte and the immune response or antiviral treatment is thought to drive the emergence of HBV mutants that have the capacity to escape immune responses or antiviral treatments. Analysis of genome-wide nucleotide divergence has allowed for the identification of nine genotypes (A-I) and several sub-genotypes. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. It may also progress to chronic infection, particularly if transmitted from mother to child or acquired during childhood or adolescence. In contrast, progression to chronic HBV infection is rare when infection occurs in immunocompetent adults. text: PRINCIPLES OF INFECTION PREVENTION & CONTROL IN HEALTHCARE SETTINGS (Part 1) Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Tutorial 5 Dear students & Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Define standard precautions and their application in all patient care settings 2. Describe the importance of hand hygiene and its role in breaking the chain of infection. 3. Demonstrate proper techniques for hand hygiene (handwashing and alcohol-based hand rub). 4. Explain indications for PPE, including gloves, masks, gowns. 5. Explain the different types of PPE and their appropriate use. 6. Discuss the donning and doffing procedures for PPE. 7. Identify factors to consider when selecting PPE. 8. Describe the three types of transmission-based precautions: contact, droplet, and airborne. 9. Describe respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette 10.Recognize safe sharp practices. DEFINITIONS • Standard precautions are the minimum infection prevention and control practices that apply to ALL patient care, which should be followed to reduce the transmission of healthcare - associated infections (HAI) in any setting where health care is delivered. These practices are designed to protect both health care worker (HCW) and prevent HCW from spreading infections among patients. • They should be used by ALL health care workers at ALL times when attending to ALL patients, regardless of suspected or confirmed infection status of the patient. • Standard precautions apply to blood, all body fluids , secretions and excretions (except sweat), non-intact skin and mucous membranes. Body fluids include CSF , pleural fluid, peritoneal fluid and amniotic fluid. Secretions include nasal secretions, sputum, tears and saliva. Excretions include faeces, urine and vomitus. Standard precautions include: 1. Hand hygiene 2. Personal protective equipment 3. Respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette 4. Sharps safety and safe injection practices 5. Cleaning, disinfection and sterilization of instruments and equipment 6. Aseptic techniques 7. Environmental cleaning and disinfection 8. Linen management 9. Waste management HAND HYGIENE • Hand hygiene is the most effective measure to prevent healthcare associated infections (HAI) as transmission of pathogens mainly occurs via health care workers’ hands. • Any person involved in patient care needs to be concerned about hand hygiene to: • Protect the patient from pathogens carried on their hands • Protect themselves from pathogens • Protect the health-care environment from pathogens Hand Hygiene Agents • Soap and water • Hand washing with soap and running water is essential when hands are visibly dirty or visibly soiled with body fluids. • Liquid soap is better than bar soap. However, refilling of empty containers should be discouraged. • If only bar soap is available, provide small pieces which should be just adequate for the day. Place on a clean drainable rack or soap dish so that no water is retained Hand Hygiene Agents • Alcohol hand rub • The preferred preparation for routine hand hygiene if hands are not visibly soiled. • Has a good immediate activity but residual activity is poor. • Does not require drying with a towel, or a designated area for hand washing. • A commercial product with adequate quality control is recommended. • Solutions containing 75-85%(v/v) of isopropyl alcohol or ethanol are effective. Hand Hygiene Agents • Other agents • These agents are preferred during outbreaks of HAI. • 4% w/v chlorhexidine gluconate (has a good residual activity) • 7.5% povidone iodine Just Read Just Read • Gloves do not replace the need for hand hygiene. • Hand hygiene is required before putting on gloves and immediately after removing gloves. • Hand hygiene products should not be applied to gloves. PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT • Personal protective equipment (PPE) refers to a variety of barriers used alone or in combination to protect mucous membranes, airways, skin and clothing from contact with infectious agents. • When indicated, PPE should be selected rationally and appropriately based on the anticipated risk of exposure. • It is necessary to provide appropriate types, sizes and styles of protective equipment. • Each institution should have a regular risk assessment for every health care procedure. PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT (PPE) • Gloves – protect hands • Gowns/aprons protect skin and/or clothing • Masks– protect mouth/nose • Respirators protect respiratory tract • Goggles protect eyes • Face shields protect face, mouth, nose & eyes What is Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)? ▪ “specialized clothing or equipment worn by an employee for protection against infectious materials” (OSHA) ▪ “provides a physical barrier between micro- organisms and the wearer ” (WHO, 2004)

name: PDF: Part II
ref: file:T5 Principles of Infection prevention  control in healthcare settings (part 2).pdf
text: PRINCIPLES OF INFECTION PREVENTION & CONTROL IN HEALTHCARE SETTINGS (Part 2) Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Tutorial 5 Dear students & Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Define aseptic technique and its principles. 2. Explain the importance of aseptic technique in various procedures, such as injections, wound care, and catheter insertion. 3. Apply the steps involved in performing aseptic techniques. ASEPTIC TECHNIQUES Any time we touch a patient we put them at risk for an infection! Terminology ▪ Asepsis – A process of keeping away disease producing microorganism. ▪ Aseptic technique -are practices that are designed to minimize the risk of introducing microorganisms to patients during patient care. It includes practice techniques just before , during and or after any invasive patient procedures. ▪ Antiseptic agent- an antimicrobial substance applied to the skin to reduce the number of microbialflora. AsepticT echnique • Protect patients from acquiring microorganisms from the HCWs skin and environment. Patients • Protect HCW from acquiring microorganisms from the patient and environment Health Care Workers (HCW) • Reduce risk ofinfection transmission Community& others Who are at risk? What is Aseptic Technique? • Aseptic technique aims to prevent pathogenic organisms , in sufficient quantity to cause infection, from being introduced to susceptible sites by hands, surfaces and equipment. (National Health and Medical Research Council, 2010) • Aseptic technique protects patients during invasive clinical procedures by employing infection control measures that minimise, as far as practicably possible, the presence of pathogenic microorganisms. Definition of a Safe Aseptic Technique • Does not harm the recipient, • Does not expose the provider to any avoidable risks, • Does not result in any waste that is dangerous for other people. Outcome: - Quality & Safety of Healthcare - Saves resources. • There are two categories of asepsis; • (1) General asepsis which applies to patient care procedures outside the operating theatre and • (2) Surgical asepsis relating to procedures/processes designed to prevent surgical site infection. This lecture will focus primarily on general aseptic procedures as insertion of intravenous catheters or urinary catheters and examples of “no-touch” technique. Preventing Infections using Aseptic Technique • There are several key Infection Control components to consider when performing any invasive procedure: A. Environmental Control B. Hand Hygiene C. PPE Selection D. Aseptic Field Management E. Preparation of the patient for an invasive procedure F. Non-touch technique G. Sequencing A. Environmental Control • Prior to aseptic procedures, clinicians must ensure that there are no avoidable nearby environmental risk factors, this might include (but is not limited to): 1. Use a designated special area or physical barrier e.g. for: • treatment, • procedure • or operating rooms. 2. Control activities to reduce: Airborne transmission and Distraction if procedures are performed at bedside. 3. Keep doors closed during procedures. Post a sign outside the door! 4. Limit traffic or excludes visitor and unnecessary personnel. 5. Avoid cleaning activities in the area during invasive procedures. Creating and maintaining a safe environment 1) Routine cleaning of the environment 2) Using clean equipment and supplies ( mops, water, cleaning cloths). 3) Using environmental protection agency (EPA) registered hospital detergent , disinfectants and germicides. B. HandHygiene C. Protective Personal Equipment (PPE) Glove use • Gloves are single-use items. • If it is necessary to touch key parts or key sites directly, sterile gloves must be used to minimise the risk of contamination. • If key parts or key sites are not touched directly non -sterile gloves may be necessary to protect the clinician from blood or body fluids or exposure to toxic drugs during administration. • Gloves do not replace the need for hand hygiene . Hand hygiene must be performed before and after glove use. • Selection of sterile or non -sterile gloves is also dependent upon clinician competency. • When preparing for the procedure clinicians should assess their own competence and experience in performing the procedure and determine whether touching of key parts or sites is required. • If touching may take place sterile gloves are required. Other PPE • Protective Personal Equipment (other than gloves) may be required if indicated to reduce the risk of blood and body fluid exposure to the clinician. • Maximum barrier precautions may be required during some procedures (such as CVC insertion) to reduce the risk to the patient of acquiring a healthcare associated infection. D. Aseptic Field Management • Prior to commencing a procedure requiring AT , it is imperative the clinician determines the aseptic field required and how that field will need to be managed. • The aseptic field must be managed to ensure that key parts and key sites are protected. • The aseptic field should be prepared as close as possible to the time of actual use. D. Aseptic Field Management • The clinician should select a tray or trolley of an appropriate size to ensure key parts are adequately contained within the aseptic field. • The tray or trolley must be cleaned appropriately and allowed to dry before placing any items in or on the tray or trolley. If a surface remains wet then asepsis will be compromised. • The aseptic field may also need to be extended by draping the patient . The sterile drape will provide additional work space where sterile equipment may be placed as well as protecting the key site from contamination. Preventing Infections using Aseptic Technique • Correct Aseptic Technique prevents contamination and transfer of pathogens from hands, surfaces and equipment to the patient during procedures. • Correct Aseptic Technique requires key parts and key sites to be identified and protected at all times. • Key parts must only come into contact with other key parts and / or key sites.

name: Notes - Basic concepts of infection
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 5 1 BASIC CONCEPTS OF INFECTION ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Explain the cellular and biological characteristics that distinguish major groups of medically important microorganisms and relate them to their clinical significance. 2. Differentiate resident, transient, and potentially pathogenic microbiota in relation to colonization and disease. 3. Analyze the microbiota of different body sites to distinguish normal colonization from findings suggestive of infection. 4. Apply the principles of colonization resistance, dysbiosis, and opportunistic infection to clinical situations involving disruption of normal microbiota or host barriers. MICROBIAL WORLD The spectrum of infection has widened, with discoveries that organisms earlier thought to be harmless can cause disease under certain circumstances. Who could have guessed that Helicobacter pylori, would be the major cause of gastric and duodenal ulcers and an officially declared carcinogen? Moreover, bioterrorist forces have unearthed two previously controlled infectious diseases—anthrax and smallpox—and threatened their distribution as agents of biological warfare. For students of medicine, understanding the fundamental basis of infectious diseases has more relevance than ever. The science of medical microbiology dates back to the pioneering studies of Pasteur and Koch, who isolated specific agents and proved that they could cause disease by introducing the experimental method. Microbiology is the study of all living organisms that are too small to be visible with the naked eye. This includes bacteria, archaea, viruses, fungi, prions, protozoa and algae, collectively known as 'microbes'. These microbes play key roles in nutrient cycling, biodegradation/biodeterioration, climate change, food spoilage, the cause and control of disease, and biotechnology. The major classes of microorganisms in terms of ascending size and complexity are prions, viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites. All organisms other than viruses and prions are made up of cells. Although viruses have genetic material (DNA or RNA) they are not cellular, lacking cell membranes, cytoplasm and the machinery for synthesizing macromolecules, depending instead upon host cells for this process. The agents (prions) lack nucleic acid and consist only of infectious proteinaceous particles. All other organisms have a cellular organization, being made up of single cells (most ‘microbes’) or of many cells. Each cell has genetic material (DNA) and cytoplasm with synthetic machinery, and is bounded by a cell membrane. Bacteria are prokaryotes; all other organisms are eukaryotes. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 5 Figure 1. Size of microbes Table 1. Differences between eukaryotes and prokaryotes. Eukaryotic cell Prokaryotic cell Cell size Large (10-100 µm) Small (0.5-5 µm) Organism type Multicellular Unicellular Nucleus Present (membrane bound) Absent (nucleoid region) Replication Mitotic division Binary fission Membrane bounds organelles e.g mitochondria, lysosomes Present Absent Ribosomes Large (80S) Small (70S) Cytoplasm Present Present Plasma membrane Present Present Cell wall Simple (present in fungi) Peptidoglycan (present in all prokaryotes) HUMAN MICROBIOTA The presence of microbes on or in humans is not, by itself, abnormal. In fact, from shortly after birth on, it is universal; Current estimates indicate that the numbers of microbial and human cells are of the same order of magnitude, with an approximate ratio close to 1:1. This population formerly called the normal flora is now referred to as our microbiota or microbiome. These microorganisms, which are overwhelmingly bacteria, are frequently found colonizing various body sites in healthy individuals. The constituents and numbers of the microbiota vary in different areas of the body and, sometimes, at different ages and physiologic states. Thus, each accessible area of the body presents a particular ecologic niche, colonization of which requires a particular set of properties of the colonizing microbe. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 5 Organisms of the microbiota may have a symbiotic relationship that benefits the host or may simply live as commensals with a neutral relationship to the host. The members of the human microbiota may stay for highly variable periods; 1) Residents are strains that have an established niche at one of the many body sites, which they occupy indefinitely. 2)Transients are acquired from the environment and establish themselves briefly, but they tend to be excluded by competition from residents or by the host’s innate or immune defense mechanisms. The term carrier state is used when organisms known to be potentially pathogenic are involved, although its implication of risk is not always justified. For example, Streptococcus pneumoniae, a cause of pneumonia, and Neisseria meningitidis, a cause of meningitis, may be isolated from the throat of 5% to 40% of healthy people. Whether these bacteria represent transient flora, resident flora, or carrier state is largely semantic. It is important to understand the role of the microbiota because of its significance both as a defense mechanism against infection and as a source of potentially pathogenic organisms. In addition, it is important for physicians to know the typical composition of the microbiota at various sites to avoid confusion when interpreting laboratory culture results. The composition of the human microbiota is dynamic and is influenced by age, diet, geography, medications (especially antibiotics), hormones, disease, immune status, and environmental exposures. Microbiota at different body sites 1. Blood, Body Fluids, and Tissues In health, the blood, body fluids, and tissues are sterile. Occasional organisms may be displaced across epithelial barriers as a result of trauma or during childbirth; they may be briefly recoverable from the bloodstream before they are filtered out in the pulmonary capillaries or removed by cells of the reticuloendothelial system. Such transient bacteremia may be the source of infection when structures such as damaged heart valves and foreign bodies (prostheses) are in the bloodstream. 2. Skin The skin surface provides a dry, slightly acidic, aerobic environment. It plays host to an abundant flora that varies according to the presence of its appendages (hair, nails) and the activity of sebaceous and sweat glands. The flora is more abundant on moist skin areas (axillae, perineum, and between toes). e.g. Staphylococci, Propionibacterium, and diphtheroids. Even with antiseptic scrubbing, it is difficult to eliminate bacteria from skin sites, particularly those bearing pilosebaceous units. Organisms of the skin flora are resistant to the bactericidal effects of skin lipids and fatty acids, which inhibit or kill many extraneous bacteria. 3. Gastrointestinal tract The mouth and pharynx contain large numbers of facultative and anaerobic bacteria. The stomach contains few, if any, resident organisms in health because of the lethal action of gastric hydrochloric acid and peptic enzymes on bacteria. The small intestine has a scanty resident flora, except in the lower ileum, where it begins to resemble that of the colon. The colon carries the most abundant and diverse microbiota in the body. In the adult, feces are 25% or more bacteria by weight (about 1010 organisms per gram). More than NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 4 of 5 90% are anaerobes. The remainder of the flora is composed of facultative organisms such as Escherichia coli, enterococci, and numerous other species. There are considerable differences in adult gut flora depending on the diet of the host. Those whose diets include substantial amounts of meat have more Bacteroides and other anaerobic gram-negative rods in their stools than those on a p

name: PDF: L22 Hepatitis Viruses (A, C, E)
text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 10 22 HEPATITIS VIRUSES (C, A, E) ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Analyze the structural, genomic, and replication characteristics of Hepatitis A, C, and E viruses to explain their mechanisms of antigenic variation, environmental stability, and therapeutic targets. 2. Apply principles of viral immunopathopathology to differentiate between the natural history, clinical syndromes, extrahepatic manifestations, and acute versus chronic disease outcomes of HAV, HCV, and HEV infections. 3. Interpret virologic, serologic, and molecular diagnostic profiles to accurately determine infection phases, guide post-exposure protocols, and assess therapeutic cure. 4. Formulate evidence-based prevention and management strategies, incorporating direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens, immunoprophylaxis protocols, and infection control measures for viral hepatitis. HEPATITIS C VIRUS Structure & Replication - HCV is the only member of the Hepacivirus genus of the Flaviviridae family. - HCV has a positive-sense RNA genome, and is enveloped. - The genome encodes 10 proteins, including 3 structural [one core protein and two glycoproteins (E1, E2)] as well as 7 non-structural proteins. The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase is error prone and generates mutations in the glycoprotein and other genes. This generates antigenic variability. Such variability makes development of a vaccine very difficult. - There are seven major genotypes (1-7) of HCV (clades), and between and within each genotype there is considerable genetic and antigenic diversity. Different genotypes predominate in different parts of the world. Genotype 4a is the most common in Egypt. HCV Genetic diversity is not correlated with differences in clinical disease, although differences exist in response to antiviral therapy. Figure 1. Structure and genome organization of HCV NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 10 Pathogenesis & Immunity - HCV is transmitted primarily in infected blood and sexually. Intravenous drug abusers and tattoo recipients are at highest risk to HCV infection. Screening procedures have led to a reduction in the levels of transmission by blood transfusion and organ donation. Almost all (>90%) HIV-infected people who are or were intravenous drug users are infected with HCV. - The high incidence of chronic asymptomatic infections promotes the spread of the virus in the population. - The ability of HCV to remain cell associated and prevent host cell death promotes persistent infection but results in liver disease later in life. - The virus’s ability to evade interferon action and change its antigenicity help the virus establish chronic disease. - Cell-mediated immune responses are necessary to resolve the infection but also cause tissue damage. - Antibody to HCV is not protective. Due to the selective pressure from the host, and the antigenic variations that occur in the E2/E1 proteins, the virus evade the humoral immune response and establish a persistent infection. - HCV antibodies have also been implicated in the formation of immune complexes against the liver and other tissues. During acute infection, the rise in serum transaminases is due to immune-mediated hepatocyte damage. The immune complexes are also deposited in other tissues and cause extrahepatic complications, including vasculitis, arthritis, glomerulonephritis, and others. - Chronic HCV infection results in inflammatory response that may lead to progressive fibrosis and hepatocarcinogenesis. - The chronic infection can exhaust CD8 cytotoxic T cells so they cannot resolve the infection. Clinical syndromes - A viremia can be detected within 1 to 3 weeks of infection. The viremia lasts 4 to 6 months in people with an acute infection and longer than 10 years in those with a persistent infection. - The incubation period ranges from 2 weeks to 6 months. - HCV has the highest rate of chronicity (> 75%). - More commonly (>70% of cases), the initial disease is asymptomatic or clinically mild (20–30% have jaundice; 10–20% have only nonspecific symptoms such as anorexia, malaise, and abdominal pain) but establishes chronic persistent disease. The predominant symptom is chronic fatigue. Chronic persistent disease often progresses to chronic active hepatitis within 10 to 15 years and to cirrhosis (20% of chronic cases) and liver failure (20% of cirrhotic cases) after 20 years. HCV promotes the development of hepatocellular carcinoma after 30 years in up to 5% of chronically infected patients. Virologic and serologic Response - Currently available HCV antibody tests have a window period from exposure to HCV to detection of antibody of approximately 8-11 weeks. Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAT) can detect HCV RNA approximately 1-2 weeks after exposure. This means that for the first eight weeks following exposure to HCV antibody tests may not be able to detect HCV antibodies, and for the first 1-2 weeks following HCV exposure NATs may not be able to detect HCV RNA. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 10 - In chronic hepatitis C, serum ALT concentrations may fluctuate over time and may even be intermittently normal. HCV RNA may persist for decades. Diagnosis is confirmed by finding positive anti-HCV and positive HCV-RNA for ≥ 6 months after initial infection. Figure 2. Serological events associated with HCV infection. Laboratory Diagnosis 1. Nucleic acid-based assays (eg, RT- PCR) detect the presence of circulating HCV RNA and are useful for diagnosis of acute infection soon after exposure and for monitoring patients on antiviral therapy (Confirm sustained virologic response (SVR) following treatment). Nucleic acid assays also are used to genotype HCV isolates. 2. Serologic assays are available for diagnosis of HCV infection. Seroconversion occurs within 3-6 months of infection. Antibodies are directed against core, and NS3, NS4 and NS5 proteins and tend to be relatively low in titer. Serological assays include: enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), chemiluminescence immunoassay (CIA) and point of care immunoassay tests employing multiple HCV antigens. Detection of HCV antibodies does not distinguish between acute, chronic, or resolved infection. N.B. SVR= defined as no detectable HCV-RNA at 12 or more weeks after completion of treatment. It indicates the infection has been eradicated, and the virus is highly unlikely to return, marking a viral cure. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 4 of 10 Figure 3. Recommended testing for identifying current HCV infection. (Reference. CDC) CDC Guidelines for Health Care Provider (HCP) exposed to Hepatitis C Virus (1) Test the source patient as soon as possible (preferably within 48 hours) after exposure by using Nucleic Acid Test (NAT) for HCV RNA (preferred option) or Hepatitis C antibody test (anti-HCV) with reflex to NAT if positive. • If the source patient is positive for HCV RNA, refer the patient for further care. • Follow-up testing of HCP is recommended if the source patient is: - HCV RNA positive, OR - Anti-HCV positive with HCV RNA status unknown, OR - Cannot be tested. (2) Test the HCP: Simultaneous with source-patient testing, test the HCP as soon as possible (preferably within 48 hours) after exposure. • At baseline, test the HCP with an HCV antibody test with reflex to NAT for HCV RNA if positive. • If follow-up testing is recommended based on the source patient status, conduct a test 3–6 weeks after exposure with a NAT for HCV RNA. • If the HCP is HCV RNA negative at 3–6 weeks: Test one more time at 4–6 months after exposure for HCV antibody, with reflex to RNA if positive. N.B. If the HCP was already HCV antibody positive but RNA negative at baseline, instead test for HCV RNA.) • If the HCP remains anti-HCV negative at 4-–6 months, no follow up is needed in most circumstances. However, if the HCP is immunocomp

text: PRINCIPLES OF MICROBIOLOGICAL DIAGNOSIS OF BACTERIAL INFECTIONS Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Tutorial 1 Dear students & Transfer Goal Understand microbiological methods for diagnosis of bacterial infections Students’ learning outcomes At the end of this session, the student will be able to: Recognize the different methods for diagnosis of bacterial infection Distinguish the advantages of diagnostic tests for bacterial infection Select the appropriate diagnostic test for bacterial infection Appraise the results of different microbiological tests for bacterial infections Diagnostic microbiology methods Direct microscopic examination Antigen/ nucleic acid detection Culture isolation + AST Antibody/cell mediated IR detection Ag detection: ELISA, IF, latex, … NA detection: PCR, Probes, …. 1 2 3 4 Ab mediated = serology ELISA, IF, Latex,.. Gram stain ZN stain DFA Colonial morphology Gram film B iochemical tests Direct Indirect 1. Direct microscopic examination Microscopic examination of stained or unstained specimens is a relatively simple and inexpensive, but much less sensitive method than culture for detection of small numbers of bacteria. A specimen must contain at least 10 5 organisms per milliliter before it is likely that organisms will be seen on a smear. Gram stain (all bacteria) ZN stain (mycobacteria) Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) staining Gram staining is a very useful procedure in diagnostic microbiology. Most specimens submitted when bacterial infection is suspected should be smeared on glass slides, Gram-stained, and examined microscopically. On microscopic examination of any specimen (Direct Smear) the Gram reaction (purple indicates Gram-positive organisms; red indicates Gram-negative) morphology (shape: cocci, rods, fusiform, or other) of bacteria should be noted. the presence or absence of inflammatory cells and the type of cell are important to note and quantify. The appearance of bacteria on Gram-stained smears does not permit identification of species . 1. Direct microscopic examination Gram stained smears Specimens submitted for examination for mycobacteria should be stained for acid-fast organisms by Ziehl-Neelsen stain . 1. Direct microscopic examination Immunofluorescent antibody (Fab) staining is useful in the identification of many microorganisms. Such procedures are more specific than other staining techniques. Use of monoclonal antibodies may circumvent the problem of nonspecific staining. 1. Direct microscopic examination 2. Culture and Identification Isolated colonies For diagnostic bacteriology, it is necessary to use several types of media for routine culture, particularly when the possible organisms include aerobic, facultatively anaerobic, and obligately anaerobic bacteria. 2. Culture and Identification The standard medium for specimens is blood agar , usually made with 5% sheep blood. Most aerobic and facultatively anaerobic organisms will grow on blood agar. Chocolate agar , a medium containing heated blood with or without supplements, is a second necessary medium; some organisms that do not grow on blood agar, including pathogenic Neisseria and Haemophilus , will grow on chocolate agar. A selective medium for enteric Gram-negative rods ( MacConkey agar ) is a third type of medium used routinely. These agars contain indicators that allow differentiation of lactose- fermenting organisms from non-lactose-fermenting organisms. Specimens to be cultured for obligate anaerobes must be plated on anaerobic media . Routine culture media 2. Culture and Identification S elective culture media Many other specialized media ( selective media ) are used in diagnostic bacteriology; choices depend on the clinical diagnosis and the organism under consideration upon physician request . The laboratory staff selects the specific media on the basis of the information in the culture request. For culture of mycobacteria , specialized media ( Lowenstein Jensen ) are commonly used. These media may contain inhibitors of other bacteria. Because many mycobacteria grow slowly, the cultures must be incubated and examined periodically for weeks . In addition to the above standard and selective media, agars that incorporate antibiotics and chromogenic enzyme substrates that impart color to specific organisms of interest, such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus are available. These media, while more expensive, do enhance sensitivity by inhibiting background microbiota and allowing the pathogen of interest to be more easily recognized. Typically, these chromogenic agars are used for specimens such as surveillance cultures . Chromogenic c ulture media 2. Culture and Identification When growth is detected in any medium, the process of identification begins. Identification involves methods for obtaining pure cultures from single colonies, followed by: Gram stained films, Biochemical tests designed to characterize and identify the isolate. The exact tests and their sequences vary with different groups of organisms, and the taxonomic level (genus, species, subspecies, etc ) of identification needed varies according to the medical usefulness of the information. 2. Culture and Identification Colonial morphology Gram stained films Biochemical tests T yping Colonial morphology G ram stained films Biochemical tests 3. Antigen detection Immunofluorescent tests (direct and indirect fluorescent antibody tests) , Enzyme immunoassays (EIAs), including enzyme linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA), and agglutination tests are used to detect antigens of infectious agents present in clinical specimens. EIAs are used to detect bacterial antigens in a variety of specimen types such as stool, CSF, urine, and respiratory samples. E .g. Antigen detection is used most often in the diagnosis of group A streptococcal pharyngitis . Latex agglutination tests are primarily directed at the detection of carbohydrate antigens of encapsulated microorganisms (causes of bacterial meningitis). Immunochromatography rapid test for Group A streptococci L atex agglutination for group A streptococci L atex agglutination for bacterial meningitis 4. Molecular assays Nucleic acid–based methods are generally specific and highly sensitive and can be used for all categories of microbes . Results can be provided rapidly . Because each test typically is specific to a single organism, the clinician must know the diagnostic possibilities and request tests accordingly. Recent advances have led to the development of multiplex assays , in which a single nucleic acid–based test can detect and differentiate between ≥ 2 causative microorganisms. Multiplex assays have similar sensitivity and specificity as single target assays . 4. Molecular assays Multiplex syndromic molecular assays were created to offer all the benefits that conventional molecular diagnostic tests do, as well as the benefits of quick results , portability, and user-friendliness . E.g. BioFire FilmArray ( BioMérieux ) BioFire FilmArray (BioMérieux) 5. Serological testing Detection of specific antibodies to infectious agents can be useful for diagnosis of acute or chronic infections, and for investigating the epidemiology of infectious disease. During the course of illness, IgM antibody is first produced, followed by appearance of IgG antibody. Serology is most useful when acute and convalescent sera are tested to show increases in antibody titers over time. There are a variety of serological assays available, including direct immunofluorescence, agglutination, EIA, and ELISA. 6. Mass spectrometry Mass spectrometry (MS), a technology used to analyze proteins , has revolutionized the approach to microbial identification in clinical laboratories. MS employs methods such as ionization radiation to disrupt material, forming charged particles that are identified in various ways on the basis of mass or mass-to-charge ratio. M atrix-assisted laser desorption ionization time-of- flight mass spectroscopy ( MALDI-TOF MS) . MALDI-TOF allows identif ication of bacteria and yeast isolates recovered in clinical cultures. The assays involve making a thin smear from a colony or broth culture onto a metallic slide of the organism to be identified and applying an acid matrix to it. The slide is placed into the instrument where the organism mixture is hit by laser pulses. Charged protein fragments are produced and accelerated through an electrostatic field in a vacuum tube until they contact the mass spectrometer’s detector. Molecules of different masses and charges “fly” at different speeds (“time of flight”). name: Practical  - P2. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing & interpretation
text: ANTIMICROBIAL SUSCEPTIBILITY TESTING & INTERPRETATION Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg MED217 Principles of infection Practical 2 Dear students & Transfer Goal Recognize the role of antimicrobial susceptibility testing Students’ learning outcomes At the end of this session, the student will be able to: Recognize different methods for antimicrobial susceptibility testing Differentiate between disc diffusion and dilution tests for antimicrobial susceptibility Interpret the results of antimicrobial susceptibility tests. Appraise the antibiogram according to clinical condition of the patient Introduction Deciding whether any bacterium should be considered susceptible or resistant to an antimicrobial involves an integrated assessment of: (1) in vitro activity by antimicrobial susceptibility test, (2) pharmacologic characteristics of the antibiotic (dosage, routes, frequency of administration, absorption, metabolism, excretion), (3) clinical factors of the patient. Any agent approved for clinical use has demonstrated in vitro its potential to inhibit the growth of some target group of bacteria at concentrations that can be achieved with acceptable risks of toxicity ; that is, the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). Thus, MIC is defined as the least amount of antimicrobial that will inhibit growth of an organism. In selecting therapy , clinicians must consider more than the results of laboratory tests . The clinical pharmacology of the drug, the cause of the disease, the site of infection, the immune function of the patient, the pathology of the lesion must be taken into account as well. For example, the antimicrobial must reach the subarachnoid space and cerebrospinal fluid in meningitis. Similarly, treatment may be ineffective for an infection that has resulted in abscess formation unless the abscess is surgically drained. A ccording to CLSI The Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) provides recommendations for which agents to test based on the organism recovered and the specimen type, and interpretive criteria ( susceptible, intermediate, or resistant ) based on the measured zone size. S I R Another diffusion procedure uses gradient strips to produce elliptical zones that can be directly correlated with the MIC. This method, the epsilometer test (E test) . This approach is slower and more laborious than automated broth systems. S I R E test 2. Dilution tests D etermine the MIC directly by using serial dilutions of the antimicrobial agent . The dilutions are prepared in tubes or microdilution wells , concentrations are doubled using a base of 1 μg /mL (0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on). The bacterial inoculum is adjusted to a standard ( 10 5 to 10 6 bacteria/mL ) and added to the broth. After incubation, the tubes are examined for turbidity produced by bacterial growth. B roth microdilution method The first tube in which visible growth is absent (clear) is the MIC for that organism. Guidelines available from CLSI provide interpretive criteria, defining strains as resistant, intermediate, or susceptible to a certain drug based on the MIC. Bactericidal effects can be estimated by subculturing the clear broth from MIC testing onto antibiotic-free solid media . 3. Automated tests Instruments are now available that carry out rapid, automated variants of the broth dilution test . In these systems the bacteria are incubated with the antimicrobial in specialized modules that are read automatically on a frequent basis. The multiple readings and the increased sensitivity of determining endpoints by turbidimetric or fluorometric analysis makes it possible to generate MICs in as little as 4 hours . In laboratories with sufficient volume, these methods are no more expensive than manual methods, and the rapid results have enhanced potential to influence clinical outcome , particularly when interfaced with computerized hospital information systems. Phoenix, BD VITEK, BioMerieux 4. Molecular tests Molecular techniques can provide a faster and more reliable investigation of AMR than traditional phenotypic methods in many ways. However, they often involve specialized equipment and demand professional interpretation. PCR, DNA microarray, whole-genome sequencing, and metagenomics are examples of such practices. Among molecular diagnostic techniques, PCR is a highly recognized detection tool. The strategy is to detect the resistance gene rather than to measure the phenotypic expression of that gene product. These methods offer the prospect of automation and rapid results. T he World Health Organization (WHO) published a Global Action Plan on AMR in 2015 . The plan emphasized the importance and need of “ effective, fast, and low-cost diagnostic technologies for guiding the appropriate use of antibiotics .” This action plan aims to improve the speed and accuracy of diagnosis through quick, accurate, and minimal cost point-of-care testing (POCT) diagnostic technologies . POC-based diagnostics can correctly detect AMR pathogens at the bedside with a high detection rate, allowing for the rapid initiation of appropriate therapy while avoiding antibiotic overuse or abuse. For instance, FilmArray ® ( BioFire , Salt Lake City, UT, USA) is a technological innovation that makes it possible to simultaneously identify many targets. name: Practical  - T2. Principles of microbiological diagnosis of viral infections
ref: file:T2 Principles of microbiological diagnosis of viral infections.pptx
text: PRINCIPLES OF MICROBIOLOGICAL DIAGNOSIS OF VIRAL INFECTIONS Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg MED217 Principles of infection Tutorial 2 2. Antigen detection Commercial kits are available to detect many viruses . Multiple types of assays are used as well: EIA, IF , latex agglutination, Immunochromatography, etc. In general, the antigen detection assays for viruses are less sensitive than the viral culture methods and NAATs . M any of these assays have been replaced by NAATs 3. Nucleic acid amplification techniques A wide variety of commercial assays are available to detect viral nucleic acid or to amplify and detect it. These procedures are rapidly becoming the standards for diagnostic virology , supplanting the traditional virus culture and antigen detection techniques. The methods include PCR, reverse transcriptase PCR, others. The procedures allow detection as well as quantitation of the viruses . Data from quantitative assays are used to guide antiviral therapy in multiple viral diseases. E.g. RT-PCR for HCV. RT-PCR PCR Multiplex syndromic molecular assays were created to offer all the benefits that conventional molecular diagnostic tests do, as well as the benefits of quick results, portability, and user-friendliness. Many of these test platforms allow non-laboratorians to operate them successfully, which makes them suitable for deployment in patient care settings like clinics and hospital emergency rooms. Microbiology laboratories frequently use syndromic panel testing since the procedure can identify several pathogens linked to various infection symptoms (respiratory, gastrointestinal, and central nervous system). E.g. BioFire FilmArray ( BioMérieux ) BioFire FimArray 4. Cultivation in cell culture D etection of viral growth Identification of virus in cell culture C ytopathic effect (CPE) in cell culture ( shrinking, swelling, rounding of cells, formation of syncytia or clusters), e.g. respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) : multinucleated giant cells (syncytia). H emadsorption and hemagglutination . e.g. Influenza viruses may be detected within 24–48 hours if erythrocytes are added to infected cultures. Viruses produce a hemagglutinin that enables the erythrocytes to adsorb at the cell surface . Interference : the virus that infects the susceptible cell culture produces no CPE or hemagglutinin, but can be detected by “ challenging” the cell culture with a different virus that normally produces a characteristic CPE . The second, or challenge, virus fails to infect the cell culture because of interference by the first virus, which is thus detected. CPE (Syncitia formation) CPE (Balloning) 4. Cultivation in cell culture D etection of viral growth Identification of virus in cell culture The identity of a virus isolate is established with: type-specific antiserum, which inhibits virus growth ( neutralization test, hemagglutination inhibition; HAI ) or which reacts with viral antigens ( ELISA, IF ) Neutralisation test Dear students & Hemagglutination inhibition test Cell culture techniques are being replaced by antigen detection methods and NAATs . However, they are still useful and are still practiced in clinical, research, and public health virology laboratories. 5. Measuring immune response to viral infection = Serological tests Establishing the diagnosis of a viral infection is accomplished serologically by demonstrating: (1) a fourfold or greater increase in antibody titer or (2) by demonstrating antiviral antibodies of the IgM class . The methods used include ELISA, IF test, the neutralization test, HAI … Measurement of antibodies by different methods does not necessarily give parallel results. Humoral IR Cellular IR TO BE DISCUSSED IN ANOTHER CONTEXT 5. Measuring immune response to viral infection Serological tests Uses: when the virus has a long incubation period prior to the appearance of clinical manifestations. E.g. Epstein-Barr virus, the hepatitis viruses, and HIV. Typically, testing for antibodies to these viruses is the first step in diagnosis and may be followed later, in most cases, by nucleic acid amplification that is used to assess the levels of circulating virus as an estimate of the level of infection and/ or response to specific antiviral therapies. Another important utility of serologic tests is to assess an individual’s vaccination status, vulnerability or prior exposure to a virus and the potential for reactivation in the context of immunosuppression or organ transplantation. Indirect ELISA Indirect IF Immunoblot technique Western blot is used to identify an antigen in a complex mixture of proteins . The complex mixture of proteins is subjected to gel electrophoresis (PAGE). This separates the proteins according to charge and molecular size. The gel is then blotted to a nitrocellulose membrane. The membrane is incubated with a serum sample. If the serum contains specific antibody that reacts with a protein on the membrane, the immobilized proteins capture virus-specific antibody and are visualized with an enzyme-conjugated antihuman antibody. The antigen–antibody complex is visible as a separate band. This method is widely used as a secondary test for HCV, HIV. Name three methods that can be used for viral antigen detection. EIA/ELISA Immunofluorescence Immunochromatography Transfer Goal Understand microbiological methods for diagnosis of viral infections A patient has a negative viral antigen test but strong clinical suspicion of infection. Does the negative result necessarily exclude infection? No. Antigen detection assays are generally less sensitive than NAATs and other methods. A negative antigen result therefore needs to be interpreted in the clinical context and may warrant another diagnostic approach. A patient presents with symptoms suggestive of a viral infection. A tissue smear is examined microscopically, but no characteristic inclusion bodies are identified. The clinician asks whether this negative result excludes viral infection. Q1. Does a negative direct microscopic examination exclude viral infection? Q2. Why is direct microscopic examination not considered the primary diagnostic method for most viral infections? Q3. Which modern method would generally provide greater diagnostic sensitivity? No Many viruses do not produce readily recognizable inclusion bodies, and the sensitivity of direct microscopy is relatively low. Nucleic acid amplification testing (e.g., PCR/NAAT) is generally more sensitive. Suspected new influenza outbreak in a dorm → Patient with suspected chronic HCV → Animal bite, suspected rabies → Infant with bronchiolitis in winter → Suspected HIV exposure, screening then confirmation → W hat test to choose in the following case scenarios? NAAT/antigen test, not serology (acute) S erology first, then NAAT for viral load. D irect IF/microscopy on brain tissue (Negri bodies) R apid antigen or multiplex NAAT panel for RSV. ELISA (screen) → confirmatory NAAT . A 28-year-old patient presents with fever, sore throat, cough, and fatigue. Symptoms started 3 days ago. The physician suspects a viral respiratory infection. A respiratory specimen and blood sample are collected for laboratory investigation. Three laboratory results are subsequently available: Result 1: Viral NAAT/PCR — Positive Result 2: Serum IgG — Positive Result 3: Viral antigen detection test — Positive Q1. Which laboratory result most directly demonstrates the presence of viral nucleic acid in the respiratory specimen? Q2. Which result could indicate previous exposure to the virus rather than necessarily indicating the current infection? Q3. Which laboratory result demonstrates RAPID easy cheap detection of the virus? NAAT Serum IgG Ag detection Q5. If the patient is only on day 3 of illness, why might the positive PCR result be more useful for diagnosing the current infection than the positive IgG result? Because PCR/NAA

name: Practical  - T3. Principles of microbiological diagnosis of fungal infections
ref: file:T3 Principles of microbiological diagnosis of fungal infections.pptx
text: PRINCIPLES OF MICROBIOLOGICAL DIAGNOSIS OF FUNGAL INFECTIONS Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg MED217 Principles of infection Tutorial 2 Dear students & Transfer Goal Understand microbiological methods for diagnosis of fungal infections Students’ learning outcomes At the end of this session, the student will be able to: Recognize the different methods for diagnosis of fungal infection Distinguish the advantages of different diagnostic tests for fungal infection Select the appropriate diagnostic test for specific fungal infection Appraise the results of different microbiological tests for fungal infections A. Direct methods Potassium hydroxide (KOH) G ram stain India ink 1. Direct microscopic examination Types of specimen: 10% solution of potassium hydroxide (KOH) on a microscope slide under a coverslip (Wet mount) The strong alkali digests the tissue elements (epithelial cells, leukocytes, debris), but not the rigid cell walls of either yeasts or molds. Negative stain India Ink For Capsulated organisms This technique is mainly used to examine CSF samples for Cryptococcus neoformans. Gram stain (gram positive) A few yeasts including Candida albicans can be visualized using the Gram stain. (Gram positive oval bodies) 2. Histopathologic examination Routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histopathological stain. Specialized fungal cell wall stains are more sensitive The Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) BLACK Periodic acid- Schiff (PAS) red Formalin-fixed biopsy specimens A- (GMS) of bronchoalveolar lavage showing black stained cysts of Pneumocystis jirovecii . B. (GMS) showing branching septate hyphae. C-Periodic acid- Schiff (PAS) showing septate branching hyphae 3. Antigen detection The major targets are mannans, mannoproteins, glucan, chitin, or some other structure unique to the fungal pathogens. Examples include: Cryptococcus neoformans capsular polysaccharide antigen test (cryptococcal antigen) is sensitive and specific. Serum antigen tests for Aspergillus species (galactomannan) , Candida (mannan antigen) and other fungal pathogens (β-d-glucan) are less sensitive for diagnosing infection but can be useful in some cases. 4. Molecular methods Most DNA-based methods use PCR to amplify fungus-specific sequences or conserved sequences. PCR to detect fungal DNA (mostly Candida or Aspergillus) in blood and other specimens. Automated commercial instruments for the DNA-based identification of pathogenic fungi have been developed by several companies. B. Culture The traditional mycological medium, Sabouraud’s dextrose agar (SDA), contains glucose and modified peptone (pH 7.0), supports the growth of fungi, and restricts the growth of bacteria. SDA can be made fungal-selective by the addition of antibacterial antibiotics such as chloramphenicol and gentamicin . Cycloheximide , an antimicrobial that inhibits some saprophytic fungi, is sometimes added to Sabouraud’s agar to prevent overgrowth of contaminating molds from the environment, particularly for skin cultures. Yeasts grow better at 37°C and molds at 30°C . The texture and color of the colony are examined on its front and back sides, the presence of diffusible pigments in the medium should be noted. The type of colony is observed, yeast or filamentous. Molds are most often identified by the morphology of their conidia and conidiophores. Other features such as the size, texture, and color of the colonies help characterize molds. Yeasts colonies resemble that of bacterial colonies. Microscopic examination: For filamentous colonies, a “ Needle Mount ” is made using lactophenol cotton blue . Points to be noted are size, shape, septation, color of spores or the type of specialized structures upon which spores are borne. For yeast colonies: Gram stain is performed. Gram-positive oval budding with or without pseudomycelium are observed. Identification: Once a fungus is isolated, identification procedures depend on whether the growing fungus is a yeast or a mold . Yeasts are identified by biochemical tests analogous to those used for bacteria, including some that are identical ( eg , urease production). The observation of specific fungal structures such as pseudohyphae is also diagnostically useful among the yeasts. Molds are usually identified by their macroscopic morphology. C. Antibody Detection (Serology) Serum antibodies directed against a variety of fungal antigens can be detected in patients infected with those agents. These tests are rarely useful for diagnosing acute infections. A ll types of fungal microscopic examination I dentify M ention the type of stain/preparation (KOH, india ink, Gram stain, lactophenol cotton blue) Histopathological examination Identify Identify the type of stain A ll types of fungal cultures I dentify t h e fungus in the figure M ention the type fungal colony (Yeast/Filament) Mention the type of culture medium (SDA) A patient presents with severe headache and fever. A lumbar puncture is performed. An India Ink CSF smear shows the organism presented in the associated Figure. Q1. Interpret the smear findings. Q2. What antigen test can be performed to confirm this diagnosis? Cryptococcal capsular polysaccharide antigen test. A BAL specimen is examined using special stain and shows cystic structures consistent with Pneumocystis jirovecii . What type of diagnostic method is being used? Histopathological/GMS staining examination. THANK YOU

name: Practical  - T4. Disinfection & sterilisation in healthcare settings
ref: file:T4 Disinfection  sterilization procedures in healthcare settings.pptx
text: DISINFECTION & STERILIZATION PROCEDURES IN HEALTHCARE SETTINGS Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Tutorial 4 S emicritical items R espiratory equipment Laryngoscopes Flexible endoscopes C ritical items Single use items R eusable items Factors that affect the efficacy of both disinfection and sterilization include : Prior cleaning of the object; O rganic and inorganic load present; T ype and level of microbial contamination; C oncentration of and exposure time to the germicide; P hysical nature of the object (e.g., crevices, hinges, and lumens); P resence of biofilms ; T emperature and pH of the disinfection process . STERILIZATION Techniques of sterilization 1. Heat 2. Low temperature Dry heat Sterilization by oxidation of the cell components. Incineration (This is an efficient method for the sterilization and disposal of contaminated materials; pathological waste materials, surgical dressings, sharp needles and other clinical waste) and the use of the laboratory Bunsen burner are examples of sterilization by dry heat. H ot air oven at 160–180°C for 1 -2 h : This method is applicable to metals, glassware, and some heat-resistant oils and waxes that are immiscible in water and, therefore, cannot be sterilized in the autoclave. Moist heat I n the form of water or steam is far more rapid and effective in sterilization than dry heat because m oist heat destroys microorganisms by the irreversible coagulation and denaturation of enzymes and structural proteins. Autoclave : it consists of a chamber in which the air can be replaced with pure saturated steam under pressure. Recognized minimum exposure periods for sterilization of wrapped healthcare supplies are 30 minutes at 121°C in a gravity displacement sterilizer or 4 minutes at 132°C in a prevacuum sterilizer. A utoclaves 1. Pre-vacuum autoclaves are used for sterilization of sterilization of all critical and semicritical items that are heat and moisture resistant (surgical instruments, surgical dressings, bed linen,..) suitable for wrapped items. Temperature and duration for sterilization: 132 °C for 4 minutes. 2. Gravity displacement autoclaves used to process non-porous articles whose surfaces have direct steam contact ( unwrapped items e.g. laboratory media, water, pharmaceutical products). Temperature and duration for sterilization: 121°C for 20 minutes. P revaccum autoclave Gravity displacement Dear students & E thylene oxide sterilizer The microbicidal activity of ETO is considered to be the result of alkylation of protein, DNA, and RNA , preventing normal cellular metabolism and replication. The main advantage is that it can sterilize heat- or moisture-sensitive medical equipment without deleterious effects on the material used in the medical devices. The main disadvantages are the lengthy cycle time, the cost, and its potential hazards to patients and staff. ETO sterilizers resemble autoclaves and expose the load to 10% ETO in carbon dioxide at 50 - 60°C under controlled conditions of humidity. Exposure times, usually, are approximately 4 to 6 hours and must be followed by a prolonged period of aeration to allow the gas to diffuse out of substances that have absorbed it. H ydrogen peroxide (plasma) sterilizer This process inactivates microorganisms primarily by the combined use of hydrogen peroxide gas and the generation of free radicals during the plasma phase of the cycle. Uses . Materials and devices that cannot tolerate high temperatures and humidity , such as some plastics, electrical devices, and corrosion-susceptible metal alloys, can be sterilized by hydrogen peroxide gas plasma. I onizing radiation It has been used for a number of heat sensitive medical products (e.g., tissue for transplantation, pharmaceuticals, medical devices). Because of high sterilization costs, this method is an unfavorable alternative to ETO and plasma sterilization in healthcare facilities but is suitable for large-scale sterilization . It is widely used in industrial processes, including the sterilization of many disposable surgical supplies such as gloves, plastic syringes, specimen containers . M onitoring the sterilization process 1. Mechanical monitors for steam sterilization include the daily assessment of cycle time and temperature by examining the temperature record chart (or computer printout) and an assessment of pressure via the pressure gauge. M onitoring the sterilization process 2. Chemical indicators are convenient, are inexpensive, and indicate that the item has been exposed to the sterilization process. Chemical indicators usually are either heat-or chemical-sensitive inks that change color when one or more sterilization parameters (e.g., saturated steam) are present. An air-removal test (Bowie-Dick Test) must be performed daily in an empty prevacuum steam sterilizer to ensure air removal. M onitoring the sterilization process 3 . Biological indicators measure the sterilization process directly by using the most resistant microorganisms (i.e., Bacillus spores) , and not by merely testing the physical and chemical conditions necessary for sterilization. DISINFECTION D isinfection 1. Physical methods 2. Chemical methods Disinfectants AND Antisptics UV radiation Inactivation of microorganisms results from destruction of nucleic acid . The application of UV radiation in the health-care environment (i.e., operating rooms, isolation rooms, and biologic safety cabinets ) is limited to destruction of airborne organisms or inactivation of microorganisms on surfaces. Flushing- washer disinfector Flushing- and washer-disinfectors are automated and closed equipment that clean and disinfect objects from bedpans to surgical instruments and anesthesia tubes. They have a short cycle (20-30 min) . They clean by flushing with warm water ( 80-90°C) , possibly with a detergent, and then disinfect by flushing the items with hot water or with steam. Transfer Goal Recognize the importance of disinfection and sterilization procedures Chemical Disinfectant kill all microorganisms except large numbers of bacterial spores (e.g., 2% glutaraldehyde), might be cidal for mycobacteria, vegetative bacteria, most viruses, and most fungi but do not kill bacterial spores (e.g., Alcohol 70%). Can kill most vegetative bacteria, some fungi, and some viruses but NOT bacterial spores or mycobacteria. (e.g., Quaternary ammonium compounds) Chemical Disinfectant Article Disinfectant or antiseptic Level of disinfection Comment I. Disinfectants Floors, walls, surfaces Quaternary ammonium compounds (QUATS) LLD Used in environmental decontamination of non-critical surfaces, as floors, furniture, and walls as well as neonatal ICU incubators, monitors in ICU -General environmental disinfection -Decontamination of blood spills Sodium hypochlorite solution (1000 ppm or 5000 ppm) ILD - HLD - 1000 ppm is prepared by diluting 5% solution (1:50) (environmental disinfection & small blood spill) - 5000 ppm is prepared by diluting 5% solution (1:10) (large blood spill) Contact time: 10 minutes Thermometers, stethoscopes Alcohol (70-90%) ILD Alcohol evaporates so no rinsing is required. Endoscopes Glutaraldehyde (2%) Hydrogen peroxide (7.5%) Peracetic acid (0.2%) HLD Glutaraldehyde ( cidex ) 2% Contact time: 45 min II. Antiseptics ICU/Ward staff hands Soap and water (for visibly dirty hands) or Alcohol based hand rubs (for visibly clean hands) LLD ILD Alcohol based hand rub (70-90% ethyl or isopropyl alcohol) Contact time: 20-30 seconds. Surgeons’ hands Alcohols (70-90% ethyl and isopropyl alcohols) Alcohol-chlorhexidine Povidone iodine (10%) ILD Products with chlorhexidine in combination with alcohol are more effective than alcohol alone with residual effect up to 24 hours.
