name: ppt  - Basic concepts of infection
text: BASIC CONCEPTS OF INFECTION Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 1 Dear students & Transfer Goal Recognize the importance of medical microbiology Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Understand the definition of medical microbiology. 2. Recognize the types of human microbiota. 3. Differentiate between resident and transient microbiota. 4. Relate the role of microbiota in different body sites with health and disease. • The spectrum of infection has widened , with discoveries that organisms earlier thought to be harmless can cause disease under certain circumstances. • Who could have guessed that Helicobacter pylori, would be the major cause of gastric and duodenal ulcers and an officially declared carcinogen? • Moreover, bioterrorist forces have unearthed two previously controlled infectious diseases —anthrax and smallpox—and threatened their distribution as agents of biological warfare. • For students of medicine, understanding the fundamental basis of infectious diseases has more relevance than ever. • The science of medical microbiology dates back to the pioneering studies of Pasteur and Koch , who isolated specific agents and proved that they could cause disease by introducing the experimental method. • Microbiology is the study of all living organisms that are too small to be visible with the naked eye. This includes bacteria, archaea, viruses, fungi, prions, protozoa and algae, collectively known as 'microbes’. • These microbes play key roles in nutrient cycling, biodegradation/biodeterioration, climate change, food spoilage, the cause and control of disease, and biotechnology. Classification of medically important microbes 13 • All organisms other than viruses and prions are made up of cells. • Although viruses have genetic material (DNA or RNA) they are not cellular, lacking cell membranes, cytoplasm and the machinery for synthesizing macromolecules, depending instead upon host cells for this process. • The agents ( prions) lack nucleic acid and consist only of infectious proteinaceous particles. • All other organisms have a cellular organization, being made up of single cells (most ‘microbes’) or of many cells. Each cell has genetic material (DNA) and cytoplasm with synthetic machinery, and is bounded by a cell membrane. Bacteria are prokaryotes; all other organisms are eukaryotes. The major classes of microorganisms in terms of ascending size and complexity are prions, viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites. Eukaryotic cell Prokaryotic cell Cell size Large (10-100 µm) Small (0.5-5 µm) Organism type Multicellular Unicellular Nucleus Present (membrane bound) Absent (nucleoid region) Replication Mitotic division Binary fission Membrane bounds organelles e.g mitochondria Present Absent Ribosomes Large (80S) Small (70S) Cytoplasm Present Present Plasma membrane Present Present Cell wall Simple (present in fungi) Peptidoglycan (present in all prokaryotes) • Eukaryotes vs prokaryotes Human Microbiota • The presence of microbes on or in humans is not, by itself, abnormal. • Current estimates indicate that the numbers of microbial and human cells are of the same order of magnitude, with an approximate ratio close to 1:1. . • This population formerly called the normal flora is now referred to as our microbiota or microbiome. • These microorganisms, which are overwhelmingly bacteria, are frequently found colonizing various body sites in healthy individuals. • The constituents and numbers of the microbiota vary in different areas of the body and, sometimes, at different ages and physiologic states. Thus, each accessible area of the body presents a particular ecologic niche, colonization of which requires a particular set of properties of the colonizing microbe. • Organisms of the microbiota may have a symbiotic relationship that benefits the host or • may simply live as commensals with a neutral relationship to the host. • The members of the human microbiota may stay for highly variable periods: 1) Residents are strains that have an established niche at one of the many body sites, which they occupy indefinitely. 2) Transients are acquired from the environment and establish themselves briefly, but they tend to be excluded by competition from residents or by the host’s innate or immune defense mechanisms.

name: ppt - Bacterial structure, classification & growth
text: BACTERIAL STRUCTURE, CLASSIFICATION & GROWTH Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 2 Dear students & Transfer Goal Recognize the structure and growth of bacteria Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Describe and classify different types of bacteria 2. Distinguish between structure of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria 3. Interpret the role of different bacterial structures in infection 4. Correlate bacterial growth curve with infectious disease course Bacterial size and shape • The small size (0.5 – 5 µm) • Nearly colorless nature of bacteria require the use of stains (Gram stain) for visualization with a light microscope. Hence, bacteria are generally referred to Gram positive (violet) and Gram negative (red). • The major morphologic forms are spheres, rods, bent or curved rods, and spirals. Spherical or oval bacteria are called cocci and are typically arranged in clusters or chains. Rods are called bacilli and may be straight or curved. Bacilli that are small and pleomorphic to the point of resembling cocci are often called coccobacilli. Bacterial size and shape Structure of bacteria • The major structures of the bacterial cell consists of 1. the multilayered envelope and its appendages and 2. the interior core consisting of the nucleoid (or nuclear body) and the cytoplasm. 1. Envelope and appendages • A rigid cell wall surrounds all bacterial cells except bacteria lacking cell walls such as the mycoplasmas. The structure and function of the bacterial wall is a hallmark of the prokaryotes; it is absent in human cell. • It protects the cell from mechanical disruption and from bursting caused by the internal pressure of the cell. • It also provides a barrier against certain toxic chemical and biologic agents. • Its form is responsible for the shape of the cell. • Site of action of beta lactams (penicillin binding proteins; PBP) • Contains receptor for phages. A. Cell wall Gram positive bacteria Gram negative bacteria Envelope Cell wall - Peptidoglycan layer Thicker Thinner - Teichoic acid Present Absent - Outer membrane Absent Present - Periplasmic space Absent Present - Cell membrane Present Present - Lysozyme Sensitive Resistant - Penicillin Sensitive Less sensitive - Gram stain reaction Violet Red • Peptidoglycan consists of a linear glycan chain of two alternating sugars, N -acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N -acetylmuramic acid (NAM). Adjacent glycan chains are cross - linked into sheets by peptide amino acids side chains. A. Cell wall 1. Envelope and appendages • Most enzymes found in mammalian hosts and other biologic systems do not degrade peptidoglycan; one important exception is lysozyme, the hydrolase in tears and other secretions . Treatment of a gram-positive cell with penicillin (which blocks formation of the peptide cross-links) destroys the peptidoglycan, and bacteria is lysed, but If the cell is protected from lysis by suspension in a medium isotonic with the cell interior, the cell becomes round and forms a sphere called a protoplast surrounded by cell membrane 1. Envelope and appendages A. Cell wall Protoplasts • Teichoic acid are polymers of either glycerol phosphate or ribitol phosphate. A type of teichoic acid called lipoteichoic acid and appears to play a role in anchoring the wall to the cell membrane and as an epithelial cell adhesin. The major antigen of Gram positive bacteria. 1. Envelope and appendages A. Cell wall • LPS consists of: (1) lipid A (the endotoxin), (2) a core polysaccharide, and (3) O antigen polysaccharide side chains (the major surface antigen of gram-negative bacteria). • LPS of the outer membrane of the cell wall of gram-negative bacteria is endotoxin. It is responsible for many of the features of disease, such as fever and shock (especially hypotension), caused by these organisms. 1. Envelope and appendages A. Cell wall • The cell (plasma) membrane of bacteria is similar to the familiar bi-leaflet membrane of most cells, containing phospholipids . However, bacterial cell membrane does not contain sterols (except mycoplasmas). 1. Envelope and appendages B. Cell membrane The bacterial cell membrane is therefore the functional equivalent of most of the organelles of the eukaryotic cell and is vital to the growth and maintenance of the cell. 1. Envelope and appendages The cell membrane: • plays a role in the segregation of daughter chromosomes at cell division. • is the site of synthesis of DNA, cell wall polymers. • It contains the entire electron transport system of the cell (and, hence, is functionally analogous to the mitochondria of eukaryotes). • It contains receptor proteins that function in chemotaxis. • it is a permeability barrier and contains proteins involved in the selective and active transport of solutes. • It is also involved in secretion of proteins including exotoxins and hydrolytic enzymes involved in the pathogenesis of disease. B. Cell membrane

name: ppt - Pathogenesis of bacterial infection
text: PATHOGENESIS OF BACTERIAL INFECTION Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 3 Dear students & Transfer Goal Understand pathogenesis of infections caused by bacteria Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Define bacterial colonization and infection 2. Recognize the steps of bacterial pathogenesis 3. Relate the virulence mechanisms of bacteria to its pathogenesis 4. Differentiate bacterial exotoxins and endotoxins • Adherence (adhesion, attachment): The process by which bacteria stick to the surfaces of host cells. It is a major initial step in the infection process. • Colonization: the presence of multiplying bacteria on a body surface (like on the skin, mouth, intestines or airway) without causing disease in the person. • Infection: Invasion and Multiplication of an infectious agent within the body to cause disease. • Pathogenicity: The ability of any bacterial species to cause disease in a susceptible human host. • Pathogen: A bacterial species able to cause such disease when presented with favorable circumstances (for the organism). • Opportunistic pathogen: An agent capable of causing disease only when the host resistance is impaired ( ie, when the patient is “immunocompromised”). Important definitions Important definitions • Virulence: A term which presumes pathogenicity, but allows expression of degrees from low to extremely high, for example: Low virulence Moderate virulence High virulence Extremely high virulence Streptococcus salivarius oropharyngeal flora, if during a transient bacteremia cause infective endocarditis. Escherichia coli in the colon, but if displacement regularly causes acute infection. Bordetella pertussis , the cause of whooping cough, is not found in the resident flora, highly infectious and causes disease in almost every nonimmune person it contacts. Yersinia pestis, the cause of plague, is also highly infectious, but in addition leads to death in a few days in over 70% of cases. Attributes of bacterial pathogenicity 1. Entry 2. Adherence 3. Invasion 4. Evading the immune system 5. Injury and tissue damage sIgA Lactoferrin Human have various protective mechanisms to prevent microbial entry. 1. Entry • How efficiently bacterial pathogens navigate all these barriers before their initial encounter with their target cell type is in some ways measured by their infecting dose. How many organisms must be given to a host to ensure infection in some proportion of the individuals? • In general, pathogens that have environmental or animal reservoirs can overwhelm innate defenses with large numbers. • Pathogens with no reservoir or amplification mechanism must be transmitted human-to-human and thus require the lowest infecting doses 1. Entry 2. Adherence • Adherence requires the participation of two factors: 1. An adhesin on the invading microbe 2. A receptor on the host cell. • The adhesin must be exposed on the bacterial surface either alone or in association with appendages like pili. In gram - negative bacteria, the outer membrane is a major site for adhesins. Most adhesins are proteins, but carbohydrates and teichoic acids may also be involved. • Two of the most common receptors, mannose and fibronectin , are widely present on human epithelial cell surfaces. • Biofilms may also act as an adherence mechanism by binding to catheters, prosthetic devices, or mucosal surfaces. 2. Adherence 3. Invasion • A few bacteria (as Chlamydia), like viruses, are obligate intracellular pathogens. Other bacteria are facultative intracellular pathogens and can grow as free -living cells in the environment as well as within host cells. • invasive organisms adhere to host cells by one or more adhesins but use a class of molecules, called invasins, which interact with integrins or other families of cell adhesion molecules. The integrins in turn interact with elements of the cell cytoskeleton stimulating modifications which end in uptake of the bacterial cell. 3. Invasion Invasive bacteria enter cells initially within a membrane-bound, host-vesicular structure but then follow one of two pathways Some bacteria ( Listeria, Shigella ) enzymatically lyse the phagosome membrane and escape to the nutrient -rich host cell cytoplasm. These bacteria may continue to multiply there, infect adjacent cells, or move through the cell to the submucosa. Other invasive pathogenic species ( Salmonella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis ) remain in the phagosome and replicate even in phagocytes by preventing phagosome–lysosome fusion or, if fused, blocking acidification to the optimum pH for digestive enzyme activity. lyse the phagosome membrane and escape to the nutrient-rich host cell cytoplasm. 3. Invasion 3. Invasion remain in the phagosome and replicate even in phagocytes by preventing phagosome–lysosome fusion or, if fused, blocking acidification 4. Evading the immune system • Innate immunity Manipulating PAMPs • In some pathogens (Helicobacter, Legionella) the lipid A (toxic) component of LPS is simply a variant poorly recognized by TLR-4 • Other pathogens (Salmonella, Pseudomonas) are able to modulate their lipid A pattern. • Gram-positive bacteria may accomplish a similar benefit by altering their cell wall teichoic acids. Disrupting complement 4. Evading the immune system • Innate immunity Manipulating PAMPs • These polysaccharide capsules of pathogens interfere with effective complement deposition on the bacterial cell surface by binding regulators of C3b that are present in serum (factor H). When one of these, serum factor H, is concentrated on the capsular surface, it accelerates the degradation of C3b deposited from the host serum. This negates both direct complement injury and makes the receptors recognized by phagocytes unavailable. Disrupting complement Opsonisation

name: ppt - Bacterial genetics
text: Bacterial Genetics Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 4 Dear students & Transfer Goal Appraise the role of bacterial genetics in medicine Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Recognize all types of bacterial DNA 2. Interpret consequences of genetic change in bacteria 3. Differentiate different types of genetic transfer and exchange 4. Appraise the role of genetic engineering in medicine Types of bacterial DNA Chromosome Plasmid Transposable elements Single circular double stranded supercoiled DNA molecule. Extrachromosomal, double-stranded, circular DNA molecules Pieces of DNA that move readily from one site to another either within or between the DNAs of bacteria, plasmids, and bacteriophages. “jumping genes.” Plasmids carry the genes for the following functions: 1. Antibiotic resistance, (e.g. R plasmids) which is mediated by a variety of enzymes, such as the beta-lactamases. 2. Exotoxins, such as the exfoliative toxin of S. aureus and tetanus toxin of Clostridium tetani. 3. Pili (fimbriae), which mediate the adherence of bacteria to epithelial cells. Types of bacterial DNA Transmissible plasmid • Transposons are not capable of independent replication; they replicate as part of the DNA in which they are integrated. • Transposons can code for drug- resistant enzymes, toxins, or a variety of metabolic enzymes and can either cause mutations in the gene into which they insert or alter the expression of nearby genes. Types of bacterial DNA Genetic change in bacteria • Mutation • recombination • Transformation • Transduction • Conjugation Genomic Change Exchange of genes • Transposition Within one bacterial cell Between 2 bacterial cells • The spontaneous development of mutations is a major factor in the evolution of bacteria. Mutations occur in nature at a low frequency (one mutation in every million cells for any one gene ), but the large size of microbial populations ensures the presence of many mutants. • Because bacteria are haploid, the consequences of a mutation, are immediately evident in the mutant cell. Genomic change in bacteria 1. Mutation • Because the generation time of bacteria is short, it does not take many hours for a mutant cell that has arisen by chance to grow to the dominant cell type if the mutation gives it a survival advantage. • Recombination is the process in which nucleic acid molecules from different sources are combined or rearranged to produce a new nucleotide sequence . The source of recombinant DNA may be another part of the same chromosome or from outside the cell from one of the genetic transfer mechanisms described later. Genomic change in bacteria 2. Recombination • There are two types of recombination: a. Homologous recombination occurs between closely related DNA sequences and generally substitutes one sequence for another . The process requires a set of enzymes produced by the rec genes. b. Site-specific recombination occurs between dissimilar DNA sequences and generally produces insertions or deletions or both. This process usually requires specialized recombination enzymes, such as those produced by many transposons and lysogenic bacteriophages. Genomic change in bacteria 2. Recombination • Transposition involves transposable elements that are genetic units capable of mediating their own transfer from one chromosome to another, from one location to another on the same chromosome, or between chromosome and plasmid within the same bacterial cell . This transposition relies on their ability to synthesize their own site -specific recombination enzymes , called transposases. Genetic transfer within bacteria cell Transposition (1) when inserted in a new site they cause insertional mutation. (2) Sometimes they insert into genes and inactivate gene that encodes an essential protein, then the cell dies. (3) The transfer of a transposon to a plasmid and the subsequent transfer of the plasmid to another bacterium by conjugation contributes significantly to the spread of antibiotic resistance. Genetic transfer within bacteria cell Transposition • It involves the release of DNA into the environment by the lysis of some bacterial cells, followed by the direct uptake of that DNA by the recipient cells. The ability to take up DNA from the environment is called competence, and in many species of bacteria. • The fate of the internalized DNA fragment then depends on whether it shares homology (the same or similar base sequences) with a portion of the recipient cell’s DNA. If so, recombination can occur. Heterologous DNA is degraded and causes no heritable change in the recipient cell. Genetic transfer between bacterial cells 1. Transformation • Transduction is the transfer of genetic information from donor to recipient cell by viruses of bacteria called bacteriophages. Transduction can be classified as specialized if the phages in question transfer particular genes (usually those adjacent to their integration sites in the genome) or generalized if incorporation of DNA sequences is random because of accidental packaging of host DNA into the phage capsid. The encapsulated DNA, instead of phage DNA, is injected into a new host cell, where it can recombine with the homologous host DNA. Genetic transfer between bacterial cells 2. Transduction Generalized transduction Specialized (Restricted) transduction • The transfer of DNA from the donor to a recipient bacterial cell in a process that requires intimate cell contact . By themselves, bacteria cannot conjugate. Only when a bacterial cell contains a self - transmissible plasmid does DNA transfer occur. In most cases, conjugation involves transfer only of plasmid DNA. Genetic transfer between bacterial cells 3. Conjugation F plasmid

name: ppt - Viral structure & classification
text: VIRAL STRUCTURE & CLASSIFICATION Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 7 Dear students & Transfer Goal Recognize viral structure & classification Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Analyze the structural and genomic features of clinically relevant viruses to predict their behavior during infection and transmission. 2. Differentiate enveloped from naked viruses and interpret how their structural differences influence environmental stability, disinfectant susceptibility, and host-cell entry. 3. Apply principles of defective viruses and viral classification to clinical situations involving viral coinfection and viral taxonomy. 4. Evaluate bacteriophage characteristics and propagation patterns to select appropriate phages for potential therapeutic use against bacterial infections. • Viruses are the smallest replicating intracellular microorganisms that are comprised of sets of genes either DNA (DNA viruses) or RNA (RNA viruses) packaged in a capsid (protein shell) or in a capsid and an outer lipid bilayer envelope. • The resulting complete virus particle is called a virion. • Viruses have an obligate requirement for intracellular growth and a heavy dependence on host cell structural and metabolic components. Therefore, viruses are also referred to as obligate intracellular parasites. Viruses do not have a nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, or other cell organelles. Structure of virus • Viruses are approximately 20-400 nm in diameter . • The basic structure of all viruses places the nucleic acid genome ( DNA or RNA) • on the inside of a protein shell called a capsid. • Some human viruses are further packaged into a lipid membrane, or envelope, which is usually acquired from the plasma or cytoplasmic membrane of the infected cell during release from the cell. Structure of virus • The genomes of enveloped viruses form a protein complex and a structure called a nucleocapsid, • which is often surrounded by a matrix protein that serves as a bridge between the nucleocapsid and the inside of the envelope. • Viruses that are not enveloped have a defined external capsid and are referred to as naked viruses. • Protein or glycoprotein structures called spikes, which often protrude from the surface of virus particles, are involved in the initial contact with receptor on host cells Viral genomes • Viral genomes can be made of either RNA or DNA and also can be either single-stranded or double - stranded. • The RNA viruses can be either positive sense (+) ( same polarity of mRNA) or negative sense (–) (complementary to or antisense of mRNA), double- stranded (one strand + and the second strand –) or ambisense (both + and – polarity on the same strand). • Although the RNA genomes of most viruses are linear, some RNA viruses may also have segmented genomes (several segments or pieces of RNA), with each segment responsible for encoding a protein. The DNA genome of viruses can be both linear and circular genomes. • Most viruses contain a single copy of their genome, except that retroviruses (e.g HIV) carry two identical copies of its genome and are, therefore, diploid. Viral capsids • The capsids or nucleocapsids are virus -encoded specific proteins that protect the genome and confer shapes to viruses. The capsids of all viruses are composed of many copies of one or, at most, several different kinds of protein subunits . The presence of many identical protein subunits in viral capsids or the existence of many identical spikes in the membrane of enveloped viruses has important implications for adsorption, hemagglutination, and recognition of viruses by neutralizing antibodies. The protein shell forming the capsid or the nucleocapsid assumes one of two basic shapes: helical or icosahedral. Helical Icosahedral Virus envelope • Many human viruses have an outer lipid bilayer membrane that is derived from host plasma membrane. The viral envelope lipid layer membrane contains virus -encoded glycoproteins called “ spikes” or “peplomers” or “viral envelope proteins .” The envelope spikes bind to the receptor on the host cells, help the virus envelope membrane fuse with the cellular membrane of the host cells, and act as principal antigens against which the host mounts immune response for the recognition of the virus. • Enveloped viruses are more sensitive to detergents, solvents, ethanol, ether, and heat compared with nonenveloped (naked capsid) viruses whose outer coat is capsid protein. • Both envelope glycoproteins, and naked capsid viruses’ spikes become antigens after infection and the host mounts both cell -mediated and humoral immune responses for the elimination of virus -infected cells and cell -free virus, respectively. These antigens also determine the viral serotypes that are based on antigenic variation and are type -specific such as poliovirus serotypes 1, 2, and 3. • The capsid or envelope of viruses functions • (1) to protect the nucleic acid genome from damage during the extracellular passage of the virus from one cell to another, • (2) to aid in the process of entry into the cell, and • (3) in some cases, to package viral enzymes essential for the early steps of the infection process. Defective viruses • Viruses which lack a complete genome so that they cannot completely replicate or cannot form a protein coat. 1. Some are host-dependent defectives, meaning they can replicate only in cell systems which provide the particular genetic function which they lack. 2. Others, called Satellite viruses, are able to replicate only when their genetic defect is complemented by a helper virus (is the hepatitis D virus which replicates only in the presence of surface antigen from a co-infecting hepatitis B virus). Reaction to physical & chemical agents Heat and cold Naked viruses tend to be stable, losing little infectivity after several hours at 37 °C. Enveloped viruses are much more heat labile , rapidly at 37 °C. Viral infectivity is generally destroyed by heating at 50 –60°C for 30 minutes, although there are some exceptions (eg, hepatitis B virus) Viruses can be preserved by storage at freezing temperatures, pH Viruses are usually stable between pH values of 5 – 9. Some viruses ( eg, enteroviruses) are resistant to acidic conditions. All viruses are destroyed by alkaline conditions. Radiation Ultraviolet, x-ray inactivate viruses. Formaldehyde It destroys viral infectivity by reacting with nucleic acid. Viruses with single-stranded genomes are inactivated much more readily than those with double -stranded genomes. Formaldehyde has minimal adverse effects on the antigenicity of proteins and therefore has been used in the production of inactivated viral vaccines. Chlorine Larger concentrations of chlorine are required to destroy viruses than to kill bacteria, especially in the presence of extraneous proteins. For example, the chlorine treatment of stools adequate to inactivate typhoid bacilli is inadequate to destroy poliomyelitis virus present in feces. Quaternary ammonium compounds and organic iodine compounds not effective against viruses Alcohol Alcohols, such as isopropanol and ethanol, are relatively ineffective against certain viruses, especially picornaviruses. Reaction to physical & chemical agents Classification of viruses • The International Committee for Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) considered various properties, including virions, genome, proteins, envelope, replication, and physical and biologic properties. Based on these properties: • virus families are designated with the suffix, -viridae (as in Herpesviridae), • virus subfamilies with suffix virinae (Herpesvirinae), • virus genera with suffix virus (Herpesvirus), and • virus species designated by a virus type (herpes simplex virus 1).

name: ppt - Viral replication
text: VIRAL REPLICATION Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 8 Dear students & Transfer Goal Understand viral and phage replication cycles Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Outline the major stages of the viral replication cycle and predict the consequence of disruption at each stage. 2. Analyze how differences in viral genome type and cellular machinery determine the strategy of DNA and RNA viral replication. 3. Interpret how viral attachment, entry, replication, assembly, and release contribute to viral pathogenesis and potential immune protection. 4. Differentiate lytic and lysogenic bacteriophage replication and explain their clinical consequences, including lysogenic conversion. Viral replication • Virus replication depends on virus–host cell interaction and the type of cells it infects—whether permissive or nonpermissive cells. 1. Permissive cells are those that permit production of progeny virus particles and/or viral transformation. 2. Nonpermissive cells do not allow virus replication, but may allow virus transformation. Some viruses enter cells that do not support virus replication, but some early viral proteins cause cell death; this infection is termed abortive infection. Viral replication cycle • Virus replication cycle typically consists of six discrete phases: (1) adsorption or attachment to the host cell, (2) penetration or entry, and uncoating to release the genome, (3) synthetic or virion component production, (4) assembly, and (5) release from the cell. • Eclipse phase: in virus replication is the time interval between when a virus infects a host cell and when the first new, infectious virus particles (virions) are assembled inside the cell. 1. Adsorption or attachment • The first step in every viral infection • A prerequisite for this interaction is a collision between the virion and the cell. • It involves interaction between virion attachment proteins (VAP) or spikes and cell receptors. • For some viruses, two different surface molecules, receptor and coreceptors, are involved in adsorption (ex; HIV). • A particular kind of virus is capable of infecting only a limited spectrum of cell types called its host range. • In many cases, human viruses infect only a particular subset of the cells found in their host organism. This kind of tissue tropism is clearly an important determinant of viral pathogenesis. In most cases studied, the specific host range of a virus and its associated tissue tropism are determined at the level of the binding between the cell receptors and VAP . • When a virus particle has penetrated to the inside of a cell, it is hidden from the host immune system . Thus, if protection from a virus infection is to be accomplished at the level of antibody binding to the virions, it must occur before adsorption and prevent the virus from attaching to and penetrating the cell. Thus, most neutralizing antibodies —whether elicited as a result of natural infection or vaccination— are specific for virion attachment proteins. 2. Penetration and uncoating Uncoating step (capsid dissasembly from the viral genome) may be simultaneous with entry or may occur in a series of steps. There are two basic mechanisms for the entry of an enveloped virus into the cell. 1. Some viruses (ex; measles, HIV) enter by a process called direct fusion . The envelopes of these viruses contain protein spikes that promote fusion of the viral membrane with the plasma membrane of the cell, releasing the nucleocapsid directly into the cytoplasm. There are two basic mechanisms for the entry of an enveloped virus into the cell. 2. Other enveloped viruses (influenza virus, coronavirus), after adsorption, the virus particles are taken up by receptor- mediated endocytosis. When it involves viruses, the process is referred to as viropexis. The nucleocapsid is now surrounded by two membranes: the original viral envelope and the newly acquired endosomal membrane. Low pH of the endosome leads to a conformational change in a viral spike protein, which results in the fusion of he two membranes and release of the nucleocapsid into the cytoplasm. Naked viruses, also appear to enter the cell by viropexis 3. Synthetic or virion component production • Most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm—the immediate site of entry with the exception of influenza viruses and the retroviruses that replicate in the nucleus. • All DNA viruses must move from the cytoplasm to the nucleus to replicate, except the poxviruses that replicate in the cytoplasm. 3. Synthetic or virion component production Transcription and translation Genome replication An essential step in every virus infection is the production of virus-specific mRNAs synthesize viral proteins. Viral gene expression is often temporally regulated. Early proteins commonly include regulatory proteins and enzymes needed for genome replication, whereas late proteins are predominantly structural proteins required for assembly of progeny virions. 3. Synthetic or virion component production Transcription and translation Genome replication The genomes of most DNA viruses are transcribed by the host DNA -dependent RNA polymerase (RNA polymerase II) in the nucleus to yield the viral mRNAs which are exported to the cytoplasm for translation. The (+) sense RNA viruses , possess genomes that can be used directly as mRNAs and are translated immediately on entry into the cytoplasm of the cell. The ( –) sense RNA viruses , to make mRNAs must provide their own transcription machinery (RNA- dependent RNA polymerase) to produce the viral mRNAs at the beginning of the infection process. DNA viruses DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RNA polymerase II) 3. Synthetic or virion component production Transcription and translation Genome replication DNA viruses • The smallest of the DNA viruses (parvoviruses) are completely dependent on host machinery that they require the infected cells to be dividing to ensure that a normal S phase occurs and replicates the viral DNA together with the cellular DNA. • The largest DNA viruses (poxviruses) are independent of the host . Because they replicate in the cytoplasm, they must code for almost all of the enzymes and other proteins required for replicating their DNA. • All other DNA human viruses are at least partially dependent on host cell machinery for the replication of their genomes (code for a protein expressed early in infection that induces an unscheduled cycle of cellular DNA replication (S phase). The extent to which viruses use the cell replication machinery depends on their protein-coding potential and, thus, on the size of their genome.

name: ppt - Antibacterial agents
text: ANTIBACTERIAL AGENTS Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 5 Dear students & Transfer Goal Recognize all antibacterial agents in clinical practice Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Classify the mechanisms of action of antibacterial agents 2. Recognize the action of each class of antibiotics 3. Relate the action of antibiotic to its spectrum of activity 4. Select the appropriate antibiotic according to bacterial infections • Clinically effective antimicrobial agents exhibit selective toxicity toward the microbe rather than the host. In most cases, selectivity is explained by action on microbial processes or structures that differ from those of mammalian cells. • For example, some agents inhibit the synthesis of the bacterial cell wall (an organelle not present in human cell). Classification of bacteria Gram negative Gram positive Non-gram stainable Cocci Staphylococci Streptococci Enterococci Bacilli Corynebacterium Bacillus Clostridium Cocci Neisseria Bacilli Enterobacterales Pseudomonas Acinetobacter ❑ Atypical bacteria ❑ Mycobacteria ❑ Spirochetes 1. Antimicrobials acting on cell wall synthesis A. beta lactams • Action • The targets of all the β-lactams are penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs). • The β-lactam antibacterial agents interfere with the transpeptidation reactions that seal the peptide crosslinks between glycan chains. The PBP interacts with β-lactam ring and are not available for the synthesis of new peptidoglycan. • The disruption of peptidoglycan layer leads to the lysis of bacterium (bactericidal effect). • It is important to remember that all antibiotics inhibiting cell wall synthesis are effective only on growing cells (metabolically active cells). 1. Antimicrobials acting on cell wall synthesis • β-lactam antimicrobial agents comprise: 1. Penicillins 2. Cephalosporins 3. Carbapenems 4. Monobactams. • They are named after the β -lactam ring in their structure; this ring is essential for their antibacterial activity. The cephalosporins are classified by generation —first, second, third, fourth, fifth, or “unclassified.” In general, a cephalosporin of a higher generation has a wider spectrum. • The carbapenems imipenem, meropenem, have the broadest spectrum of all β -lactam antibiotics due to the combination of easy penetration of gram -negative and gram-positive bacterial cells and high level of resistance to β-lactamases. 1. Antimicrobials acting on cell wall synthesis 1. Antimicrobials acting on cell wall synthesis B. Glycopeptides • Action: Vancomycin and teicoplanin belong to this group. The effect is the same as with β-lactams: they inhibit cell wall peptidoglycan synthesis by blocking transpeptidation but by a mechanism different from that of the β -lactam drugs. Vancomycin binds directly to the d -alanyl-d-alanine portion of the pentapeptide, which blocks the transpeptidase from binding, whereas the β -lactam drugs bind to the transpeptidase itself. 1. Antimicrobials acting on cell wall synthesis 1. Antimicrobials acting on cell wall synthesis 2. Inhibitors of protein synthesis Cidal Tigecycline has no reliable activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and is not appropriate for treatment of bloodstream infections because of its low serum concentrations. To sum up 2. Inhibitors of protein synthesis Antibiotic Mechanism of action Spectrum of activity Uses Toxicity Aminoglycosides 30S and 50S bactericidal Aerobic Gram negative Gram positive: in combination with beta lactams BSI, intraabdominal infections, UTI Ototoxicity Nephrotoxicity Tetracyclines 30S bacteriostatic Gram positive and Gram negative (aerobic & anaerobic) Intracellular bacteria Skin infections, tissue infections, STI, Bone and teeth discoloration GIT disturbance Macrolides 50S bacteriostatic Mainly Gram positive Intracellular bacteria Upper & lower respiratory tract infections, STI Arrythmias GIT upset Lincosamides 50S bacteriostatic Gram positive Anaerobes Skin infection, bone infection, pneumonia GIT disturbance Oxazolidinones 50S bacteriostatic Resistant Gram positive Anaerobes Pneumonia, soft tissue infections Bone marrow suppression Chloramphenicol 50S bacteriostatic Gram positive and Gram negative (aerobic & anaerobic) Intracellular bacteria Meningitis, others Bone marrow depression

name: ppt - Antimicrobial resistance
text: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 6 Dear students & Transfer Goal Recognize the importance and mechanisms of antimicrobial resistance Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Classify the mechanisms of antibiotic resistance 2. Relate the mechanism of antibiotic resistance to the type of microbe 3. Distinguish indications for antibiotic use 4. Differentiate between empiric and targeted antibiotic therapy. • There are no direct connections between resistance and virulence: some highly drug- resistant bacteria may cause relatively indolent infections, whereas susceptible organisms may cause severe infections. • The resistance to antimicrobials may be: 1. Inherent (intrinsic) to the organism as such as permeability barriers, a lack of cell wall, 2. Acquired; appear in a previously susceptible species by mutation (chromosomal resistance) or the acquisition of new genes (plasmids and transposons) Mechanisms of antibiotic resistance Mechanisms of antibiotic resistance Exclusion Altered target Enzyme inactivation • The cell wall, particularly the outer membrane, of gram-negative bacteria presents a barrier for access to the interior of the cell. • e.g. streptococci and enterococci are intrinsically resistant to aminoglycosides • Other antimicrobials are actively transported out of the cell. • The membrane transporter systems which drive these efflux pumps often affect antimicrobials of several classes. e.g tetracycline and quinolones resistance Mechanisms of antibiotic resistance Exclusion Altered target Enzyme inactivation • If the antimicrobial target is altered in a way that decreases its affinity for the antimicrobial, the inhibitory effect will be proportionately decreased. Examples of altered antimicrobial targets MRSA: altered PBP → PBP2a → reduced β-lactam binding. Penicillin-resistant pneumococci: altered PBPs. Macrolide resistance: modification of 23S rRNA → reduced macrolide binding. Fluoroquinolone resistance: mutations affecting DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV. Mechanisms of antibiotic resistance Exclusion Altered target Enzyme inactivation • Enzymatic inactivation of antimicrobial agents is the most powerful and robust resistance mechanism. • Enzyme inactivation Mechanisms of antibiotic resistance Beta lactamases Modifying enzymes Penicillinases Extended spectrum beta lactamases Carbapenemases Adenylating enzymes Acetylating enzymes Phosphorylating enzymes Esterase Phosphotransferase Acetyl transferase Beta lactamases • Penicillinase, was discovered when penicillin-resistant strains of Staphylococcus aureus emerged and were found to inactivate penicillin in vitro. Each β-lactamase is a distinct enzyme with its own physical characteristics and substrate profile. • A class of gram -negative extended- spectrum β -lactamases (ESBLs) hydrolyses multiple cephalosporins. From a clinical perspective, they are significant because treatment with any generation of cephalosporin may lead to clinical failure. • Most concerning of all among the gram -negative are the carbapenemases. These genes have made carbapenem- resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) one of the most important challenges facing infectious diseases medicine today. Beta lactamases Modifying enzymes • The most common cause of acquired bacterial resistance to aminoglycosides is through the production of enzymes that acetylate, adenylate, or phosphorylate the aminoglycoside molecule. The resistance conveyed by these actions is usually high level; the chemically modified aminoglycoside no longer binds to the ribosome. • Inactivating enzymes have been described for a number of other antimicrobials; erythromycin (esterase, phosphotransferase ) and chloramphenicol (acetyltransferase). Non genetic causesof antibiotic resistance • Bacteria can be walled off within an abscess cavity (Surgical drainage) • Bacteria can be in a resting state (i.e., not growing) (penicillins) • Protoplasts insensitive to cell wall–active drugs. Later, if such organisms resynthesize their cell walls, they are fully susceptible to these drugs. • The presence of foreign bodies makes successful antibiotic treatment more difficult. • Several artifacts can make it appear that the organisms are resistant (e.g., administration of the wrong antibiotic or the wrong dose or failure of the drug to reach the appropriate site in the body). A good example of the latter is the poor penetration into spinal fluid by several early-generation cephalosporins. Problem of antibiotic resistance • Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global health threat. It requires urgent multisectoral action. WHO has declared that AMR is one of the top 10 global public health threats facing humanity. Misuse and overuse of antimicrobials are the main drivers in the development of drug - resistant pathogens. • Review on AMR estimates that by 2050, as many as ten million people could die each year as a result of AMR.

name: ppt - Pathogenesis of viral infection
text: PATHOGENESIS OF VIRAL INFECTION Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 9 Dear students & Transfer Goal Understand the pathogenesis of viral infection in relation to disease process Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Distinguish the major routes of viral transmission and entry and relate them to the clinical presentation of viral infections. 2. Explain how viral tropism and host -cell receptor/coreceptor interactions determine the cells and tissues susceptible to viral infection. 3. Analyze the relationships among viral pathogenicity, virulence, cytopathogenicity, and patterns of viral infection in determining clinical disease. 4. Appraise the contribution of host immune responses to virus -induced immunopathology and immunosuppression in selected viral diseases. 1. Transmission and entry of the virus into the host 2. Spread in the host 3. Tropism 4. Virulence and cytopathogenicity 5. Patterns of viral infection and disease 6. Virus-induced immunopathology 7. Virus-induced immunosuppression Viral pathogenesis comprises of several stages, including: (1) Transmission and entry of the virus into the host Horizontal Vertical Vector Direct and indirect contact Air-borne Droplet Sexual Feco-oral Pre-natal: In utero, Natal: during delivery (via birth canal), Post natal: through breast-feeding. • Zoonotic (animal-to-human) transmission of viral infections can occur from: • bite of animals (eg, rabies) • insects (eg, dengue, yellow fever) • inhalation of animal excreta (eg, roboviruses). (1) Transmission and entry of the virus into the host • After virus entry into the host, viruses have variable incubation periods. • Incubation period is the time between exposure to the organism and appearance of the first symptoms of the disease. Viruses generally multiply at the site of entry to establish infection in the host. • Some viruses have short incubation periods (influenza—2-4 days), whereas others have long incubation periods (eg, hepatitis B virus—weeks to several months). (1) Transmission and entry of the virus into the host (2) Spread in the host Localized Disseminated • At the site of entry. • spreads mainly by infecting adjacent or neighboring cells. • e.g. influenza, parainfluenza, common cold (rhinoviruses, coronaviruses), gastrointestinal infections (rotaviruses), and skin infections (papillomaviruses). Spread throughout the body. Hematogenous e.g. poliovirus, rabies virus, HBV, HCV, HIV, measles, varicella zoster virus, and others. Neural Portal of entry → local replication → lymphatic/hematogenous/neural spread → target-cell tropism → cell injury and/or immune-mediated disease. Hematogenous spread Localized infection Systemic (diseeminated) infection Neural spread (3) Tropism • Tropism is the capability of viruses to infect a discrete population of cells within an organ. • Cellular or tissue tropism is most often determined by the specific interaction of viral surface proteins (spikes) and cellular receptors on the host cells (3) Tropism • The presence of a receptor for a virus is not always sufficient for viral infection in the target cells. For example, the presence of CD4 (HIV receptor) alone on target cells does not allow virus entry into these cells, but it requires that target cells also express coreceptors, CXCR4 or CCR5 (chemokine receptors) for efficient viral attachment. (3) Tropism • Different viruses may use the same cellular molecule as receptors . Some examples are sialic acid residues functioning as important components of the receptor for influenza, corona. (4) Virulence & Cytopathogenicity • Pathogenicity: The ability of a virus to cause disease in an infected host. • Viral virulence is the degree of pathogenicity of a virus. A virus may be of high or low virulence for a particular host. Different strains of the same virus may differ in the degree of pathogenicity. • Cytopathogenicity: The ability of a virus to cause degenerative changes in cells or cell death . • Virulent viruses: Viral strains that kill target cells and cause disease. • Avirulent or attenuated strains: strains that have mutated and lost their ability to cause cytopathic effects (CPE) and disease. Some attenuated strains can be used as live vaccines. • Interference: If two closely related viruses infect a host, then infection by the first virus can inhibit the function of the second virus. • Replication of the virus results in alterations of cellular morphology and function as well as antigenicity of the virus. When a lytic virus infects a permissive cell, lots of daughter viruses are produced and this is followed by lysis of the infected cells, called cytopathic effects (CPE) • inclusion bodies, • thickening of the nucleus, • swelling, • cell fusion [syncytia]), • followed by cellular lysis. (4) Virulence & Cytopathogenicity Some viruses encode a new class of proteins called virokines and viroreceptors, which contribute to viral virulence by mimicking cellular proteins. Virokines are secreted from infected cells and act as cytokines, helping the cells to proliferate and increase virus production. Viroreceptors resemble cytokine receptors and attract cellular cytokines. E.g Herpes viruses (4) Virulence & Cytopathogenicity (5) Patterns of viral infection & disease Three major outcomes can be attributed to a viral infection Abortive Lytic Persistent No progeny virus particles are produced, but the cell may die because early viral functions can occur. Active virus production is followed by cell death. Small numbers of virus particles are produced with little or no CPE. Latent Chronic viral genetic material remains in host cell without production of virus and may be activated at a later time to produce virus and/or transform the host cell. low level of virus production with little or no CPE; and viral transformation Viral infections can be divided into five categories (5) Patterns of viral infection & disease In acute infection, the virus enters the host, then multiplies at the site of entry and in the target tissue, and this is followed by viremia and cytopathic effects. This type of infection is a lytic infection . The immune system mounts both cellular and humoral responses and successfully eliminates the virus from the host. Examples of acute viral infections followed by clearance of the virus from the host by immune responses are hepatitis A, influenza, parainfluenza, rhino, and corona viruses.

name: ppt - Antiviral agents & resistance
text: ANTIVIRAL AGENTS & RESISTANCE Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 10 Dear students & Transfer Goal Recognize different antiviral drugs and their resistance mechanisms Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Classify antiviral agents according to their molecular target and stage of the viral replication cycle. 2. Explain the relationship between the mechanism of action of selected antiviral agents and their clinical indications. 3. Select an appropriate antiviral agent for a patient according to the causative virus, mechanism of action, and clinically relevant drug characteristics. 4. Analyze the causes and clinical consequences of antiviral resistance and appropriate strategies to minimize or manage it. Why it is difficult to develop antiviral drugs? • Because viruses are obligate intracellular parasites, antiviral agents must be capable of selectively inhibiting viral functions without damaging the host, making the development of such drugs very difficult. • Another limitation is that many rounds of virus replication occur during the incubation period and the virus has spread before symptoms appear , making drug treatment after the development of clinical symptoms relatively ineffective. • The challenges in the development of antiviral agents is identification of the steps in viral replication that are unique to the virus and not used by the normal cell. Among the unique viral events are: • attachment, • penetration, • uncoating, • RNA-directed DNA synthesis (reverse transcription) or RNA -directed RNA synthesis (RNA viruses), • assembly and release of the intact virion. • There is a need for antiviral drugs active against viruses for which: • vaccines are not available or not highly effective because of a multiplicity of serotypes (eg, rhinoviruses) • because of constantly changing viral antigens (eg, influenza, HIV). • Antivirals are usually most effective when started early, because viral replication may peak before or around symptom onset. Clinical benefit depends on the virus, site of infection, host factors, and timing. • Combination therapy is particularly important for viruses with high mutation rates, such as HIV and HCV, because it suppresses replication more effectively and reduces the probability of resistance. Selected antiviral drugs ANTIVIRAL DRUGS Inhibition of early events Inhibition of viral nucleic acid synthesis Inhibition of late events Inhibitors of Uncoating Fusion inhibitors Polymerase inhibitors Reverse transcriptase inhibitors Protease inhibitors Neuraminidase inhibitors Nucleoside analogs Non-nucleoside 1. Inhibitors of uncoating • Amantadine and rimantadine • They are extremely selective, with activity against only influenza A, • they act as inhibitors of the viral M2 protein. • They have been used either as prophylaxis or for therapy. • Unfortunately, since 2001, the rates of resistance to amantadine/rimantadine have increased so sharply (up to 100% for some strains) that they are no longer routinely recommended. 2. Fusion inhibitors • HIV fusion inhibitors act by disrupting the fusion of viral envelope with the cell membrane, preventing cellular infection. The prototype agent is enfuvirtide. 3. Inhibitors of nucleic acid synthesis Nucleoside analogues Nucleotide analogues Non- Nucleoside inhibitors Acyclovir Ganciclovir Zidovudine Lamivudine Ribavirin Idoxuridine and Trifluorothymidine Cidofovir Foscarnet 3. Inhibitors of nucleic acid synthesis (A) Nucleoside analogues • Most antiviral agents are nucleoside analogs that are active against virus -specific nucleic acid polymerases or reverse transcriptases and have much less activity against analogous host enzymes. Some of these agents serve as nucleic acid chain terminators after incorporation into nucleic acids. • Nucleoside analogs cause selective inhibition of viral replication by: • binding better to viral DNA polymerase, rather than to the cellular DNA polymerase; • by being utilized more extensively in virus -infected cells due to the more rapid synthesis of DNA in infected cells. Nucleoside analogues 1. Acyclovir • A guanosine analog. • The key to its benefit is that it must be phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase to be active. Therefore, the compound is essentially nontoxic because it is not phosphorylated or activated in uninfected host cells. Viral thymidine kinase catalyzes the phosphorylation of acyclovir to a monophosphate, then host cell enzymes complete the progression to the diphosphate and, finally, the triphosphate. • Acyclovir triphosphate inhibits viral replication by competing with guanosine triphosphate and inhibiting the function of the virally encoded DNA polymerase. • Susceptible strains of herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 (HSV- 1 and -2) are the most active thymidine kinase inducers and are the most readily inhibited by acyclovir. • Resistant strains of HSV have been recovered from immunocompromised patients, including patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); in most instances, resistance results from mutations in the viral thymidine kinase gene or viral DNA polymerase. 1. Acyclovir Nucleoside analogues • A guanosine analog. • It confers activity against cytomegalovirus ( CMV), because another viral-encoded phosphorylating enzyme (UL97) is present in CMV-infected cells that is, capable of phosphorylating ganciclovir and converting it to the monophosphate. Then, cellular enzymes convert it to the active compound, ganciclovir triphosphate, which inhibits the viral DNA polymerase. • Since ganciclovir can be phosphorylated in normal, uninfected, host cells, toxicity, especially neutropenia, frequently limits therapy. 2. Ganciclovir Nucleoside analogues Nucleoside analogues 3. Zidovudine • Thymidine analog • inhibits the reverse transcriptase of HIV by terminating the developing DNA chain. As with other nucleosides, AZT must be phosphorylated; host cell enzymes carry out the process. • The basis for the relatively selective therapeutic effect of AZT is that HIV reverse transcriptase is more than 100 times more sensitive to AZT than is host cell DNA polymerase. • It is also used for treatment of pregnant HIV-infected women. It has been shown to reduce or prevent the transmission of HIV from the mother to the baby. The drug, however, is toxic and costly. Nucleoside analogues 4. Lamivudine Lamivudine is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor with activity agains t HIV and HBV to disrupt viral DNA synthesis. Lamivudine is phosphorylated intracellularly to its active triphosphate metabolite . This nucleoside analogue is incorporated into viral DNA by HIV reverse transcriptase and HBV polymerase, resulting in DNA chain termination. Nucleoside analogues 5. Ribavirin • A guanosine analog. • Similar to other nucleoside analogs, ribavirin must be phosphorylated to mono, di-, and triphosphate forms, but cellular enzymes can carry out each of these, thus, heightening the risk of toxicity. • It is an inhibitor of RNA polymerase. • It was used used in treatment of HCV. Aerosol administration is used for treatment of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).

name: Online Microbiology Revision (1)
text: NMD3101 · PRINCIPLES OF INFECTION Viral Structure, Classification & Replication Revision session · Lectures 7 & 8 Summarised from the lectures of Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University TODAY'S SESSION What we will revise NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 2 01 Structure Virion, capsid, envelope, genomes, defective viruses, resistance to agents 02 Classification ICTV naming; DNA vs RNA; naked vs enveloped families 03 Replication Five stages, DNA vs RNA strategies, assembly and release 04 Bacteriophages Lytic vs lysogenic cycles, phage therapy, lysogenic conversion 05 Self-test Eight exam-style questions with answers By the end you should be able to… 1 Predict how structure and genome type affect stability, disinfectant susceptibility and entry 2 Outline the replication stages and predict the effect of disrupting each one 3 Differentiate lytic from lysogenic phage replication, and explain lysogenic conversion PART 1 · STRUCTURE What is a virus? NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 3 Smallest replicating microorganisms A set of genes (DNA or RNA) packaged in a capsid, with or without an outer lipid envelope. The complete particle is the virion. Obligate intracellular parasites They can only grow inside cells and depend heavily on host structural and metabolic components. No cell machinery of their own No nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria or other organelles. Typical diameter: 20–400 nm. Ebola virus is filamentous (about 970 nm long), so it is left off the scale. Sizes from the lecture figure. PART 1 · STRUCTURE Naked vs enveloped viruses NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 4 Naked (non-enveloped) Genome inside a defined protein capsid Structure Nucleic acid + capsid (nucleocapsid); no lipid membrane Stability Stable: little loss of infectivity after hours at 37 °C; resistant to detergents, solvents, ethanol, ether Entry Viropexis (receptor-mediated endocytosis) Release Cell lysis: the cell dies and bursts Enveloped Nucleocapsid wrapped in a host-derived lipid bilayer Structure Nucleocapsid + matrix protein inside a lipid envelope studded with glycoprotein spikes Stability Heat-labile; sensitive to detergents, solvents, ethanol, ether and heat Entry Direct fusion, or viropexis Release Budding through the cell membrane PART 1 · STRUCTURE Building blocks of a virion NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 5 Genome DNA or RNA; single- or double-stranded Capsid Protein shell of many identical subunits; protects the genome and gives shape Nucleocapsid Genome + capsid protein complex Envelope Host-derived lipid bilayer carrying viral glycoproteins Matrix protein Bridges the nucleocapsid and the inner face of the envelope Spikes (peplomers) Bind host receptors, drive fusion, and are the main antigens Capsid symmetry Helical Icosahedral Jobs of the capsid / envelope 1 Protect the genome between cells 2 Help entry into the cell 3 Sometimes package early enzymes Many identical subunits and spikes matter for adsorption, hemagglutination and neutralizing antibodies. Helical Icosahedral PART 1 · STRUCTURE Viral genomes NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 6 DNA or RNA, single- or double-stranded. RNA genomes are classed by polarity: + (+) sense Same polarity as mRNA, so it can be translated directly − (–) sense Complementary (antisense) to mRNA; must be copied to make mRNA = Double-stranded One (+) strand paired with one (–) strand ± Ambisense Both (+) and (–) polarity on the same strand Segmented genomes Most RNA genomes are linear; some are segmented into several RNA pieces, each encoding a protein. DNA genomes Can be linear or circular. Diploid retroviruses Most viruses carry one genome copy. Retroviruses (e.g. HIV) carry two identical copies. PART 1 · STRUCTURE Antigens, serotypes & defective viruses NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 7 Antigens & serotypes Envelope glycoproteins and capsid spikes become antigens after infection The host mounts cell-mediated responses (kill infected cells) and humoral responses (clear cell-free virus) Serotypes: type-specific antigenic variants, e.g. poliovirus types 1, 2 and 3. Defective viruses Lack a complete genome, so they cannot fully replicate or cannot form a protein coat. Host-dependent defectives Replicate only in cells that supply the missing genetic function. Satellite viruses Replicate only when a helper virus complements the defect. HBV = helper + HDV = satellite Hepatitis D replicates only in the presence of surface antigen from a co-infecting hepatitis B virus. PART 1 · STRUCTURE Reaction to physical & chemical agents NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 8 Physical agents Heat Naked viruses are stable; enveloped viruses are heat-labile. Most are inactivated at 50–60 °C for 30 min (exception: hepatitis B virus). Cold Freezing temperatures preserve viruses. pH Stable at pH 5–9; enteroviruses resist acid; all viruses are destroyed by alkali. Radiation Ultraviolet light and X-rays inactivate viruses. Chemical agents Formaldehyde Reacts with nucleic acid (single-stranded genomes are inactivated more readily). Spares protein antigenicity, so it is used for inactivated vaccines. Chlorine Higher doses are needed than for bacteria, especially with protein present: poliovirus survives stool treatment that kills typhoid bacilli. QACs & iodine Quaternary ammonium and organic iodine compounds are not effective against viruses. Alcohols Ethanol and isopropanol are relatively ineffective against some viruses, especially picornaviruses. PART 2 · CLASSIFICATION How viruses are named (ICTV) NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 9 The International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses considers: Virion Genome Proteins Envelope Replication Physical & biological properties Family -viridae Herpesviridae Subfamily -virinae Herpesvirinae Genus -virus Herpesvirus Species virus type Herpes simplex virus 1 PART 3 · REPLICATION The viral replication cycle NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 11 1 Adsorption Attachment proteins (spikes) bind cell receptors 2 Penetration & uncoating Virus enters; capsid disassembles to free the genome 3 Synthesis Genome replication, viral mRNA and protein production 4 Assembly Genome is enclosed in a capsid (encapsidation) 5 Release Lysis (naked) or budding (enveloped) Eclipse phase the interval between a virus infecting a cell and the first new infectious virions being assembled inside it. The outcome also depends on the type of cell infected: Permissive cells Permit production of progeny virus and/or viral transformation. Nonpermissive cells Do not allow virus replication, but may allow viral transformation. Abortive infection The cell cannot support replication, but some early viral proteins still cause cell death. PART 3 · REPLICATION Step 1 · Adsorption (attachment) NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 12 Spike (VAP) meets receptor: lock and key Host cell membrane receptors First step of every infection A collision between virion and cell, then VAP–receptor binding. Some viruses need a receptor plus a coreceptor (e.g. HIV). Sets host range and tissue tropism Which cells a virus can infect is decided at VAP–receptor binding: a key determinant of pathogenesis. Last chance for antibodies Once inside a cell the virus is hidden from the immune system, so protection must block attachment or penetration. Exam pearl Most neutralizing antibodies, from natural infection or vaccination, are specific for virion attachment proteins. PART 3 · REPLICATION Step 2 · Penetration & uncoating NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 13 Direct fusion e.g. measles, HIV 1 Spikes on the envelope promote fusion with the plasma membrane. 2 The nucleocapsid is released straight into the cytoplasm. Key contrast: no endosome and no pH trigger. The spike drives fusion at the cell surface. Viropexis Receptor-mediated endocytosis. e.g. influenza, coronavirus; naked viruses also appear to enter this way 1 After adsorption the particle is taken up into an endosome. 2 The nucleocapsid is now inside two membranes: the viral envelope and the endosomal membrane. 3 Low endosomal pH changes a spike protein, so the two membranes fuse. 4 The nucleocapsid is released into the cytoplasm. Uncoating capsid disassembly from the genome; it may occur simultaneously with entry or in a series of steps. PART 3 · REPLICATION Step 3 · Synthesis: where and when NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 14 Cytoplasm THE RULE Most RNA viruses replicate here, the immediate site of entry. THE EXCEPTION Poxviruses (DNA) also replicate in the cytoplasm, so they code for almost all their own replication enzymes. Nucleus THE RULE All other DNA viruses must move from the cytoplasm to the nucleus. THE EXCEPTION Influenza viruses and retroviruses (RNA viruses) replicate in the nucleus. Gene expression is timed Every infection needs virus-specific mRNAs to make viral proteins. EARLY Regulatory proteins and enzymes needed for genome replication LATE Mostly structural proteins needed to assemble progeny virions PART 3 · REPLICATION Step 3 · Genome type decides the strategy NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 15 DNA viruses Transcribed by the host DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RNA pol II) in the nucleus; mRNA is exported to the cytoplasm for translation. Reliance on host machinery depends on genome size (coding potential) Fully host-dependent Host-independent Parvoviruses Smallest. Need dividing cells so a normal S phase copies viral DNA. Most DNA viruses Partly dependent. An early protein induces an unscheduled S phase. Poxviruses Largest. Cytoplasmic and independent; code their own enzymes. RNA viruses Human cells cannot copy RNA from an RNA template, so RNA viruses must supply their own replicase or polymerase (RdRP) to duplicate the genome. (+) sense RNA The genome acts directly as mRNA and is translated immediately on entry into the cytoplasm. Genome = mRNA (–) sense RNA Must bring its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase to make mRNA at the start of infection. Carries RdRP DNA Viruses Parvovirus replication they require the infected cells to be dividing to ensure that a normal S phase occurs and replicates the viral DNA together with the cellular DNA. DNA Viruses they must code for almost all of the enzymes and other proteins required for replicating their DNA. Picornaviruses RNA viruses must provide the replicases or polymerases required to duplicate the RNA genome into daughter RNA genomes. RNA viruses PART 3 · REPLICATION Steps 4 & 5 · Assembly and release NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 16 Assembly (encapsidation) Enclosing the genome in a protein capsid follows four principles: 1 Self-assembly of the component parts 2 Stepwise and ordered 3 Protomers are preformed into capsomeres 4 Begins at a packaging site on the genome Release NAKED Cell lysis. The cell dies and bursts, releasing virions into the environment. ENVELOPED Budding through the cell membrane 1 Viral glycoprotein spikes cluster in the cell membrane 2 Matrix (M) protein coats the inner face 3 M protein attracts the finished nucleocapsid 4 Envelopment; particle is released PART 4 · BACTERIOPHAGES Bacteriophages: viruses of bacteria NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 17 Head nucleic acid inside a protein coat Tail sheath injects the genome into the host Tail fibers bind specific surface receptors Found in more than 140 bacterial genera, in many habitats Genome: single- or double-stranded DNA or RNA Many have syringe-like tails that inject their nucleic acid Prophage: a phage genome integrated into the bacterial genome Lytic phages Make many copies of themselves while killing the host cell. e.g. T-even phages (T2, T4) of E. coli Temperate phages Enter a non-lytic prophage state, replicating along with host DNA. Bacteria carrying prophages are lysogenic; a physiological signal can trigger the lytic cycle, killing the host and releasing phages. e.g. E. coli phage λ (lambda) PART 4 · BACTERIOPHAGES Phage therapy NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 18 Why phages are back Rising antimicrobial resistance has revived interest in phages: the natural predators of bacteria, discovered over 100 years ago. A therapeutic phage should… Preferably be lytic Kill the bacterial host efficiently Be fully characterised to exclude side effects Advantages over antibiotics Strongly host-specific No off-target harm from disrupting the microbiota. Co-evolve with the host They develop new infectivity and mutate alongside their host bacteria. Abundant and diverse Easily isolated, shaped and manipulated from an endless variety of sources. PART 4 · BACTERIOPHAGES Phage replication: lytic vs lysogenic NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 19 Both start the same way. Tail fibers bind specific receptors; the base plate coordinates attachment; a rigid tube is pushed out of the sheath, punctures the membrane and injects the genome (DNA or RNA). Lytic cycle Kills the host 1 Attachment Phage binds the bacterial surface 2 Penetration Viral DNA enters the host cell 3 Biosynthesis Phage DNA replicates; phage proteins are made 4 Maturation New phage particles are assembled 5 Lysis Cell bursts, releasing new phages Lysogenic cycle Dormant prophage 1 Integration Integrase inserts phage DNA into the host genome: a prophage 2 Dormancy Lytic genes are repressed; no progeny made 3 Passive copying Prophage is replicated with the host at each division 4 Stress signal UV light, low nutrients or chemicals 5 Induction Prophage excises and enters the lytic cycle PART 4 · BACTERIOPHAGES Lysogenic conversion & transduction NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 20 Lysogenic conversion A prophage gene alters the bacterium's phenotype. The toxin gene sits in the phage DNA and is expressed together with the repressor gene in the lysogenic state. Toxins from bacteria "converted" by a temperate phage: Diphtheria Scarlet fever Botulism Induction: stress (UV light, low nutrients, chemicals) makes a prophage leave the chromosome and enter the lytic cycle. Transduction Phages carry bacterial DNA from one bacterium to another. Generalized Host DNA is cut into pieces; a random bacterial fragment is occasionally packaged into a phage capsid and delivered to a new host, where recombination can occur. Specialized A prophage excises incorrectly and takes neighbouring bacterial genes with it; these travel with the phage DNA to the next host. Think Why should phages used in therapy be lytic and fully characterised? SELF-TEST Test yourself (1/2) NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 21 1 A mutant virus keeps its genome and capsid but loses its envelope glycoproteins. Which function is lost most directly? A Recognition of host-cell receptors B Segmentation of the genome C Replication of host-cell DNA D Synthesis of peptidoglycan 2 A specimen containing an enveloped virus is left at 37 °C for several hours and loses most of its infectivity. Why? A Enveloped viruses resist desiccation B Enveloped viruses are always solvent-resistant C Enveloped viruses are heat-labile D Enveloped viruses cannot acquire host membranes 3 Hepatitis D virus replicates only in a person co-infected with hepatitis B. HDV is best described as: A A naked capsid virus B A satellite (defective) virus C A temperate phage D A lytic phage 4 After receptor binding, particles are internalised into endosomes; acidification changes a spike protein and membranes fuse. This entry mechanism is: A Direct fusion B Budding C Viropexis D Transduction SELF-TEST Test yourself (2/2) NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 22 5 Capsid assembly begins at a specific genomic locus. It is called the: A Promoter region B Packaging site C Integration (int) locus D Repressor-binding site 6 A cell first makes regulatory proteins and replication enzymes, then abundant structural proteins. The late proteins are needed for: A Genome replication B Attachment to receptors C Maintaining a prophage D Assembly of progeny virions 7 Phage DNA is integrated into the bacterial chromosome and copied passively at each division; no phage is made. The phage is in the: A Lysogenic cycle B Lytic cycle C Eclipse phase D Assembly phase 8 Diphtheria, scarlet fever and botulism toxins are encoded by phage DNA in the bacteria. This phenomenon is called: A Viropexis B Generalized transduction C Induction D Lysogenic conversion SELF-TEST Answers & why NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 23 1 A Recognition of host-cell receptors Envelope glycoproteins (spikes) mediate attachment. 2 C Heat-labile Enveloped viruses lose infectivity fast at 37 °C; naked viruses are stable. 3 B Satellite (defective) virus It needs a helper: HDV depends on HBV surface antigen. 4 C Viropexis Receptor-mediated endocytosis; endosomal low pH triggers fusion. 5 B Packaging site Assembly starts at this locus; it is self-assembling and stepwise. 6 D Assembly of progeny virions Late proteins are mostly structural; early ones are regulatory or replication enzymes. 7 A Lysogenic cycle The prophage is copied passively with the host genome; lytic genes are repressed. 8 D Lysogenic conversion Toxin genes on temperate-phage DNA change the bacterium's phenotype.

text: A 28-year-old female presents with dysuria and urinary frequency. A clean-catch midstream urine culture yields>105 CFU/mL of Escherichia coli. The patient asks how a bacterium normally found in her digestive tract caused a bladder infection. Which concept best explains this clinical scenario? A. Opportunistic infection caused by disruption of normal mucosal barriers B. Primary infection caused by acquisition of an environmental transient pathogen C. Vector-borne transmission from host skin flora D. Dysbiosis resulting from an absolute loss of anaerobic commensals E. Malfunction of the mucociliary escalator leading to systemic colonization ANSWER: A A 65-year-old male receiving broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics for severe pneumonia develops severe watery diarrhea and abdominal cramping. Stool testing confirms Clostridioides difficile colitis. Which mechanism primarily enabled C. difficile to cause disease in this patient? A. Loss of colonization resistance due to disruption of normal gut microbiota B. Direct neutralization of gastric hydrochloric acid by antibiotic agents C. Destruction of the ciliated epithelial lining in the colon D. Eradication of transient environmental flora from the lower ileum E. Translocation of resident skin staphylococci into the systemic circulation ANSWER: A • A 32-year-old woman presents to the clinic with vaginal itching and a thick, white discharge following a course of oral amoxicillin for a sinus infection. Loss of glycogen deposition driven by decreased systemic estrogen B. Disruption of skin lipids and fatty acids in the perineal region C.
