How should this microorganism be classified? A. Eukaryote B. Prokaryote C. Virus D. Prion E. Protozoan ANSWER: B A 45-year-old patient undergoing chemotherapy develops a central venous catheter - associated bloodstream infection. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus epidermidis . The patient asks if this organism was contracted from the hospital environment. Which statement best describes the normal niche of this organism? A. It is a resident microorganism of the human skin flora B. It is a transient pathogen restricted to the lower respiratory tract C. It is an environmental microbe that cannot survive on human epithelia ANSWER: A A medical student evaluates a routine Gram stain from an endotracheal tube aspirate of a ventilated patient. The laboratory report notes the presence of a few transient bacterial cells. Which anatomical clearance mechanism normally keeps the lower trachea and large bronchi free of permanent microbial colonization? A. Ciliary movement of the mucociliary blanket B. Secretion of hydrochloric acid and peptic enzymes C. Lactic acid production maintaining an environmental pH of 4 D. High concentration of bile salts and anaerobic fermentation E. Continuous desquamation of heavily keratinized squamous cells ANSWER: A A 19 -year-old college student presents with fever, severe headache, and neck stiffness. A nasopharyngeal swab reveals Neisseria meningitidis . A asymptomatic roommate also tests positive for the same organism in her nasopharynx. What term best describes the roommate's status? A. Latent eukaryotic infection B. Dysbiosis-induced colitis C. Vector-borne amplification D. Active systemic bacteremia E. Carrier state ANSWER: E A 72-year-old male with a history of rheumatic heart disease undergoing a dental extraction develops subacute bacterial endocarditis two weeks later. The isolated pathogen is part of the normal oral flora. Which event initiated the pathogenesis of this patient's endocarditis? A. Overgrowth of spore-forming anaerobes in the stomach B. Loss of cutaneous fatty acid bactericidal activity C. Transient bacteremia following mucosal trauma D. Colonization resistance failure in the distal urethra E. Shift of gut microbiota from Bacteroides to Lactobacillus ANSWER: C A healthy 24-year-old medical student undergoes a screening nasal swab. The laboratory reports colonization with Staphylococcus aureus. Which anatomical site serves as the primary reservoir for S. aureus in approximately 25% to 30% of healthy humans? A. Anterior nares / Nasopharynx B. Distal 1 cm of the urethra C. Mid-jejunum D. Gastric antrum E. Renal pelvis ANSWER: A A patient in the intensive care unit with a central line develops high fever, hypotension, and generalized purpura. Blood cultures yield Gram-negative bacilli. Which specific structural component of these bacteria is directly responsible for triggering endotoxic shock and fever? A. Lipid A component of lipopolysaccharide B. Flagellar hook proteins ANSWER: A A 22-year-old student presents with dry cough, low-grade fever, and fatigue. Chest radiography shows patchy interstitial infiltrates. Sputum culture confirms Mycoplasma pneumoniae. The attending physician avoids prescribing beta-lactam antibiotics because Mycoplasma species natively lack which target structure? A. Plasma membrane B. 70S Ribosomes C. Circular chromosome D. Cell wall E. Cytoplasmic enzyme ANSWER: D A 60-year-old patient undergoing chemotherapy develops systemic Streptococcus pneumoniae infection. The pathogenic strain is heavily encapsulated. What is the primary mechanism by which the capsule promotes bacterial virulence in this patient? A. Protection against host phagocytosis B. Secretion of exotoxins that lyse red blood cells C. Direct conjugation with host epithelial cells D. Facilitation of high-speed motility through viscous mucus E. Generation of ATP via the electron transport system ANSWER: A An outbreak of severe diarrhea occurs in a daycare center. Isolates of enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) are analyzed. The pathogenic strain possesses fine, hair-like surface projections that bind to specific receptors on human intestinal epithelial cells. Which bacterial structure is mediating this attachment? A. Sex pili B. Flagella C. Endospores D. Common pili (fimbriae) E. Lipoteichoic acids ANSWER: D A hospital laboratory isolates a multi-drug resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae strain. Genetic analysis demonstrates that the resistance genes are located on a small, circular, extrachromosomal double-stranded DNA molecule that replicates independently of the chromosome. What is this structure? A. Nucleoid B. Plasmid C. Endospore D. Inclusion granule E. Ribosome ANSWER: B A farmer suffers a deep puncture wound from a rusty nail soiled with dirt. Ten days later, he presents with severe muscle spasms and jaw stiffness (trismus) caused by Clostridium tetani. The organism survived in the oxygenated, dry soil for years before entry. text: HEPATITIS VIRUSES (Part 2) Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 22 Dear students & Transfer Goal Recognize the microbiology of Hepatitis C, A & E viruses Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Describe the structural and genomic characteristics of Hepatitis viruses. 2. Explain the pathogenesis and immune responses associated with Hepatitis viruses infections, and their role in acute, chronic, and fulminant disease progression. 3. Differentiate between the clinical syndromes and natural history of HBV, HCV, and HDV infections, including acute, chronic, and carrier states. 4. Interpret the diagnostic utility of virologic and serologic markers in distinguishing phases of infection and guiding clinical management. 5. Evaluate the current strategies for treatment of Hepatitis viruses infections. 6. Apply principles of prevention and control of viral hepatitis, including vaccination, post-exposure prophylaxis, infection control precautions. HEPATITIS C VIRUS Structure of HCV - HCV is the only member of the Hepacivirus genus of the Flaviviridae family. - HCV has a positive-sense RNA genome, and is enveloped. Structure of HCV • The genome encodes 10 proteins , including: • 3 structural [one core protein and two glycoproteins (E1, E2)] as well as • 7 non -structural proteins. The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase is error prone and generates mutations in the glycoprotein and other genes. This generates antigenic variability. Such variability makes development of a vaccine very difficult. Structure of HCV • There are seven major genotypes (1 -7) of HCV (clades), and between and within each genotype there is considerable genetic and antigenic diversity. Different genotypes predominate in different parts of the world. • Genotype 4a is the most common in Egypt. • HCV Genetic diversity is not correlated with differences in clinical disease, although differences exist in response to antiviral therapy. Pathogenesis & Immunity of HCV • HCV is transmitted primarily in infected blood and sexually . Intravenous drug abusers and tattoo recipients are at highest risk to HCV infection. Screening procedures have led to a reduction in the levels of transmission by blood transfusion and organ donation. Almost all (>90%) HIV -infected people who are or were intravenous drug users are infected with HCV . Pathogenesis & Immunity of HCV • The high incidence of chronic asymptomatic infections promotes the spread of the virus in the population. • The ability of HCV to remain cell associated and prevent host cell death promotes persistent infection but results in liver disease later in life. • The virus’s ability to evade interferon action and change its antigenicity help the virus establish chronic disease. • Cell-mediated immune responses are necessary to resolve the infection but also cause tissue damage. • Antibody to HCV is not protective . Due to the selective pressure from the host, and the antigenic variations that occur in the E2/E1 proteins, the virus evade the humoral immune response and establish a persistent infection. • HCV antibodies have also been implicated in the formation of immune complexes against the liver and other tissues. During acute infection, the rise in serum transaminases is due to immune -mediated hepatocyte damage. The immune complexes are also deposited in other tissues and cause extrahepatic complications, including vasculitis, arthritis, glomerulonephritis, and others. Pathogenesis & Immunity of HCV • Chronic HCV infection results in inflammatory response that may lead to progressive fibrosis and hepatocarcinogenesis. • The chronic infection can exhaust CD8 cytotoxic T cells so they cannot resolve the infection. Pathogenesis & Immunity of HCV Clinical syndromes of HCV • A viremia can be detected within 1 to 3 weeks of infection. • The viremia lasts 4 to 6 months in people with an acute infection and longer than 10 years in those with a persistent infection. • The incubation period ranges from 2 weeks to 6 months. • HCV has the highest rate of chronicity (> 75%). • More commonly (>70% of cases), the initial disease is asymptomatic or clinically mild (20–30% have jaundice; 10 –20% have only nonspecific symptoms such as anorexia, malaise, and abdominal pain) but establishes chronic persistent disease . The predominant symptom is chronic fatigue. • Chronic persistent disease often progresses to chronic active hepatitis within 10 to 15 years and to cirrhosis (20% of chronic cases ) and liver failure (20% of cirrhotic cases ) after 20 years. HCV promotes the development of hepatocellular carcinoma after 30 years in up to 5% of chronically infected patients. Clinical syndromes of HCV Virologic & Serologic Response to HCV • Currently available HCV antibody tests have a window period from exposure to HCV to detection of antibody of approximately 8-11 weeks. • Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAT) can detect HCV RNA approximately 1-2 weeks after exposure. This means that for the first eight weeks following exposure to HCV antibody tests may not be able to detect HCV antibodies, and for the first 1-2 weeks following HCV exposure NATs may not be able to detect HCV RNA. Virologic & Serologic Response to HCV • In chronic hepatitis C , serum ALT concentrations may fluctuate over time and may even be intermittently normal. HCV RNA may persist for decades. Diagnosis is confirmed by finding positive anti-HCV and positive HCV - RNA for ≥ 6 months after initial infection.

name: ppt: L21  Hepatitis Viruses (B, D)
text: HEPATITIS VIRUSES (Part 1) Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 21 Dear students & Transfer Goal Recognize the microbiology of Hepatitis B & C viruses Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Describe the structural and genomic characteristics of Hepatitis viruses. 2. Explain the pathogenesis and immune responses associated with Hepatitis viruses infections, and their role in acute, chronic, and fulminant disease progression. 3. Differentiate between the clinical syndromes and natural history of HBV, HCV, and HDV infections, including acute, chronic, and carrier states. 4. Interpret the diagnostic utility of virologic and serologic markers in distinguishing phases of infection and guiding clinical management. 5. Evaluate the current strategies for treatment of Hepatitis viruses infections. 6. Apply principles of prevention and control of viral hepatitis, including vaccination, post-exposure prophylaxis, infection control precautions. HEPATITIS B VIRUS Structure of HBV • HBV is the major member of the hepadnaviruses. Other members of this family include woodchuck, ground squirrel, and duck hepatitis viruses. HBV infects the liver and, to a lesser extent, the kidneys and pancreas of only humans and chimpanzees. Structure of HBV • HBV is a small enveloped DNA virus. Specifically, the genome is a small, circular, partly double - stranded DNA . Although a DNA virus, it encodes a reverse transcriptase and replicates through an RNA intermediate. Structure of HBV • The virion, also called the Dane particle, is 42 nm in diameter. The virions are unusually stable for an enveloped virus. They resist treatment with ether, low pH, freezing, and moderate heating . These characteristics assist transmission from one person to another and hamper disinfection. The viral genome encodes four overlapping open reading frames (ORFs), C, P , S, and X, from which functional viral proteins are produced: o Hepatitis B Core antigen HBc and its relatives such as E antigen (HBe); HBc: viral capsid protein which is only present inside hepatocytes and detected in liver biopsies and not detected in serum. HBe; It is secreted in a soluble form and detected only in infected patient’s serum. o Pol from P (Polymerase with reverse transcriptase and ribonuclease H activity); o three types of Surface antigens, L-HBs, M-HBs, and S-HBs, (Large, medium and small) from S; o HBV X protein (HBx) from X. Regulatory protein for transcription and is required for initiation of infection. It can be detected only in the cells replicating the virus. Replication of HBV • The attachment of HBV to hepatocytes is mediated by the HBsAg glycoproteins. • On penetration into the cell, the nucleocapsid delivers the genome to the nucleus, where the partial DNA strand of the genome is completed to form a complete double -stranded DNA circle (covalently closed circular DNA; cccDNA) • Transcription of the genome is controlled by cellular transcription elements found in hepatocytes. • Viral genome can be integrated randomly in the host genome . This is not required for viral replication but it is one of the important mechanisms for hepatocyte transformation and HCC development. Replication of HBV Pathogenesis & Immunity of HBV • HBV can cause acute or chronic , symptomatic or asymptomatic disease. Which of these occurs seems to be determined by the person’s immune response to the infection. Transmission of HBV • The major source of infectious virus is blood, but HBV can be found in semen, saliva, milk, vaginal secretions, and amniotic fluid. • The most efficient way to acquire HBV is through: • (1) injection of the virus into the bloodstream [Per-cutaneous transmission including intramuscular , intravenous, subcutaneous or intra-dermal injections, tattooing, ear piercing and needle stick. Contamination of skin lesions (fresh cutaneous scratch, abrasion and burns). Infected blood and blood products through transfusion or dialysis. • (2) Common but less efficient routes of infection are sexual contact and birth (Perinatal transmission when mothers are HBsAg positive due to leak of maternal blood to infant’s circulation during birth. Transplacental transmission is rare). • The virus starts to replicate in hepatocytes of the liver within 3 days of its acquisition, with minimal cytopathic effect. • Symptoms may not be observed for 45 days or longer because they are primarily caused by immunopathology. • The infectious dose, the route of infection, and the person determine the incubation period. Infection proceeds for a relatively long time without causing liver damage (i.e., elevation of liver enzyme levels) or symptoms. Pathogenesis & Immunity of HBV • Copies of the HBV genome integrate into the hepatocyte DNA and can remain latent. HBsAg particles continue to be released into the blood even after virion release has ended and until the infection is resolved. • An individual is infectious when both the HBsAg and the HBeAg components of the virion can be detected in the blood. Pathogenesis & Immunity of HBV • Cell-mediated immunity and inflammation are responsible for causing the symptoms and effecting resolution of the HBV infection by eliminating the infected hepatocyte. • An insufficient T-cell response to the infection generally results in the occurrence of mild symptoms, an inability to resolve the infection, and development of chronic hepatitis. • Chronic infection also exhausts CD8 T cells, preventing them from killing infected cells. Infants and young children have an immature cell - mediated immune response and are less able to resolve the infection, but they suffer less tissue damage and milder symptoms. • As many as 90% of infants infected perinatally become chronic carriers. Viral replication persists in these people for long periods. Pathogenesis & Immunity of HBV Immune Response to HBV inability to resolve the infection, and development of chronic hepatitis effecting resolution of the HBV infection by eliminating the infected hepatocyte.

name: PPT - Introduction to medical mycology
text: INTRODUCTION TO MEDICAL MYCOLOGY Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 11 Dear students & Transfer Goal Recognize medically important fungi Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Interpret the major morphological features of medically important fungi and relate them to their mode of growth and pathogenic potential. 2. Differentiate superficial, subcutaneous, systemic, and opportunistic mycoses using clinical presentation, host factors, and tissue involvement. 3. Apply appropriate laboratory diagnostic approaches to common superficial and opportunistic fungal infections based on specimen type and fungal characteristics. 4. Analyze the relationship between fungal virulence mechanisms, host immune status, route of transmission, and the resulting clinical manifestations. • Medical mycology is the study of fungi that cause human disease, including their morphology, classification, pathogenesis, laboratory diagnosis, treatment and prevention . Eukaryotic cell • Fungi are eukaryotes with a higher level of biologic complexity than bacteria. They reproduc e both asexually (production of spores, budding) and sexually (production of zygotes). Fungi may be unicellular or may differentiate and become multicellular by the development of long, branching filaments. Structure of fungal cell Fungal cell wall structure Fungal cells have a rigid cell wall (made of complex polysaccharides such as mannans, glucans, and chitins in close association with each other and with structural proteins) Mannoproteins of the cell wall are composed of mannan found on the cell surface where they are linked to various proteins. Mannoproteins are very important since antibodies are readily developed against these molecules on the cell surface. cytoplasmic membrane (made of ergosterol). YEAST MOLD Morphologic classification Yeasts round cellular form. reproducing by a process of asexual budding, e.g. Cryptococcus Pseudohyphae elongated yeast cells growing end-to-end. e.g. Candida Molds filamentous, tube -like structures called hyphae, mycelium . ( septate molds), others do not form septa (aseptate molds ). They reproduce asexually (spores), or sexually (zygote). e.g. Aspergillus Dimorphic can transition between morphological forms depending on environmental conditions. thermally dimorphic fungi, yeast-like (37°C) hyphae (ambient temperature) e.g. Histoplasma capsulatum yeasts Classification by diseases 1. Superficial mycoses such as the dermatophytes, cause indolent lesions of the skin and its appendages , commonly known as ringworm and athlete’s foot, without typically spreading to deeper tissues. Classification by diseases 2. Subcutaneous mycoses Rare in Egypt characteristically cause infection through the skin, followed by subcutaneous or lymphatic spread. e.g. mycetoma Tropical regions Classification by diseases 3. Opportunistic mycoses are those found in the environment or in the resident flora that produce disease primarily in immunocompromised hosts. E.g. Aspergillus, Candida, Cryptococcus, Pneumocystis, Mucor. Aspergillosis (lung) Rhinocerebral lung Meningitis Skin, mm, UTI Pneumonia Classification by diseases 4. Systemic mycoses are the most virulent fungi and may cause serious and progressive systemic disease in previously healthy persons. They are not found in the human microbiota. Although their major potential is to produce deep-seated visceral infections and systemic spread. e.g. Histoplasma capsulatum NOT in Egypt America Many opportunistic fungal infections are primarily diseases of patients with impaired host defenses rather than highly virulent pathogens in healthy individuals. Selected fungal infections 1. Dermatophytes • General term for species invading superficial layers of skin. Of the many species involved, those belonging to Epidermophyton, Microsporum and Trichophyton are of greatest importance. Transmission By contact with fungal material on skin scales. Pathogenesis Skin inflammation, pruritus – sometimes localized hypersensitivity reactions. Diseases Tinea, ringworm, athlete’s foot. Laboratory identification Examination of KOH-treated skin scrapings for hyphae; fluorescence under Wood’s lamp. Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) Treatment Topical (imidazoles) and oral antifungal agents (griseofulvin, itraconazole, terbinafine). 1. Dermatophytes

name: PPT - Antifungal agents & resistance
text: ANTIFUNGAL AGENTS & RESISTANCE Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 12 Dear students & Transfer Goal Understand antifungal agents and their resistance mechanisms Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Differentiate the mechanisms of action of major antifungal drug classes based on their fungal cellular targets. 2. Interpret the clinical spectrum and pharmacologic properties of antifungal agents to guide treatment of common and life-threatening fungal infections. 3. Select an appropriate antifungal agent for a patient according to the fungal pathogen, site/severity of infection, and important drug toxicities. 4. Analyze antifungal resistance mechanisms by relating changes in drug targets, drug uptake, efflux, or biosynthetic pathways to therapeutic failure. • Compared with antibacterial agents, relatively few antifungals are available for treatment of fungal infections. Many substances with antifungal activity have proved to be unstable, to be toxic to humans , or to have undesirable pharmacologic characteristics, such as poor diffusion into tissues. Newer antifungal agents target fungal -specific cellular features and demonstrate lower toxicity than older drug classes. Mechanism of action of antifungals I. Antifungals acting on cell membrane • Action: The polyenes nystatin and amphotericin B are lipophilic and bind to ergosterol , the dominant sterol in the cytoplasmic membrane of fungal cells. After binding, they form annular channels, which penetrate the membrane and lead to leakage of essential small molecules from the cytoplasm and cell death. 1. Polyenes I. Antifungals acting on cell membrane • Spectrum of activity: Almost all fungi are susceptible to amphotericin B , and the development of resistance is rare. Use of amphotericin B is limited to progressive, life-threatening fungal infections. • Amphotericin B is insoluble in water and must be administered intravenously as a colloidal suspension • Side effects: The major limitation to amphotericin B therapy is the toxicity created by its affinity for mammalian as well as fungal membranes. Intravenous Infusion is commonly followed by chills, fever, headache, and dyspnea. The most serious toxic effect is renal dysfunction . The even greater toxicity of nystatin limits its use to topical preparations 1. Polyenes I. Antifungals acting on cell membrane • Preparations that complex amphotericin B with lipids (liposomal amphotericin) have been used as a means to limit toxicity. 1. Polyenes I. Antifungals acting on cell membrane • Action: Their activity is based on inhibition of the enzyme “lanosterol 14-α-demethylase” responsible for conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol, the major component of the fungal cell membrane. This leads to ergosterol depletion and lanosterol accumulation, forming defective membranes. 2. Azoles Azoles are generally fungistatic against many fungi rather than uniformly fungicidal. I. Antifungals acting on cell membrane • Spectrum of activity: Fluconazole is primarily active against yeasts, including many Cryptococcus and Candida species. Mold-active azoles (itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, and isavuconazole) have extended activity against molds such as Aspergillus species . These Most of these agents can be given orally or parenterally. Topical agents (ketoconazole, clotrimazole, and miconazole) are available as topical preparations for superficial mycoses. 2. Azoles I. Antifungals acting on cell membrane • Side effects: Azoles can cause varying degrees of liver toxicity. Additionally, many systemic azoles, can adversely affect cardiac myocyte repolarization and therefore prolong the QTc interval on an E CG, placing patients at increased risk for cardiac arrhythmias. • Azoles can also affect the precursors of some hormones and may therefore cause endocrinological side effects , restricting their use in pregnancy. 2. Azoles I. Antifungals acting on cell membrane • Action: The allylamines act by inhibition of an enzyme (squalene epoxidase) in the early stages of ergosterol synthesis. 3. Allylamines Spectrum of activity: The allylamine group includes an oral and topical agent , Terbinafine is particularly effective against dermatophytes and accumulates in keratinized tissues, making it an important treatment for tinea infections and onychomycosis. II. Antifungals acting on nucleic acid synthesis • Action: 5-Flucytosine (5FC) is an analog of cytosine. It is a potent inhibitor of RNA transcription and DNA synthesis. Flucytosine II. Antifungals acting on nucleic acid synthesis • Spectrum of activity: Flucytosine is well absorbed after oral administration. It is active against most clinically important yeasts, including Candida albicans and Cryptococcus neoformans, but it has little activity against molds. • Side effects: The frequent development of mutational resistance during therapy limits its application to mild yeast infections or its use in combination with amphotericin B for cryptococcal meningitis . The primary toxic effect of flucytosine is a reversible bone marrow suppression that can lead to neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. Flucytosine III. Antifungals acting on cell wall synthesis • Action: Echinocandins inhibit a glucan biosynthetic enzyme (β-1,3- D-glucan synthase) required for the synthesis of fungal cell wall . Echinocandin administration, therefore, causes morphologic distortions and osmotic instability in yeasts and molds, similar to the effect of β-lactams on bacteria. Echinocandins III. Antifungals acting on cell wall synthesis • Spectrum of activity : Caspofungin, has activity against Candida and Aspergillus. Although highly active against many Candida species, the echinocandins tend to be used as second -line agents for invasive aspergillosis. Cryptococcus neoformans whose cell wall glucans have a slightly different structure, are more tolerant of echinocandins. • Newer echinocandins, micafungin and anidulafungin, have the same mode of action and a similar spectrum of antifungal activity. • Side effects: Since there are no similar glucans in humans, echinocandin toxicity is minimal. Echinocandins IV . Other antifungals Griseofulvin • Action: acts on the microtubules and associated proteins that make up the mitotic spindle. It interferes with cell division. • Spectrum of activity : after oral administration, it is absorbed from GIT and concentrates in the keratinized layers of the skin. It is active only against the agents of superficial mycoses. • Side effects : Clinical response is slow. Prolonged therapy may be required. To Sum Up Antifungal resistance • Many of the same resistance mechanisms observed in bacteria are also found in fungi. • Fungi tend to primarily inactivate drug activity using efflux pumps and by altering their biosynthetic pathways. • In contrast to bacteria, fungi do not make hydrolytic enzymes to inactivate antibiotics to the same extent as bacteria.

name: PPT - Principles of vaccines
text: PRINCIPLES OF VACCINES Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 13 Dear students & Transfer Goal Understand the principle and types of vaccines Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Define vaccine and Recognize the principle of vaccination 2. Classify different types of vaccines 3. Differentiate between inactivated and live attenuated vaccines 4. Identify the advantages and disadvantages of different types of vaccines 5. Relate different types of vaccines to the generated immune response What is vaccine? • The word “vaccine” originates from the Latin Variolae vaccinae (cowpox), which Edward Jenner demonstrated in 1798 could prevent smallpox in humans. Today the term ‘vaccine’ applies to all biological preparations, produced from living organisms, that enhance immunity against disease and either prevent (prophylactic vaccines) or, in some cases, treat disease (therapeutic vaccines). • Vaccines are administered in liquid form, either by injection, by oral, or by intranasal routes. Principle of vaccination • Vaccines artificially stimulate immunity through exposure to an antigenic substance. • An effective vaccine does not protect against disease until it is administered in the proper dosage to susceptible individuals. • Failure to reach all sectors of the population with complete courses of immunization is reflected in the continued occurrence of outbreaks in populations who refuse immunization. • Active immunization → vaccine → slower onset → memory → long-term protection • Passive immunization → antibody → immediate protection → temporary → no memory • Herd immunity refers to the fact that the risk of infection among susceptible individuals in a population is reduced by the presence of adequate numbers of immune individuals. However, the threshold of immunity needed for this indirect protective effect depends on many factors, including the transmissibility of the infectious agent, the nature of the vaccine- induced immunity, and the distribution of the immune individuals. Principle of vaccination Herd immunity Vaccines are composed of either the entire disease-causing microorganism or some of its components. • From living organisms that have been weakened, usually from cultivation under sub -optimal conditions (also called attenuation), or from genetic modification, which has the effect of reducing their ability to cause disease; • From whole organisms that have been inactivated by chemical, thermal or other means; Vaccines are composed of either the entire disease-causing microorganism or some of its components. • From components of the disease -causing organism, such as specific proteins and polysaccharides, or nucleic acid • From inactivated toxins of toxin-producing bacteria, called toxoid. • From the conjugation of polysaccharides to proteins (this increases the effectiveness of polysaccharide vaccines in young children) Types of vaccines 1. Live attenuated 2. Inactivated 3. Toxoid 4. Subunit 5. Conjugate 6. Recombinant 7. Naked DNA 8. mRNA 1. Live attenuated vaccines • These wild viruses or bacteria are attenuated (weakened) in a laboratory, by serial passages in animals or cell cultures. As more is learned about microbial genes involved in disease pathogenesis, attenuated vaccine s can be engineered in the laboratory. • T o produce an immune response, live, attenuated vaccines must replicate in the vaccinated person. • Advantages • Acting more like the natural infection with regard to their effect on immunity. Because live attenuated organisms replicate within the host, they can activate both MHC class I and class II pathways, resulting in both cellular and humoral immune responses. When administered through a mucosal route, live attenuated vaccines can stimulate local secretory IgA and mucosal immune responses Disadvantages • risk of reversion to greater virulence, • severe infection in immunocompromised hosts, • limited storage and shelf life in some cases (destroyed by heat and light). • interference with the vaccine virus by circulating antibody. 1. Live attenuated vaccines • The live, attenuated viral vaccines as: • MMR (measles, mumps, rubella), • varicella. • Bacterial live attenuated vaccines as: • Typhoid vaccine (Ty21a), • Bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG). 1. Live attenuated vaccines 2. Inactivated vaccines • They are made by purifying bacterial or viral preparations to a certain extent and then inactivating their infectivity in a way that does minimal damage to the important proteins; mild chemical ( formalin) or thermal treatment is frequently used. Adjuvant is added to boost the immunogenicity, as they enhance uptake by presenting cells e.g. aluminium hydroxide or aluminium phosphate.

name: PPT - Gram positive cocci of medical importance
ref: file:L14 Gram positive cocci of medical importance.pdf
text: GRAM POSITIVE COCCI OF MEDICAL IMPORTANCE Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg MED217 Principles of infection Lecture 14 Dear students & Transfer Goal Recognize Gram positive cocci of medical importance Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Recognize different Gram-positive cocci of medical importance 2. Relate the virulence factors of Gram-positive cocci to their pathogenesis 3. Interpret method of transmission of Gram-positive cocci to disease process 4. Select appropriate antibiotic treatment options for different Gram -positive cocci infections The aerobic gram-positive cocci are a heterogeneous collection of spherical bacteria that are common residents in the mouth, gastrointestinal tract, genitourinary tract, and skin surface. he most important genera are • Staphylococcus (Staph aureus, Staph epidermidis) • Streptococcus (Str pyogenes, Str agalactiae, Str pneumoniae, oral streptococci) • Enterococcus. Staphylococcus • Genus contains over 30 species, of which three are of greatest medical importance Staphylococcus aureus Staphylococcus epidermidis Staphylococcus saprophyticus Coagulase positive staphylococci Coagulase negative staphylococci Staphylococcus aureus • Gram-positive cocci in clusters. • Some strains produce capsules. • Non-fastidious • Facultative anaerobe (capable of aerobic and anaerobic respiration) • Normal habitat: humans (and animals associated with them); skin, especially nose and perineum (carriage rates higher in hospital patients and staff). • Spread: is mainly by contact. Staphylococcus aureus Protein A: interacts non-specifically with host IgG antibodies reducing opsonization and causing local activation of complement. Extracellular toxins: • enterotoxins, • exfoliative toxin, • TSST (toxic shock syndrome toxin), cell-associated: capsule, protein A, fibronectin-binding protein, collagen- binding proteins Enzymes: Coagulase & catalase, protease, nuclease • membrane- damaging toxins (haemolysins), • leukocidin Superantigens • Diseases (Infections) • Boils; skin sepsis; postoperative wound infection; osteomyelitis; pneumonia endocarditis, sepsis • Scalded skin syndrome; food- borne infection, toxic shock syndrome Staphylococcus aureus • Diseases (Infections) Staphylococcus aureus Toxic shock syndrome Fever Skin rash and desquamation Multisystem organ failure Hypotension Shock No Bacteremia Food poisoning Short incubation period No fever Vomiting Scalded skin syndrome Skin desquamation • Laboratory Identification Staphylococcus aureus White or golden colonies on blood agar Catalase positive Coagulase positive most strains ferment mannitol. • Treatment • In susceptible isolates, antibiotics of choice are beta -lactamase-stable penicillins; however, the vast majority of hospital isolates are beta-lactamase producers. • Multiple drug resistance (including methicillin and tolerance or resistance to vancomycin) is a worldwide problem. Vancomycin is the drug of choice for MRSA. • Mupirocin can be used for topical treatment of carriage. • Prevention of spread by isolation and / or treatment of carriers in high -risk areas in hospital. Staphylococcus aureus Staphylococcus epidermidis Characteristics Gram-positive cocci in clusters. Non-fastidious; facultative anaerobe Transmission Normal habitat: skin (carriage rate approximately 100%). Spread by contact with self, other patients or hospital personnel. Almost all infections acquired in hospital, but may be endogenous. Pathogenesis Extracellular slime production may be a marker of virulence and aid in the colonization of plastic implants (e.g. intravenous catheters and prostheses). Diseases Opportunist pathogen associated with device-related sepsis (e.g. catheter -related sepsis; prosthetic valve endocarditis; infection of artificial joints; shunt infections) Laboratory identification White colonies on blood agar; catalase positive, coagulase negative, mannitol not fermented. Treatment Antibiotic resistance: often multiresistant (including penicillin and methicillin). Prevention of infection: catheter care. Staphylococcus epidermidis • Laboratory Identification Staphylococcus epidermidis White colonies on blood agar Catalase positive Coagulase negative Do not ferment mannitol. Streptococcus • A large group of Gram -positive cocci distributed widely in humans and animals, mostly forming part of the normal flora , but some species responsible for some major infections. • Individual cells occur in pairs and chains. • The medically significant streptococci may be divided: 1. on the basis of either haemolysis on blood agar (complete haemolysis, beta; partial haemolysis, alpha; no haemolysis, gamma) or 2. by the presence or absence of a group - specific carbohydrate antigen (i.e. the Lancefield group labelled alphabetically A to V). Streptococcus pyogenes • Gram-positive cocci in chains • non-motile • facultative anaerobe Group A beta hemolytic streptococci • Normal habitat is the human upper respiratory tract and skin. • Spread by airborne droplets and by contact. • Elaborates many enzymes and exotoxins, which may play a role in infection: • erythrogenic toxin (lysogenic phage mediated); • TSST (Superantigen) • streptolysins; • streptokinase A and B (therapeutic applications); • deoxyribonuclease; • hyaluronidase (‘spreading factor’). Streptococcus pyogenes
